chapters.n: The Psalms open with a doorway psalm describing two paths. The happy person doesn’t drift into evil step by step — walking with, then standing with, then sitting with those who mock God.

f.g: Hebrew ’ashre — “happy” or “how fortunate”; the same idea as the Beatitudes.

f.w: sitteth in the seat of the scornful
f.g: Walking, standing, then sitting — a progression showing how gradually sin can settle in.

chapters.n: Instead, this person loves God’s teaching and thinks about it constantly. The positive habit, not just avoiding evil, is what shapes him.

f.g: Hebrew torah — instruction or teaching, not only rules.

chapters.n: Such a person is like a tree planted beside irrigation channels: it bears fruit at the right time, its leaves stay green, and it thrives.

f.w: a tree planted by the rivers of water

f.g: Irrigation channels — the tree was deliberately planted by a reliable water source.

chapters.n: The wicked are the opposite — like chaff, the light husks blown away when grain is tossed in the wind at harvest. They have no weight or root.

f.g: Worthless husks separated from grain by winnowing.

chapters.n: So the wicked will not stand firm at the judgment, nor belong in the gathering of the righteous.

f.w: shall not stand in the judgment

chapters.n: The Lord knows — personally watches over — the path of the righteous, while the path of the wicked leads to ruin.

f.g: In Hebrew, “know” implies close, caring relationship.

chapters.n: A royal psalm, probably used when a king of Israel was crowned. It asks why nations rage against God in useless rebellion. The New Testament applies it to Jesus Christ.

f.g: The nations — non-Israelite peoples.
Plot something empty and doomed to fail.

chapters.n: Earthly kings and rulers band together against the Lord and his anointed king.

f.g: Hebrew mashiach (Messiah); Greek christos (Christ). Kings were anointed with oil.

chapters.n: They say, “Let’s break free of their chains and throw off their ropes” — rejecting God’s rule as if it were slavery.

f.g: Bonds, fetters — the yoke of God’s rule.

chapters.n: God, enthroned in heaven, laughs at their plotting. Their rebellion is no real threat to him.

f.g: Scorn, mockery.

chapters.n: Then he speaks to them in anger and terrifies them in his fury.

f.g: Terrify, dismay.

chapters.n: God declares that he has installed his own king on Zion, his holy mountain in Jerusalem.

f.g: The hill of Jerusalem where the temple stood.

chapters.n: The king announces God’s decree: “You are my Son; today I have become your Father.” Every Davidic king was called God’s son at coronation; the New Testament sees its fulfillment in Christ.

f.w: Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee

chapters.n: God promises the king the nations and the ends of the earth as his inheritance.

f.w: the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession

chapters.n: He will rule them with an iron scepter and shatter rebellion like clay pottery.

f.g: An iron scepter — unbreakable authority. Lehi’s and Nephi’s “rod of iron” is the word of God.

chapters.n: The psalm now urges the world’s kings to be wise and accept correction.

f.g: Be warned, accept discipline.

chapters.n: Serve the Lord with reverence and rejoice before him with awe.
Pay homage to the Son, the king, before his anger flares. All who take refuge in him are blessed. Christians see the Son as Jesus Christ.

f.g: Kissing was a sign of homage and submission to a king.

f.w: Blessed are all they that put their trust in him

chapters.n: The heading ties this psalm to David fleeing from his son Absalom’s rebellion. David cries out: Lord, so many enemies are rising up against me!

f.w: many are they that rise up against me

chapters.n: Many say God won’t rescue him. “Selah” is a pause marker — perhaps a musical interlude or a moment to reflect.

f.w: There is no help for him in God

f.g: A Hebrew term of uncertain meaning, probably a musical or liturgical pause.

chapters.n: But David turns to God: you are my shield, my glory, and the one who lifts my head when it hangs in shame.

f.w: the lifter up of mine head
f.g: The one who restores dignity and hope.

chapters.n: He cried aloud to the Lord, and God answered him from his holy mountain.

f.g: Mount Zion, where the ark of the covenant was kept.

chapters.n: Even surrounded by danger, David lay down, slept, and woke again, because the Lord held him up. Peaceful sleep is evidence of trust.

f.w: I laid me down and slept

chapters.n: He will not fear even tens of thousands of enemies surrounding him.
David prays, “Rise up, Lord, and save me!” Striking an enemy on the jaw and breaking his teeth means making him powerless to bite.

f.g: An old battle cry used when the ark set out.

f.w: broken the teeth of the ungodly

chapters.n: Salvation belongs to the Lord alone. David ends not with his own needs but with a blessing on all God’s people.
An evening prayer. David asks the God who vindicates him to answer, recalling how God has given him room to breathe in past trouble.

f.g: The God who upholds my cause and declares me in the right.
You gave me space — relief from tight, pressing distress.

chapters.n: David asks his opponents how long they will shame his honor, love empty things, and chase lies.

f.g: Emptiness — perhaps idols or worthless plans.
Lying, falsehood (an old English word).

chapters.n: They should know the Lord has set apart the faithful for himself and hears their prayers.

f.w: set apart him that is godly for himself
f.g: “Godly” translates ḥasid — one who is loyal and devoted in covenant love.

chapters.n: Tremble and don’t sin; reflect quietly on your bed and be still. Good counsel for anyone angry or anxious at night.

f.w: Stand in awe, and sin not
f.g: Or “Be angry, and sin not,” as Paul quotes it.

chapters.n: Offer sacrifices with a right heart, and trust in the Lord.
Many ask, “Who will show us anything good?” David answers by praying for the light of God’s face to shine on them — an echo of the priestly blessing.

f.w: lift thou up the light of thy countenance upon us

chapters.n: God has filled David’s heart with more joy than others feel at a bumper harvest of grain and wine.

f.g: Grain.

chapters.n: David lies down and sleeps in peace, because the Lord alone keeps him safe.

f.w: I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep

chapters.n: A morning prayer. David asks the Lord to listen to his words and even to his unspoken sighs.

f.g: Sighing or groaning — the prayer of the heart beneath the words.

chapters.n: He calls God “my King and my God” — the true King above Israel’s earthly king.
Each morning David lays out his prayer like an offering and waits expectantly for God’s answer.

f.g: Arrange or lay out — the same word used for setting out a sacrifice.
Keep watch, wait eagerly.

chapters.n: God takes no pleasure in wickedness; evil cannot live as his guest.

f.w: neither shall evil dwell with thee

chapters.n: The arrogant cannot stand before him, and he hates all who practice evil.

f.g: The boastful or arrogant.

chapters.n: He destroys liars and despises the violent and deceitful.

f.g: Lies.

chapters.n: But by God’s great covenant love David may enter his house and bow toward the holy temple in reverence.

f.g: “Mercy” is ḥesed — God’s loyal, covenant love.

chapters.n: Because of his enemies, David asks God to lead him and make the way plain before him.

f.w: make thy way straight before my face

chapters.n: His enemies can’t be trusted: their hearts are full of destruction, and their throats are like open graves. Paul quotes this to show universal human sinfulness.

f.w: their throat is an open sepulchre

chapters.n: David asks God to hold them guilty and let their own schemes bring them down, because they rebel against God.

f.w: let them fall by their own counsels

chapters.n: Let everyone who takes refuge in God rejoice and sing forever, because God shelters them.

f.g: Take refuge in you.
Literally “you spread a covering over them.”

chapters.n: The Lord blesses the righteous and surrounds them with his favor like a large shield.

f.g: A large body-length shield that covered the whole person.

chapters.n: The first of the seven traditional “penitential psalms.” David asks the Lord not to correct him in anger.

f.w: rebuke me not in thine anger

f.g: Discipline, correct.

chapters.n: He begs for mercy and healing, for he is frail and his bones shake with pain.

f.g: Troubled, shaking with distress.

chapters.n: His whole self is in anguish. He breaks off mid-sentence: “But you, Lord — how long?”
“Turn back to me, Lord, and rescue me, because of your steadfast love.” He appeals to God’s character, not his own merit.

f.g: Because of your ḥesed — your loyal, covenant love.

chapters.n: In death no one remembers or praises God, David argues — so keep me alive to praise you. The Old Testament had a dim view of the afterlife; later revelation fills it out.

f.w: in the grave who shall give thee thanks?

f.g: Hebrew sheol, the place of the dead.

chapters.n: Exhausted by groaning, he soaks his bed with tears every night.

f.w: make I my bed to swim
f.g: Flood my bed — vivid exaggeration for intense weeping.

chapters.n: His eyes are worn out from grief and grow weak because of all his foes.

f.g: Grows weak, dim.

chapters.n: Suddenly the tone shifts: “Get away from me, evildoers, for the Lord has heard my weeping!” Jesus uses similar words in the judgment.

f.w: Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity

chapters.n: David is now confident: the Lord has heard his plea and accepts his prayer.

f.g: A humble plea for mercy.

chapters.n: His enemies will be ashamed and terrified, and will turn back in sudden disgrace.

f.g: Greatly dismayed — the same word David used of himself in verses 2–3, now turned on his foes.

chapters.n: The heading connects this psalm to “Cush the Benjamite,” possibly a follower of Saul who slandered David. David takes refuge in God and asks to be saved from his pursuers.

f.w: in thee do I put my trust
f.g: In you I take refuge.

chapters.n: Otherwise his enemy will tear him apart like a lion, with no one to rescue him.
David invites God to examine him: if he has done what he is accused of, if his hands are guilty…

f.g: A formal oath of innocence, like Job’s.

chapters.n: …if he has betrayed a friend — when in fact he spared the one who was his enemy without cause…

f.w: I have delivered him that without cause is mine enemy
f.g: Perhaps recalling how David spared Saul’s life.

chapters.n: …then let his enemy hunt him down, trample his life into the ground, and lay his honor in the dust.

f.w: lay mine honour in the dust
f.g: Honor (literally “glory”) here can also mean his very life.

chapters.n: David calls on God to rise up in anger against his raging enemies and wake to carry out the justice he has decreed.

f.g: Bold poetic language — not that God sleeps, but a plea for him to act.

chapters.n: Let the nations gather around God’s throne as he takes his seat on high to judge.

f.g: Take your judgment seat above.

chapters.n: The Lord judges the peoples. David asks to be judged by his integrity — not claiming sinlessness, but innocence of these charges.
End the evil of the wicked and secure the righteous, for God tests minds and hearts.

f.g: Reins = kidneys, thought of as the seat of emotions — God examines our deepest motives.

chapters.n: David’s shield is God, who saves the upright in heart.

f.g: Literally “my shield is upon God.”

chapters.n: God is a righteous judge and opposes evil every day.

f.w: God is angry with the wicked every day
f.g: Better “a God who expresses his displeasure every day” — his justice never sleeps.

chapters.n: If people don’t repent, God sharpens his sword and strings his bow.

f.g: If he does not repent.
Sharpen.

chapters.n: He prepares deadly weapons and makes his arrows flaming darts.

f.w: ordaineth his arrows against the persecutors
f.g: Better “makes his arrows fiery shafts.”

chapters.n: The wicked are pictured as pregnant with evil: they conceive trouble and give birth to lies.
Whoever digs a pit to trap others falls into it himself.

f.w: is fallen into the ditch which he made

chapters.n: The trouble he causes comes back on his own head; his violence lands on his own skull.

f.g: Top of the head, skull.

f.w: His mischief shall return upon his own head

chapters.n: David ends in praise, thanking the Lord for his justice and singing to the Most High.

f.g: Hebrew ‘Elyon, an ancient title for God.

chapters.n: A hymn of praise framed by the same line at beginning and end. God’s name is majestic throughout the earth, and his glory is set above the heavens.

f.g: “LORD” is Jehovah (YHWH); “Lord” is Adonai, meaning master or sovereign.
Majestic, glorious.

chapters.n: God uses the praises of little children to silence his enemies — strength from the weakest. Jesus quoted this when children praised him in the temple.

f.w: Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings

f.g: Nursing infants.

chapters.n: David gazes at the night sky — moon and stars crafted by God’s fingers, as an artisan crafts fine work.
Compared with all that, why would God care about mere humans? Yet he does — he remembers and visits us. Moses asked a similar question after his vision.

f.w: What is man, that thou art mindful of him?

f.g: Care for, attend to.

chapters.n: God made humans only a little lower than divine beings and crowned them with glory and honor. Latter-day Saints see here our divine nature as children of God.

f.w: a little lower than the angels
f.g: Hebrew ’elohim — can mean God or divine beings; the Greek Old Testament reads “angels.”

f.w: crowned him with glory and honour

chapters.n: God gave humanity stewardship over his creations, putting everything under their feet. Hebrews applies this ultimately to Christ.

f.g: Stewardship and responsible rule, not exploitation.

f.w: thou hast put all things under his feet

chapters.n: Domestic animals — sheep and cattle — and wild animals too.

f.g: Wild animals.

chapters.n: Birds, fish, and every creature that travels the ocean’s paths.
The psalm closes by repeating its opening: Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!

f.w: how excellent is thy name in all the earth!

chapters.n: Psalms 9 and 10 were likely once a single poem; together they form a broken acrostic, with sections starting on successive Hebrew letters. David begins with wholehearted thanks for God’s wonders.

f.g: Wonders — God’s great acts of deliverance.

chapters.n: He will be glad and sing praise to the Most High.

f.g: Hebrew ‘Elyon, God Most High.

chapters.n: When his enemies retreat, they stumble and perish before God’s presence.

f.g: Literally “before your face.”

chapters.n: God has upheld David’s just cause, sitting on his throne as a righteous judge.

f.w: maintained my right and my cause
f.g: Took up my case in court and ruled in my favor.

chapters.n: God has rebuked the nations and erased the names of the wicked forever.

f.w: put out their name for ever

chapters.n: The enemy’s ruin is permanent; their cities are uprooted and even the memory of them is gone.

f.w: their memorial is perished with them
f.g: Even their remembrance has vanished.

chapters.n: But the Lord reigns forever; he has set up his throne for judgment.

f.w: the LORD shall endure for ever

chapters.n: He will judge the world fairly and govern the nations with justice.
The Lord is a stronghold for the oppressed, a safe tower in times of trouble.

f.g: A high fortress, a secure height out of danger’s reach.

chapters.n: Those who know God’s name — his character — trust him, for he never abandons those who seek him.

f.w: hast not forsaken them that seek thee

f.g: Know who God is, his nature and reputation.

chapters.n: Sing praise to the Lord who lives in Zion; tell the nations what he has done.

f.w: declare among the people his doings

chapters.n: God, who avenges bloodshed, remembers the afflicted and never forgets their cry.

f.g: Investigates and avenges murder.

chapters.n: David pleads for mercy: see how my enemies afflict me, you who lift me from the gates of death.
…so that he can praise God in the gates of Zion and rejoice in God’s salvation. Death’s gates contrast with Zion’s gates.

f.g: A poetic name for Jerusalem and its people.

chapters.n: The nations have fallen into the pit they dug; their feet are caught in the net they hid.

f.w: sunk down in the pit that they made

chapters.n: God is known by his justice: the wicked are trapped by their own deeds. “Higgaion” may be a musical direction.

f.g: Possibly a musical term — a meditative interlude or resounding chord.

f.w: snared in the work of his own hands

chapters.n: The wicked and the nations that forget God will return to the realm of the dead.

f.g: Hebrew sheol — the grave or world of departed spirits.

chapters.n: The needy will not always be forgotten; the hope of the poor will not die.

f.w: the needy shall not alway be forgotten

chapters.n: Rise up, Lord! Don’t let mortals triumph; let the nations be judged before you.

f.g: Don’t let mere humans win out against you.

chapters.n: Strike them with awe, Lord, so the nations realize they are only human.

f.w: know themselves to be but men
f.g: Hebrew ’enosh — frail, mortal humanity.

chapters.n: A cry many people feel: why, Lord, do you seem so far away? Why hide when we are in trouble? Scripture allows honest questions in prayer.
In arrogance the wicked hunt down the poor. The psalmist asks that they be caught in their own schemes.

f.g: Plots, schemes.

chapters.n: The wicked boast about their cravings; the greedy curse and despise the Lord.

f.g: Better “the greedy man curses and spurns the Lord.”

chapters.n: In pride the wicked don’t seek God; there is no room for God in any of their thoughts.

f.w: God is not in all his thoughts
f.g: His whole outlook is “There is no God.”

chapters.n: He prospers at all times; God’s judgments are far beyond his notice, and he scoffs at his enemies.

f.g: Better “his ways always prosper.”
Sneers, scoffs.

chapters.n: He tells himself, “Nothing will shake me; I’ll never have trouble.” This is the self-confidence of the proud.
His mouth is full of curses, lies, and threats; trouble and evil sit under his tongue. Paul quotes this verse.

f.w: His mouth is full of cursing

chapters.n: He hides in ambush near villages, murdering the innocent from hiding, his eyes secretly watching for the helpless.

f.g: Secretly.

chapters.n: Like a lion in a thicket he waits to seize the poor, then drags them off in his net.

f.w: as a lion in his den

chapters.n: The helpless are crushed and collapse, falling under his strength.

f.g: The Hebrew is unclear; it may describe the victim being crushed, or the predator crouching to pounce.

chapters.n: He tells himself, “God has forgotten; he has hidden his face and will never see.”
The psalmist cries, “Arise, Lord! Lift your hand! Don’t forget the afflicted.”

f.g: A gesture of power and action.

chapters.n: Why does the wicked person despise God, thinking, “He won’t hold me accountable”?

f.g: Treat with contempt.
You won’t call me to account.

chapters.n: But God does see the trouble and grief and takes it into his own hands. The helpless entrust themselves to him, for he helps the fatherless.

f.w: thou art the helper of the fatherless

chapters.n: Break the power of the wicked; call evil to account until none is left.

f.w: Break thou the arm of the wicked
f.g: The arm symbolizes power.

chapters.n: The Lord is King forever; the nations will perish from his land.

f.w: The LORD is King for ever and ever

chapters.n: The Lord hears the longing of the humble, strengthens their hearts, and listens closely.

f.g: You will strengthen and encourage them.

chapters.n: He will defend the orphan and the oppressed, so that mere mortals of the earth will terrify no more.

f.g: Mortal man made of dust — weak compared with God.

chapters.n: Frightened advisers urge David to run and hide like a bird in the mountains. David replies that he has already taken refuge in the Lord.

f.w: In the LORD put I my trust
Flee as a bird to your mountain

chapters.n: The advisers point out that the wicked are aiming arrows from the shadows at the upright.

f.g: Secretly, from the dark.

chapters.n: “When the foundations of society are crumbling, what can a righteous person do?” It is the voice of discouragement.

f.g: When law, order, and justice collapse.

chapters.n: David’s answer: the Lord is still in his holy temple and on his heavenly throne. His eyes see and test everyone.

f.w: The LORD is in his holy temple

f.g: He examines closely, as if narrowing his eyes.

chapters.n: The Lord tests the righteous, but he hates the wicked and anyone who loves violence.
He will rain fiery coals and sulfur on the wicked, with a scorching wind as their portion — as at Sodom.

f.g: Their allotted share — the cup they must drink.

chapters.n: The Lord is righteous and loves righteousness; the upright will see his face.

f.w: his countenance doth behold the upright
f.g: Or “the upright shall behold his face.”

chapters.n: “Help, Lord!” David feels as if faithful people have vanished, leaving no one trustworthy.

f.g: Loyal, trustworthy people have disappeared.

chapters.n: Everyone lies to their neighbor, speaking with flattering lips and a double heart.

f.g: Literally “a heart and a heart” — two-faced, saying one thing and meaning another.

chapters.n: May the Lord silence all flattering lips and boastful tongues.
They boast, “Our tongues will win; our lips are our own — who is master over us?”
God himself speaks: because the poor are plundered and the needy groan, “Now I will arise” to protect them.

f.w: now will I arise, saith the LORD

f.g: Sneers at him, or longs to snatch him.

chapters.n: In contrast with human lies, God’s words are pure, like silver refined seven times in a clay furnace — completely pure.

f.w: The words of the LORD are pure words

f.g: Seven signals completeness — perfectly refined.

chapters.n: The Lord will keep and guard his people from this wicked generation forever.
Even so, the wicked strut about whenever vileness is honored among people. David ends realistically, trusting God’s word despite the world around him.

f.w: when the vilest men are exalted
f.g: When what is worthless is praised.

chapters.n: A short lament that moves from despair to trust. “How long?” is asked four times in two verses. Will God forget David forever and hide his face?

f.w: How long wilt thou forget me

f.g: Withdraw your favor and presence.

chapters.n: How long must David wrestle with his thoughts and carry sorrow every day while his enemy triumphs?

f.g: Agonize over plans in my mind.

chapters.n: Look at me and answer, Lord; brighten my eyes, or I will sleep the sleep of death.

f.g: Restore my strength and life — dim eyes were a sign of weakness.

chapters.n: Otherwise his enemy will say, “I beat him,” and his foes will celebrate when he stumbles.

f.g: When I am shaken or fall.

chapters.n: The turn: “But I have trusted in your steadfast love; my heart will rejoice in your salvation.” Nothing outward has changed — David has chosen trust.

f.w: I have trusted in thy mercy
f.g: “Mercy” is ḥesed — God’s faithful covenant love.

chapters.n: He will sing to the Lord, because God has been good to him.
The fool says in his heart, “There is no God” — usually meaning not a philosophical atheist but someone who lives as if God doesn’t matter. Psalm 53 is nearly identical.

f.g: Hebrew nabal — morally foolish, someone who rejects God’s ways (compare Nabal in 1 Samuel 25:25).

chapters.n: The Lord looks down from heaven to see if anyone understands and seeks him.

f.w: The LORD looked down from heaven

chapters.n: All have turned aside and become corrupt; no one does good, not even one. Paul quotes this to show that everyone needs Christ’s grace.

f.w: there is none that doeth good, no, not one

f.g: Corrupt, gone bad like spoiled milk.

chapters.n: Don’t evildoers ever learn? They devour God’s people as casually as eating bread and never call on the Lord.

f.w: who eat up my people as they eat bread

chapters.n: Then they will be overwhelmed with terror, for God stands with the righteous.

f.w: God is in the generation of the righteous

chapters.n: The wicked mock the plans of the poor, but the Lord is their refuge.
Oh, that salvation for Israel would come from Zion! When the Lord restores his people, Jacob will rejoice. Latter-day Saints also connect this hope with the latter-day gathering.

f.w: the salvation of Israel were come out of Zion
bringeth back the captivity of his people
f.g: Restores the fortunes of his people.

chapters.n: A temple-entrance psalm: worshippers ask, “Lord, who may stay in your tent and live on your holy hill?” The answer lists qualities of character, not ritual.

f.w: who shall abide in thy tabernacle?

f.g: Mount Zion, where God’s sanctuary stood.

chapters.n: The one whose life is blameless, who does what is right, and who speaks truth from the heart.

f.g: Lives with integrity, whole and blameless.

f.w: speaketh the truth in his heart

chapters.n: Who doesn’t slander, doesn’t harm a neighbor, and doesn’t spread gossip about friends.

f.g: Slanders, speaks evil of someone behind their back.

chapters.n: Who rejects the contemptible but honors those who revere the Lord, and keeps a promise even when it costs him.

f.g: Despised, rejected.

f.w: sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not
f.g: Keeps his word even when it hurts him.

chapters.n: Who doesn’t charge interest to exploit the poor or take bribes against the innocent. Such a person will never be shaken.

f.g: Interest on a loan; Israel’s law forbade charging interest to a needy fellow Israelite.
Accepts a bribe to pervert justice.

chapters.n: A psalm of trust that the apostles Peter and Paul later applied to Christ’s resurrection. David begins, “Keep me safe, O God, for I take refuge in you.”

f.g: Guard me, keep me.

chapters.n: He tells the Lord, “You are my Lord; I have nothing good apart from you.”

f.w: my goodness extendeth not to thee
f.g: Better “I have no good besides you.”

chapters.n: His delight is in the holy people of the land — God’s faithful are his true companions.

f.g: The holy ones — those set apart for God.
The noble, majestic ones.

chapters.n: Those who chase other gods multiply their own sorrows. David will not join their offerings or even speak their gods’ names.

f.g: Pagan libations, possibly involving blood, which Israel’s law forbade.

f.w: nor take up their names into my lips

chapters.n: The Lord himself is David’s inheritance and his cup; God holds his future secure.

f.g: Like the Levites, who received no land because the Lord was their inheritance.
My allotted share, as land was distributed by lot.

chapters.n: The boundary lines of his life have fallen in pleasant places; his heritage is beautiful.

f.g: Measuring cords used to mark out land allotments.

chapters.n: David blesses the Lord, who counsels him; even at night his inner self instructs him.

f.g: Reins = kidneys, the seat of conscience and emotion — his heart teaches him at night.

chapters.n: He keeps the Lord always before him; with God at his right hand he will not be shaken.

f.w: I have set the LORD always before me

f.g: The place of a protector or defender in battle.

chapters.n: So his heart is glad and his whole being rejoices; even his body will rest secure in hope.

f.g: My soul or inner self (the Greek translation reads “my tongue,” as quoted in Acts 2:26).

f.w: my flesh also shall rest in hope

chapters.n: God will not abandon him to the grave or let his Holy One see decay. Peter taught that this was fulfilled in Jesus Christ, whose body rose before it could decay.

f.w: thou wilt not leave my soul in hell

f.g: Hebrew sheol — the world of the dead.

f.w: thine Holy One to see corruption

chapters.n: God will show him the path of life; in his presence is fulness of joy, and at his right hand are pleasures forever. A beautiful picture of eternal life.

f.w: in thy presence is fulness of joy

chapters.n: David asks the Lord to hear his just cause and his honest prayer — words from sincere lips.

f.g: Hear my just case.
Deceitful, insincere speech.

chapters.n: Let God’s verdict come from his presence; let his eyes see what is right.

f.g: Verdict, judgment.
Upright, fair.

chapters.n: God has examined David’s heart at night and tested him, finding nothing wrong. David has resolved not to sin with his mouth.

f.w: I am purposed that my mouth shall not transgress

chapters.n: Guided by God’s word, David has avoided the ways of violent people.

f.w: by the word of thy lips

f.g: The violent person.

chapters.n: His steps have held to God’s paths, and his feet have not slipped. (Hebrew can be read as a statement or a prayer.)
David calls on God, confident he will answer: “Turn your ear to me and hear.”

f.g: Bend down to listen.

chapters.n: Show your wonderful steadfast love, you who save those who seek refuge at your right hand.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — loyal, covenant love, shown in a wondrous way.
The hand of power and favor.

chapters.n: A tender plea: guard me like the pupil of your eye, hide me in the shadow of your wings. God protects what is most precious to him.

f.g: The pupil — the most guarded, precious part of the eye.
Like a mother bird sheltering her young.

chapters.n: …from the wicked who attack him and from deadly enemies who surround him.

f.g: Surround me.

chapters.n: They have closed their hearts — callous and fat with prosperity — and speak arrogantly.

f.g: Their hearts are hardened and insensitive.

chapters.n: They track David’s steps and surround him, watching for a chance to throw him to the ground.

f.w: set their eyes bowing down to the earth
f.g: They are intent on bringing him down.

chapters.n: They are like a lion hungry for prey or a young lion crouching in ambush.

f.w: as a lion that is greedy of his prey

chapters.n: Rise up, Lord! Confront them and bring them down; rescue me from the wicked by your sword.

f.g: Confront him, meet him head-on.
Better “by your sword.”

chapters.n: Save me by your hand from people whose only reward is in this life. God gives them plenty, and they pass wealth on to their children — but that is all they have.

f.w: men of the world, which have their portion in this life

f.g: Treasured provisions — God’s good gifts.

chapters.n: But David’s hope is higher: he will see God’s face in righteousness and, when he awakes, be satisfied with his likeness. Many read this as a hope beyond death.

f.w: I will behold thy face in righteousness
I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness

chapters.n: The heading says David sang this after the Lord rescued him from Saul and all his enemies. Nearly the same song appears in 2 Samuel 22. It opens with a deeply personal “I love you, Lord.”

f.g: A rare, tender Hebrew word for love, related to the word for womb or compassion.

chapters.n: David piles up images of protection: rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, horn, and high tower. God is every kind of safety at once.

f.g: A small shield.
The horn symbolizes strength; Zacharias used this phrase of Jesus.

chapters.n: He calls on the Lord, who deserves praise, and is saved from his enemies.
The cords of death wrapped around him, and torrents of destruction terrified him.

f.g: Better “the cords of death” — death pictured as a hunter’s ropes.
Torrents of destruction (Hebrew belial, worthlessness or ruin).

chapters.n: The ropes of the grave surrounded him; the snares of death confronted him.

f.g: Hebrew sheol — the grave.
Came to meet, confronted.

chapters.n: In distress he cried to God, and God heard him from his temple — his heavenly dwelling.

f.w: he heard my voice out of his temple

chapters.n: God’s response is pictured as a cosmic storm: the earth quakes and mountains shake because he is angry at what was done to his servant.
Smoke rises from his nostrils and devouring fire from his mouth — poetic images of God’s fierce intervention.
He parts the heavens and comes down, with dark clouds under his feet.

f.w: He bowed the heavens also, and came down

chapters.n: He rides on a cherub and soars on the wings of the wind.

f.g: A winged heavenly being, guardian of God’s holy presence.

chapters.n: He wraps himself in darkness, with dark rain clouds as his canopy.

f.g: A canopy or tent.

f.w: He made darkness his secret place

chapters.n: Out of the brightness before him, clouds burst with hail and lightning.

f.g: Lightning bolts.

chapters.n: The Lord thunders from heaven; the Most High’s voice sounds amid hail and fiery bolts.
He shoots his arrows — lightning — and scatters the enemy in confusion.

f.g: Threw into panic, routed.

chapters.n: At his rebuke the sea bed is exposed and the foundations of the world laid bare — echoing the Red Sea crossing.

f.w: the channels of waters were seen

f.g: Uncovered, laid bare.

chapters.n: God reached down from above, took hold of David, and drew him out of deep waters — as Moses (whose name means “drawn out”) was drawn from water.

f.w: he drew me out of many waters

chapters.n: God rescued him from a powerful enemy — probably Saul — and from foes too strong for him.
They attacked him on his worst day, but the Lord was his support.

f.g: Support, prop.

chapters.n: God brought him into a wide-open place of freedom and rescued him because he delighted in him.

f.g: Spaciousness — freedom from confinement and distress.

chapters.n: The Lord rewarded him according to his righteousness and clean hands. David is speaking of his loyalty to God against Saul, not claiming lifelong perfection.
He kept the Lord’s ways and did not turn away from his God.

f.w: have not wickedly departed from my God

chapters.n: All God’s laws were before him, and he didn’t set aside his decrees.

f.g: Decrees, ordinances.

chapters.n: He was blameless before God and kept himself from sin.

f.g: Blameless, whole-hearted — the same word used of Noah and Job.

chapters.n: So the Lord repaid him according to his righteousness — the clean hands God himself saw.

f.g: As God sees it, not merely as people judge.

chapters.n: God responds in kind: to the faithful he shows faithfulness, to the blameless he shows himself blameless.

f.w: With the merciful thou wilt shew thyself merciful

chapters.n: To the pure he shows himself pure, but to the crooked he shows himself shrewd.

f.g: Perverse, crooked, twisted.

chapters.n: He saves the humble but brings down those with proud looks.
The Lord keeps David’s lamp burning and turns his darkness into light.

f.g: Keep my lamp burning — preserve my life and line.

chapters.n: With God’s help he can charge an army troop and leap over a city wall.

f.w: I have run through a troop
f.g: Or “crushed a troop.”

chapters.n: God’s way is perfect, his word proven true. He shields all who take refuge in him.

f.w: the word of the LORD is tried
f.g: Refined, tested and proven.

chapters.n: Who is God except the Lord? Who is a rock besides our God?

f.w: who is a rock save our God?

chapters.n: God arms him with strength and makes his path secure.

f.g: Wraps strength around me like a belt.

chapters.n: He makes David’s feet as nimble as a deer’s, able to stand on the heights.

f.g: The sure-footed feet of a deer.

chapters.n: He trains David’s hands for battle so he can bend a bronze bow.

f.g: A bow of bronze — hard to draw.

chapters.n: God gives him the shield of salvation, upholds him, and makes him great by stooping down to help.

f.w: thy gentleness hath made me great
f.g: Literally “your humility” or “your stooping down” — God’s condescension lifts David up.

chapters.n: God widened the path under him so his ankles wouldn’t give way.

f.g: Gave me a broad, secure path.

chapters.n: David pursued his enemies and did not turn back until they were finished.

f.w: neither did I turn again till they were consumed

chapters.n: He struck them down so they couldn’t rise; they fell beneath his feet.

f.w: they are fallen under my feet

chapters.n: God armed him for battle and humbled his attackers.

f.w: girded me with strength unto the battle

chapters.n: God made his enemies turn their backs in flight, and he destroyed those who hated him.

f.w: given me the necks of mine enemies
f.g: Made them turn and flee, or placed his foot on their necks — a sign of victory.

chapters.n: They cried for help, even to the Lord, but no one saved them — they had not sought him before.

f.w: even unto the LORD, but he answered them not

chapters.n: He ground them fine as dust in the wind and trampled them like mud in the streets.

f.w: as the dust before the wind

chapters.n: God rescued him from attacks by the people and made him head of nations; foreign peoples now serve him.

f.g: Ruler over foreign nations.

chapters.n: As soon as they hear of him they obey; foreigners come cringing to him.

f.g: Foreigners will feign obedience or come cringing.

chapters.n: Foreigners lose heart and come trembling out of their fortresses.

f.g: Strongholds, fortresses.

chapters.n: The Lord lives! Praise to my Rock! Exalted be the God who saves me.
It is God who avenges David and subdues nations under him.

f.w: It is God that avengeth me

chapters.n: He rescues David from his enemies, exalts him above his attackers, and delivers him from violent men.

f.g: Possibly Saul, or any violent foe.

chapters.n: So David will praise God among the nations. Paul quotes this verse to show that the gospel was meant for Gentiles too.

f.w: will I give thanks unto thee, O LORD, among the heathen

chapters.n: God gives great victories to his king and shows covenant love to his anointed, David, and his descendants forever — a promise fulfilled ultimately in Christ, the Son of David.

f.g: Messiah — the anointed king.

f.w: to David, and to his seed for evermore

chapters.n: This psalm has two halves: God revealed in creation (vv. 1–6) and God revealed in his law (vv. 7–14). The skies themselves proclaim God’s glory and craftsmanship.

f.w: The heavens declare the glory of God

f.g: The expanse of the sky.

chapters.n: Each day passes the message on to the next, and each night shares knowledge with the next — a constant, silent sermon.

f.g: Literally “pours out” speech like a bubbling spring.

chapters.n: They use no words or language; no voice is heard — and yet their message is clear.

f.w: There is no speech nor language
f.g: Many read this as “they have no speech, no words; their voice is not heard” — creation speaks without words.

chapters.n: Their message goes out to the whole earth. Paul applied this to the spread of the gospel. In the heavens God has pitched a tent for the sun.

f.w: Their line is gone out through all the earth

f.g: A tent — the sun pictured resting at night before rising again.

chapters.n: The sun comes out like a joyful bridegroom from his room, or like a champion eager to run his course.

f.w: as a bridegroom coming out of his chamber

chapters.n: It rises at one end of the sky and circles to the other; nothing is hidden from its heat. So nothing escapes God’s presence.

f.w: there is nothing hid from the heat thereof

chapters.n: Now the law: God’s instruction is perfect, restoring the soul; his testimony is reliable, making the simple wise. Notice the six names for God’s word in verses 7–9.

f.g: Restoring or reviving the inner life.
The “simple” are inexperienced, open-minded people.

chapters.n: His precepts are right and bring joy; his commandment is pure and gives light to the eyes.
Reverence for the Lord is pure and lasts forever; his judgments are true and completely righteous.

f.w: The fear of the LORD is clean

chapters.n: They are more desirable than the finest gold and sweeter than honey dripping from the comb.
God’s words warn his servant, and keeping them brings great reward.

f.w: in keeping of them there is great reward

chapters.n: Who can see all their own mistakes? David asks to be cleansed from faults he doesn’t even know about.

f.g: Hidden, unintentional sins — faults unknown even to oneself.

chapters.n: He also asks to be kept from willful, arrogant sins so they don’t rule him. Then he will be blameless and innocent of great transgression.

f.g: Deliberate, defiant sins.

f.w: let them not have dominion over me

chapters.n: A beloved closing prayer: may my words and my heart’s thoughts please you, Lord, my Rock and my Redeemer.

f.g: Hebrew go’el — kinsman-redeemer; Latter-day Saints see Jesus Christ as the Redeemer.
Literally “my rock.”

chapters.n: The people pray for their king before battle: may the Lord answer you in trouble, and may the name of Jacob’s God protect you.

f.w: the name of the God of Jacob
f.g: God’s “name” stands for his presence and power.
Set you securely on high.

chapters.n: May he send help from his sanctuary and support you from Zion.
May he remember your offerings and accept your burnt sacrifices — kings often offered sacrifices before battle.

f.g: Literally “find your burnt offering fat” — accept it as rich and pleasing.

chapters.n: May he grant your heart’s desire and make all your plans succeed.

f.g: Bring your plans to success.

chapters.n: The people promise to shout for joy at his victory and raise their banners in God’s name.

f.w: we will set up our banners
f.g: Raise flags — a sign of victory and identity.

chapters.n: A single voice — perhaps a priest or the king — declares confidence: now I know the Lord saves his anointed and answers from heaven with mighty power.

f.g: The king; also Messiah.

f.w: the saving strength of his right hand

chapters.n: A memorable contrast: some trust in chariots and horses — the tanks of the ancient world — but we trust in the name of the Lord our God.
Those who rely on military power collapse and fall, but God’s people rise and stand firm.

f.w: we are risen, and stand upright

chapters.n: The closing plea: “Lord, save the king! Answer us when we call.”

f.g: Or “O King (God), answer us when we call.”

chapters.n: A thanksgiving that pairs with Psalm 20: the prayer has been answered. The king rejoices in the Lord’s strength and victory.

f.w: The king shall joy in thy strength

chapters.n: God has granted the king’s heart’s desire and not refused his request — an echo of Psalm 20:4.

f.w: Thou hast given him his heart's desire

chapters.n: God came to meet him with rich blessings and set a crown of pure gold on his head.

f.g: Went before, came to meet (old meaning).

chapters.n: The king asked for life, and God gave him length of days forever. For Christians this points beyond David to the eternal reign of Christ.

f.w: length of days for ever and ever

chapters.n: Through God’s help the king’s glory is great; God has given him splendor and majesty.
God has made him a blessing forever and filled him with joy in his presence.

f.g: Literally “made him blessings forever” — a source of blessing to others.
Your face — God’s presence.

chapters.n: The king trusts in the Lord; because of the Most High’s steadfast love he will not be shaken. This is the center of the psalm.

f.w: the mercy of the most High
f.g: God’s ḥesed — loyal covenant love.

chapters.n: Now the people address the king (or God): your hand will find all your enemies.

f.g: Will reach and seize.

chapters.n: When you appear, they will burn as in a blazing furnace; the Lord will swallow them up in his anger.
Their descendants will be wiped from the earth.

f.g: Their offspring.

chapters.n: Though they plot evil and scheme against God, they cannot succeed.

f.w: a mischievous device, which they are not able to perform

chapters.n: God will make them turn and run when he aims his arrows at their faces.

f.g: Put them to flight.

chapters.n: The psalm ends in praise: be exalted, Lord, in your strength; we will sing of your power.

David’s cry of abandonment became the words Jesus spoke on the cross. By quoting the first line, Jesus may have pointed to the whole psalm, which ends in triumph. Feeling forsaken, the sufferer still says “my God.”

f.w: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?

f.g: Groaning, anguished cries.

chapters.n: He cries day and night, yet hears no answer and finds no rest.

f.g: Better “you do not answer.”

chapters.n: Still he affirms that God is holy, enthroned on Israel’s praises. Faith holds even in silence.

f.g: God is pictured as seated on a throne made of his people’s praise.

chapters.n: Israel’s ancestors trusted God, and he rescued them.
They cried to him and were saved; they trusted and were not disappointed. Why, then, is he left alone?

f.g: Were not put to shame.

chapters.n: He feels like a worm, not even a man — scorned and despised by everyone. Isaiah describes the Messiah in similar terms.
Everyone who sees him mocks him, sneering and shaking their heads — exactly what onlookers did at the crucifixion.

f.g: Sneer, curl the lip in contempt.

chapters.n: They taunt, “He trusted the Lord — let the Lord rescue him!” The chief priests used nearly these words at the cross.

f.w: He trusted on the LORD that he would deliver him

chapters.n: Yet God brought him safely from the womb and made him trust while still nursing.

f.g: You made me feel safe, gave me trust.

chapters.n: From birth he has been cast on God’s care; God has been his God from his mother’s womb.

f.w: I was cast upon thee from the womb

chapters.n: “Don’t be far from me, for trouble is near and no one else will help.”
His enemies surround him like huge, strong bulls from Bashan.

f.g: Bashan, east of the Jordan, was famous for well-fed, powerful cattle.

chapters.n: They open their mouths at him like roaring, ravenous lions.

f.g: Tearing, devouring.

chapters.n: His strength drains away like spilled water; his bones are out of joint; his heart melts like wax — vivid images of physical agony.

f.w: all my bones are out of joint
f.g: An apt description of the strain of crucifixion.

chapters.n: His strength is dry as a broken piece of pottery; his tongue sticks to his mouth with thirst. God has laid him in the dust of death.

f.w: my tongue cleaveth to my jaws

f.g: A fragment of broken, baked clay.

chapters.n: A pack of evildoers circles him like dogs; they pierce his hands and his feet — strikingly fulfilled in the crucifixion of Jesus.

f.w: they pierced my hands and my feet
f.g: Most ancient translations read “pierced”; the standard Hebrew text reads “like a lion,” and scholars debate the original.
In that culture, scavenging street dogs — a term for outsiders and enemies.

chapters.n: He can count all his bones, and people stare and gloat over him.

f.w: I may tell all my bones
f.g: Tell = count; his bones are visible, stretched and exposed.

f.w: they look and stare upon me

chapters.n: They divide his clothes among them and cast lots for his garment — fulfilled when soldiers gambled for Jesus’s robe.

f.w: They part my garments among them

chapters.n: “But you, Lord, don’t be far away! My strength, hurry to help me!”
Rescue my life from the sword, my one precious life from the dogs.

f.g: My only one — my precious, irreplaceable life.

chapters.n: Save me from the lion’s mouth and the wild oxen’s horns — and here the psalm turns: “You have answered me!”

f.g: In Hebrew, the verse suddenly ends with “you have answered me,” marking the turn from lament to praise.
Wild oxen.

chapters.n: Now praise: “I will declare your name to my brothers; in the congregation I will praise you.” Hebrews applies this to the risen Christ.

f.w: I will declare thy name unto my brethren

chapters.n: All who revere the Lord, all of Jacob’s and Israel’s descendants — praise and honor him!

f.w: Ye that fear the LORD, praise him

chapters.n: For he did not despise the suffering of the afflicted one or hide his face; when he cried, God heard. The sufferer was not abandoned after all.

f.w: neither hath he hid his face from him

chapters.n: He will praise God in the great assembly and fulfill his vows before the faithful.

f.g: Offer the thanksgiving sacrifices promised in a time of need.

chapters.n: The humble will eat and be satisfied — perhaps a thanksgiving feast. Those who seek the Lord will praise him, and live forever.

f.w: The meek shall eat and be satisfied
your heart shall live for ever

chapters.n: All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord; all the families of the nations will worship him.

f.w: All the ends of the world shall remember and turn unto the LORD

f.g: Families, clans.

chapters.n: For kingship belongs to the Lord, and he rules over the nations.
Rich and poor, living and dying — all will bow before him. No one can keep himself alive; all depend on God.

f.w: all they that go down to the dust shall bow before him

chapters.n: Future generations will serve him and will be told about the Lord.
They will proclaim his righteousness to people not yet born: “He has done it!” Some hear in this an echo of Jesus’s final cry, “It is finished.”
Perhaps the best-loved psalm. David, once a shepherd himself, calls the Lord his shepherd. With God caring for him, he lacks nothing he truly needs. Jesus later called himself the Good Shepherd.

f.g: I will not lack anything.

chapters.n: The shepherd lets his sheep rest in green pastures and leads them to quiet waters — rare and precious in the dry land of Israel. Sheep won’t drink from rushing streams.

f.g: Grassy meadows — precious in a dry land.
Literally “waters of rest” — calm, refreshing water.

chapters.n: He renews my life and guides me along right paths, because his own name and reputation are at stake in caring for me.

f.g: Brings me back, revives me — can also mean brings back a wandering sheep.
Right paths — trails that lead safely home.

chapters.n: Even walking through the darkest valley, David fears no harm, because the Shepherd is with him. His rod defends and his staff guides. Notice the shift from “he” to “you” — David now speaks to God directly.

f.w: the valley of the shadow of death
f.g: A valley of deep darkness — any frightening, dangerous place, including death itself.
The rod was a club for defense; the staff, a long crook for guiding and rescuing sheep.

chapters.n: The image shifts to a generous host: God sets a feast before David while his enemies watch, anoints his head with oil like an honored guest, and fills his cup to overflowing.

f.w: Thou preparest a table before me
thou anointest my head with oil
f.g: Anointing a guest’s head with oil was a sign of welcome and honor.
Abundant blessing, more than enough.

chapters.n: God’s goodness and steadfast love will pursue David all his life, and he will live in the Lord’s house forever. Latter-day Saints may think of the temple and of returning to dwell with God.

f.w: goodness and mercy shall follow me
f.g: “Follow” is literally “pursue” — God’s love chases after us. “Mercy” is ḥesed, covenant love.

f.w: dwell in the house of the LORD for ever

chapters.n: A processional psalm, perhaps sung as the ark of the covenant was carried up to Jerusalem. It opens by declaring that the whole earth and everyone in it belong to the Lord.

f.w: The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof

f.g: Everything that fills it.

chapters.n: For he founded it on the seas and set it firmly on the waters — he created order over chaos.
The key question: who may climb the Lord’s hill and stand in his holy place? This was asked at the temple gate.

f.w: Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD?

chapters.n: The answer: those with clean hands (right actions) and a pure heart (right desires), who don’t worship what is false or make deceitful promises.

f.w: clean hands, and a pure heart
lifted up his soul unto vanity
f.g: Set his heart on what is empty or false — possibly idols.

chapters.n: They will receive blessing and vindication from the God who saves them.

f.g: Here, vindication or a right standing granted by God.

chapters.n: Such are the people who seek him, who seek the face of the God of Jacob.

f.w: that seek thy face, O Jacob
f.g: The ancient Greek and Syriac read “seek the face of the God of Jacob.”

chapters.n: A dramatic call to the city gates: lift up your heads, ancient doors, so the King of glory may enter! The gates are personified as if they must grow taller for so great a King.

f.w: Lift up your heads, O ye gates

chapters.n: The gatekeepers ask, “Who is this King of glory?” The answer: the Lord, strong and mighty in battle — the divine warrior.
The call is repeated for emphasis: open wide, ancient doors, for the King of glory to come in. Christians apply this to Christ’s ascension and his Second Coming.
Who is he? The Lord of Hosts — he is the King of glory. Latter-day Saints recognize the Lord Jehovah as the premortal Jesus Christ, who will come again in glory.

f.g: “Hosts” means armies — heavenly and earthly — under God’s command.

f.w: he is the King of glory

chapters.n: David opens with a gesture of total trust: he lifts his whole inner self up to the Lord. This psalm is an acrostic in Hebrew — each verse begins with the next letter of the alphabet, like an A-to-Z of prayer.

f.g: An idiom for longing for and trusting someone completely; the same phrase opens Psalms 86:4 and 143:8.
Small capitals translate God’s covenant name YHWH (Jehovah). Latter-day Saints understand Jehovah as the premortal Jesus Christ.

chapters.n: Trust is the reason David dares to ask for help. To be “ashamed” here means to be publicly let down — to have relied on God and seem to have been wrong. He asks that his enemies never get to gloat.

f.g: In the Psalms, shame often means disappointment or disgrace when a hope fails, more than inner embarrassment.

chapters.n: David widens the prayer to everyone who waits on God: may none of them be let down. Those who betray others for no reason are the ones who should end up disappointed.

f.g: To wait on the Lord is to hope in him with patient, expectant trust.

chapters.n: A simple, teachable request: show me how you walk, so I can walk the same way. “Ways” and “paths” repeat the same idea, a common feature of Hebrew poetry called parallelism.
David asks God to guide him step by step in truth, because God is the one who saves him. He is willing to keep waiting “all the day,” not just for a quick answer.

f.g: Salvation in the Psalms includes rescue from present danger as well as deliverance of the soul.

chapters.n: David reminds God of his own character — his tender mercies and steady love have existed from the beginning. Asking God to “remember” is a way of appealing to his covenant faithfulness.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — loyal, covenant love; kindness that keeps its promises.

chapters.n: A tender plea: don’t keep my old sins in view; look at me through your mercy instead. David bases forgiveness on God’s goodness, not his own record.

f.w: Remember not the sins of my youth

chapters.n: Because the Lord is good and upright, he doesn’t abandon sinners — he teaches them the right way. God’s goodness is exactly what gives a struggling person hope.
The meek — the humble and teachable — are the ones God can guide. Meekness here is not weakness but a willingness to be led.

f.g: Hebrew ʿanawim — the humble or lowly, those who depend on God.

chapters.n: Every road God leads people on is marked by mercy and faithfulness for those who keep their covenant with him. Even hard paths are guided by love.

f.g: God’s solemn decrees or commandments, his witnessed word.

chapters.n: David makes no excuses: his iniquity is great. He asks for pardon “for thy name’s sake” — because forgiving is true to who God is.

f.g: For the sake of God’s reputation and character; God acts in keeping with who he has revealed himself to be.

chapters.n: Anyone who reverences the Lord will be taught the path they should choose. God respects agency but gives guidance to those who seek it.

f.g: To fear the Lord is to reverence, honor and obey him, not to be terrified of him.

chapters.n: The one who reverences God will live with inner peace, and his descendants will receive the land. “Inherit the earth” echoes God’s promise to Abraham’s family.

f.w: his seed shall inherit the earth

chapters.n: God shares his confidences with those who reverence him, like a close friend. He makes his covenant known to them personally.

f.g: Hebrew sod — intimate counsel or friendship, the inner circle of trust.

chapters.n: David keeps his eyes on the Lord the way a trapped animal watches for rescue. Only God can pull his feet out of the hunter’s net.

f.g: A hunter’s snare; a common image in the Psalms for the hidden traps of enemies.

chapters.n: The tone turns personal and lonely. David feels isolated and afflicted and asks God to turn toward him.

f.g: Alone, solitary — left without support.

chapters.n: His troubles have grown bigger and bigger, and he asks God to lead him out of the tight place he is in.

f.g: Here it means the troubles have multiplied; some translate “relieve the troubles of my heart.”

chapters.n: David links his pain with his sins and asks God to see both — and to forgive. He trusts that God cares about his whole condition.
He asks God to take note of how many enemies he has and how fiercely they hate him. David brings his real situation honestly before God.
Repeating the opening plea (verse 2), David asks God to guard his life and not let his trust end in disgrace.

f.w: I put my trust in thee

chapters.n: David asks that his own integrity and honesty act like guards around him while he waits for God. Living rightly is a kind of protection.

f.g: Wholeness or completeness — a life that is undivided in loyalty to God.

chapters.n: The psalm ends by widening from one man to the whole nation: redeem all Israel from their troubles. Personal prayer becomes a prayer for God’s people.

f.g: To buy back or rescue, as a kinsman would ransom a family member — an image later fulfilled in Christ the Redeemer.

chapters.n: David asks the Lord to be his judge and vindicate him. He isn’t claiming to be sinless, but that he has lived with wholehearted loyalty and trusted God, so he won’t slip.

f.g: Here it means “vindicate me” or “defend my cause,” as a judge clears an innocent person.
Slip or waver, like losing one’s footing.

chapters.n: He invites God to test him thoroughly, the way metal is tested in fire, down to his deepest feelings and motives.

f.g: Literally the kidneys; in Hebrew thought, the seat of emotions and inner motives.
Test me, put me to the proof.

chapters.n: What keeps David steady is that God’s loyal love is always in front of his eyes. Keeping God’s kindness in view shapes how he walks.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — steadfast, covenant-keeping love.

chapters.n: David has avoided spending his time with empty, deceitful people. The company we keep shapes who we become.

f.g: Hypocrites; people who hide their true intentions.
Worthless or false people; literally “men of emptiness.”

chapters.n: He refuses to join the gatherings of evildoers. To “sit with” someone in Hebrew idiom means to share their counsel and way of life.

f.w: will not sit with the wicked

chapters.n: Washing hands was a sign of innocence and purity before worship. David pictures himself, clean, walking around the altar in procession.

f.g: Go around, encircle — likely a procession around the altar.

chapters.n: His purpose in coming to the altar is to praise God out loud and tell others about his wonderful works.

f.g: Make known, proclaim aloud.

chapters.n: David loves the place where God’s glory dwells — the sanctuary. For Latter-day Saints this echoes a love of the temple as the house of the Lord.

f.w: the place where thine honour dwelleth
f.g: Literally “the place where your glory dwells” — the presence of God in the tabernacle.

chapters.n: He asks not to be swept away in the same fate as violent sinners when judgment comes.

f.g: Men guilty of bloodshed; murderers.

chapters.n: These are people who plot harm and take bribes — corrupt in both their schemes and their dealings. The right hand stands for one’s actions and power.

f.g: Wicked plans, evil schemes — much stronger than today’s sense of playful trouble.

chapters.n: “But as for me” marks David’s choice: he will keep walking with integrity, while still asking God to redeem him and be merciful. Integrity and grace go together.

f.g: Rescue or ransom me.

chapters.n: David now stands on level, solid ground, and he will praise the Lord among the gathered worshippers. The psalm ends in confident, public gratitude.

f.g: Level ground — safe footing, in contrast to slipping (verse 1).

chapters.n: A bold declaration of faith: if the Lord is my light, my rescue, and my fortress, what is left to fear? Light pushes back darkness, and God pushes back fear.

f.g: Hebrew maʿoz — a stronghold or fortress.

chapters.n: Enemies came at David like wild beasts ready to devour him, but they tripped and fell instead. God turned the attack back on the attackers.

f.g: A vivid image of enemies acting like predators eager to destroy.

chapters.n: Even if an entire army camped around him, David would stay confident. His courage rests on God, not on the odds.

f.g: An army.

chapters.n: Above everything, David wants one thing: to live near God, to gaze on his beauty, and to seek him in his house. Many Latter-day Saints love this verse as an expression of devotion to the temple.

f.g: To seek God’s guidance, or to meditate and reflect in his sanctuary.

chapters.n: In trouble, God hides his people like a king sheltering a guest in his tent. Then he sets them high on a rock where enemies can’t reach.

f.g: A booth or shelter; a covering place.

chapters.n: With his head lifted in victory, David offers joyful sacrifices and songs. His deliverance becomes worship.

f.g: Literally “sacrifices of shouting” — offerings accompanied by glad cries.

chapters.n: The mood shifts from confidence to pleading. Faith doesn’t mean never needing to cry out for help.
God had invited, “Seek my face,” and David’s heart answered, “I will.” Seeking God’s face means seeking his presence and closeness.
David asks God not to turn away from him. He recalls that God has helped him before, and pleads with him to keep doing so.

f.g: To hide one’s face is to withdraw favor or presence.

chapters.n: Even if the closest human bonds fail — father and mother — God will gather him up. The Lord’s care is deeper than any earthly family’s.

f.g: Gather me in, receive me — as one takes in an abandoned child.

chapters.n: Surrounded by people watching for him to stumble, David asks for a clear, level path. Enemies make guidance all the more urgent.

f.g: A level, smooth road without stumbling-blocks.

chapters.n: False accusers are breathing out threats of violence. David asks not to be handed over to their wishes.
David would have collapsed if he hadn’t believed he would see God’s goodness in this life. Hope for good in “the land of the living” keeps him going.

f.g: The words “I had fainted” are added by the KJV translators; the Hebrew breaks off, as if too much to say.

chapters.n: David turns to counsel his own heart and the listener: wait on the Lord, take courage, and he will give you strength. The repeated “wait” frames the whole promise.
David calls the Lord his rock and begs him not to stay silent. If God doesn’t answer, David feels he will be like the dead.

f.g: The grave or the realm of the dead (Sheol).

chapters.n: Raising hands was the ancient posture of prayer. David stretches his hands toward the innermost room of the sanctuary where God’s presence dwelt.

f.g: The Most Holy Place (Holy of Holies), the inner sanctuary where the ark rested.

chapters.n: He asks not to be dragged off with hypocrites who speak friendly words while plotting harm. Their smooth talk hides cruel hearts.

f.w: speak peace to their neighbours, but mischief is in their hearts

chapters.n: David asks that the wicked receive what their deeds deserve. This is a plea for justice, leaving vengeance in God’s hands rather than his own.

f.g: Give them what they deserve.

chapters.n: Because they ignore what God is doing in the world, they will be torn down rather than built up. Blindness to God leads to ruin.

f.g: A building image: God tears down and builds up nations and people.

chapters.n: The turning point: David blesses the Lord because his prayer has been heard. The psalm moves from plea to praise.
God is both strength and shield — power to act and protection from harm. Trusting him brings help, and help brings a song.
God strengthens all his people and especially his anointed king. “Anointed” in Hebrew is mashiaḥ — Messiah — pointing beyond David to Christ.

f.g: Hebrew mashiaḥ; Greek christos — the root of the titles Messiah and Christ.

chapters.n: David ends praying for the whole nation: save them, bless them, and shepherd them forever. “Feed them” pictures God as a shepherd carrying his flock.

f.g: Shepherd them, tend them as a flock.
Israel, God’s own treasured people.

chapters.n: David calls on the “mighty” — possibly heavenly beings or earthly rulers — to give glory to the Lord. Even the powerful must recognize where real power lies.

f.g: Literally “sons of God” (bene elim) — likely the heavenly hosts or angels.

chapters.n: Worship should be offered with the honor God’s name deserves, in holy attire or holy splendor.

f.g: Possibly “holy attire” or “the splendor of holiness” — worship that reflects God’s purity.

chapters.n: Now a thunderstorm rolls in from the sea. Seven times the psalm repeats “the voice of the LORD,” picturing thunder as God speaking with power over the waters.

f.g: In ancient imagery, the vast, chaotic sea — which God rules.

chapters.n: God’s voice carries both power and majesty. What he says, happens.

f.w: The voice of the LORD is powerful

chapters.n: Lebanon’s cedars were the mightiest trees known; God’s voice snaps them like twigs. Nothing proud or tall stands against him.

f.g: Tall, prized trees used in Solomon’s temple, symbols of strength and pride.

chapters.n: The storm makes whole mountains seem to leap like young animals. Sirion is another name for Mount Hermon.

f.g: The Sidonian name for Mount Hermon.
Hebrew reʾem — a wild ox, not a mythical horned horse.

chapters.n: The lightning flashes like flames split apart. God commands even the fire of the storm.

f.g: Hews out or splits flames — a picture of forked lightning.

chapters.n: The storm sweeps south into the desert, shaking the wilderness of Kadesh. God’s voice reaches from the northern mountains to the southern wilderness — the whole land.

f.g: Kadesh-barnea, in the southern wilderness where Israel camped during the Exodus.

chapters.n: The storm’s force strips forests bare and startles deer into labor. Meanwhile, in his temple, worshippers cry “Glory!”

f.g: Female deer.
Strips bare, uncovers.

chapters.n: God sits enthroned above the flood — perhaps recalling Noah’s flood. He reigns as King forever, unshaken by any storm.

f.g: Hebrew mabbul, used elsewhere only for Noah’s flood.

chapters.n: The psalm that began with thunder ends with peace. The same mighty voice that shakes the earth gives strength and peace to God’s people.
David praises the Lord for drawing him up, like water lifted from a well, so his enemies had no reason to celebrate. The heading calls it a song for the dedication of the house.

f.g: The Hebrew pictures drawing up a bucket from a well.
Praise highly, exalt.

chapters.n: A short, simple testimony: I cried, and you healed me. Healing may be physical, emotional, or spiritual.
David had been near death, almost in the grave, but God brought him back. Being rescued from the pit is a preview of resurrection hope.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the realm of the dead.

chapters.n: David invites the faithful to join him in thanks. Personal deliverance becomes a reason for the whole community to praise.

f.g: Hebrew ḥasidim — the faithful, loyal ones who keep covenant.
Literally “his holy name” or memorial.

chapters.n: One of the most comforting verses in scripture: God’s discipline is brief, but his favor lasts a lifetime. Sorrow may stay overnight like a guest, but joy arrives with the morning.
David confesses that when things were going well, he grew self-confident and thought nothing could shake him.
He realizes his strength had been God’s gift all along. When God hid his face, David was immediately shaken.

f.g: An image of a secure position or stronghold — possibly his kingdom.
To withdraw his presence and favor.

chapters.n: In his trouble David returned to prayer, pleading for mercy.

f.g: Humble, earnest prayer for help.

chapters.n: David reasons with God: what good would my death do you? The dead can’t sing praise. Ancient Israel’s hope beyond the grave was still developing; later revelation teaches that the dead hear the gospel.
A short, honest cry: hear me, have mercy, help me.
God turned grief into celebration. Sackcloth was rough mourning clothing; God took it off and dressed David in joy instead.

f.g: Coarse goat-hair cloth worn in mourning or repentance.

chapters.n: The purpose of deliverance is praise. David vows his whole being will sing and give thanks forever.

f.g: Often understood as “my soul” or “my whole self.”

chapters.n: David begins with trust and asks God, who always does what is right, to rescue him so his faith is never put to shame.

f.g: God’s righteousness here means his faithfulness to rescue those in covenant with him.

chapters.n: Like a person leaning down to hear a quiet voice, God is asked to bend close and act quickly. David wants God to be his fortress.

f.g: A tender idiom: lean in to listen.
A fortress or stronghold.

chapters.n: Since God already is his rock and fortress, David asks him to lead and guide him — not because David deserves it, but because it fits God’s own name and character.

f.g: For the honor of God’s character and reputation.

chapters.n: His enemies have secretly set a trap. David asks God to pull him free, since God is his strength.

f.g: Secretly.

chapters.n: David entrusts his very life into God’s hands. Jesus spoke these words on the cross as he died, making this verse a perfect picture of trust in the Father.

f.w: Into thine hand I commit my spirit

f.g: Ransomed, rescued.

chapters.n: David rejects people who devote themselves to worthless idols. His trust is in the Lord alone.

f.g: Worthless idols — empty things that cannot help.

chapters.n: He rejoices in God’s loyal love because God has truly seen his troubles and known him personally in hard times.

f.w: thou hast known my soul in adversities
f.g: God cares for and understands him in his distress.

chapters.n: Instead of trapping him in the enemy’s grip, God set him in an open, spacious place where he could move freely.

f.g: A broad, open place — the opposite of being hemmed in.

chapters.n: Now a lament begins. David’s grief affects him eyes to stomach — his whole body aches with sorrow.

f.g: The body or inner being; grief felt physically.

chapters.n: Years of sorrow have worn him down. David admits some of his weakness comes from his own sin, and he feels it even in his bones.

f.g: Wasted away — a picture of deep exhaustion in body and spirit.

chapters.n: Enemies mock him, neighbors shame him, and acquaintances avoid him — people cross the street rather than meet him. Isolation adds to his pain.

f.g: An object of scorn or disgrace.

f.w: they that did see me without fled from me
f.g: Those who saw him outside, in the street, ran away from him.

chapters.n: He feels forgotten like the dead and as useless as a smashed clay jar. These are honest words of depression, and the Psalms make room for them.

f.g: A shattered pot, worthless and thrown away.

chapters.n: Rumors swirl and terror is everywhere as his enemies plot to kill him. Jeremiah later used the same phrase, “fear on every side.”
“But I trusted” — the turning point. In the middle of the storm, David holds onto one simple confession: you are my God.
All the moments and seasons of his life are in God’s hands, not the enemy’s. This is a quiet statement that God, not chance, governs his life.

f.w: My times are in thy hand

chapters.n: David asks God to smile on him, echoing the priestly blessing. A shining face means favor and approval.
He asks that his trust not end in disappointment, and that the wicked be the ones silenced — sent quiet to the grave.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol, the realm of the dead.

chapters.n: David prays that arrogant, lying mouths that insult the righteous would be shut.

f.g: Insolent, hard, arrogant words.

chapters.n: An outburst of wonder: God has goodness stored up like treasure for those who reverence him, and he shows it openly before others.

f.g: Stored away like treasure.

chapters.n: God hides his people in the safety of his presence, sheltering them from human pride and from quarrelsome, wounding speech.

f.g: Disputes, accusations and harmful words.
A shelter or booth.

chapters.n: David blesses the Lord, who showed him wonderful loyal love — as if placing him inside a fortified city.

f.g: A walled, fortified city; possibly recalling a real refuge such as Keilah.

chapters.n: David confesses that in his panic he concluded God had cut him off. Yet God heard him anyway. Our fears don’t limit God’s hearing.

f.g: In my alarm or panic.

chapters.n: He calls all the faithful to love the Lord, who protects the loyal and fully repays the proud.

f.g: Hebrew ḥasidim — the faithful covenant people.
Pays back in full those who act arrogantly.

chapters.n: The psalm closes with encouragement to all who hope in the Lord: take heart, and he will make you strong.
True happiness belongs to the one whose sin has been forgiven and covered by God. Paul quotes this psalm to teach that forgiveness is a gift of grace.

f.g: Happy, fortunate — the same word that opens Psalm 1.
Hidden from view; atoned for. The Hebrew idea of atonement includes covering sin.

chapters.n: Blessed is the person God no longer charges with guilt — and who is honest, without deceit. Forgiveness and honesty go together.

f.g: Does not count or charge against him.
Deceit, trickery.

chapters.n: David remembers what it was like when he hid his sin: his body felt old and he groaned all day long. Unconfessed sin weighs on the whole person.

f.g: Grew old, wasted away.
Groaning or crying out in anguish.

chapters.n: He felt God’s hand pressing on him day and night, and his strength dried up like plants in summer heat. Conviction of sin can be a merciful pressure.

f.g: A musical or liturgical marker of uncertain meaning, possibly a pause or a lift in the music.

f.w: thy hand was heavy upon me

chapters.n: The turning point: “I said, I will confess” — and God forgave. Healing came the moment David stopped hiding. This is a model of repentance.

f.w: I acknowledged my sin unto thee

chapters.n: Because of this, every faithful person should pray while God may be found. When floods of trouble come, they won’t sweep him away.

f.w: in a time when thou mayest be found

f.g: Hebrew ḥasid — faithful, devoted.

chapters.n: God is a hiding place who surrounds the forgiven person with songs of rescue, like a choir all around.

f.g: Surround me.

chapters.n: Now God himself seems to speak: I will teach you the way and keep my eye on you. Guidance follows forgiveness.

f.w: I will guide thee with mine eye
f.g: Possibly “I will counsel you with my eye upon you” — watching over you as you go.

chapters.n: Don’t be like a stubborn horse or mule that must be steered with bit and bridle. God wants willing, understanding followers, not ones dragged along.
The wicked face many sorrows, but the one who trusts the Lord is wrapped around by his loyal love.

f.g: God’s ḥesed (steadfast love) will surround him.

chapters.n: The psalm ends in celebration: the forgiven and upright should shout for joy. Repentance leads to gladness, not gloom.
The psalmist calls the righteous to rejoice. Praise fits the upright naturally, like well-made clothing.

f.g: Fitting, beautiful, appropriate.

chapters.n: Praise is to be made with music — harps and stringed instruments. Worship in Israel was often musical and joyful.

f.g: A stringed instrument like a lyre or harp.
Possibly a ten-stringed harp.

chapters.n: A “new song” celebrates fresh experiences of God’s goodness. The musicians are to play with skill and joyful shouts.

f.g: Shouts of joy, as at a festival.

chapters.n: Here is the reason for praise: what God says is upright, and everything he does is faithful and true.

f.g: In faithfulness — reliably.

chapters.n: God loves what is right and just, and the whole earth overflows with his loyal love.

f.g: Justice, fair dealing.
Hebrew ḥesed — steadfast, covenant love.

chapters.n: God created the heavens and all their stars simply by speaking. His word is creative power.

f.w: By the word of the LORD were the heavens made

f.g: The stars and heavenly bodies.

chapters.n: God piles up the sea like water gathered into a heap and stores the deep oceans like grain in a barn — a picture of complete control over nature.
Because God is the Creator, all people everywhere should reverence and stand in awe of him.
Creation was immediate: God spoke and it happened; he commanded and it held firm.

f.w: he spake, and it was done

chapters.n: Human nations make plans, but God can frustrate any scheme that opposes him.

f.w: bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought

f.g: The nations; peoples outside Israel’s covenant.

chapters.n: In contrast, God’s plans never fail. What he intends stands across all generations — a reminder of his eternal plan.

f.w: The counsel of the LORD standeth for ever

chapters.n: Blessed is the nation that makes the Lord its God, and the people he chose as his own treasured inheritance.

f.w: Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD

chapters.n: God looks down from heaven and sees every person — no one is overlooked.
From his dwelling place he watches over everyone living on earth.

f.g: Dwelling place, home.

chapters.n: God formed every human heart, so he understands every heart and notices every deed.

f.g: Forms, shapes as a potter does.

chapters.n: No king is saved by having a big army, and no warrior by his own strength. Real safety lies elsewhere.

f.g: An army.

chapters.n: Even the war horse — the ancient world’s most powerful military weapon — is a false hope for rescue.

f.w: An horse is a vain thing for safety

chapters.n: Instead, God’s eye is watching over those who reverence him and hope in his loyal love.
God watches over them to rescue them from death and keep them alive even in famine.
The community answers: we wait for the Lord, our help and shield.

f.g: Waits with hope and expectation.

chapters.n: Our hearts rejoice in him because we trust his holy name — his revealed character.
The closing prayer: may your loyal love rest on us, in the same measure as our hope in you.

f.w: according as we hope in thee
f.g: Just as, or because, we put our hope in you.

chapters.n: According to its heading, David wrote this after pretending to be insane to escape a Philistine king. Having escaped, he vows to praise the Lord always. Like Psalm 25, it is an alphabet acrostic in Hebrew.

f.w: I will bless the LORD at all times

f.g: To bless God is to praise him with gratitude.

chapters.n: David boasts — not in himself, but in the Lord. The humble will hear his story and be encouraged.

f.w: make her boast in the LORD

chapters.n: An invitation to praise together: “magnify” means to make God great in our eyes and words.

f.g: Make great; enlarge in honor.

chapters.n: David testifies simply: I sought the Lord, he answered, and he freed me from every fear.

f.w: delivered me from all my fears

chapters.n: Those who look to God are lit up with joy, their faces radiant instead of ashamed.
