f.g: Made radiant, glowing — like Moses’ face after being with God.

chapters.n: David calls himself “this poor man” — humble and in need. God heard and saved him from all his troubles.
The angel of the Lord sets up camp around those who reverence God, guarding them like a protecting army.

f.w: The angel of the LORD encampeth

chapters.n: A beloved invitation: don’t just hear about God’s goodness — experience it for yourself, like tasting food.

f.w: O taste and see that the LORD is good

chapters.n: Those who reverence God lack nothing truly needed.

f.g: Holy ones — God’s set-apart people.
No lack.

chapters.n: Even strong young lions can go hungry, but those who seek the Lord won’t lack any good thing. Strength is not the same as security.

f.w: they that seek the LORD shall not want any good thing

chapters.n: David turns teacher, like a parent gathering children: let me teach you what it means to reverence the Lord.

f.g: Reverent awe and loyal obedience toward God.

chapters.n: A teacher’s question: Who wants a long, good life? The next verses give the answer.
First, guard your speech — no evil words, no deception.
Second, turn from evil and do good. Don’t just wait for peace — chase after it.
God is attentive to the righteous; his eyes watch over them and his ears hear their cries.

f.w: his ears are open unto their cry

chapters.n: But God sets his face against evildoers, and their memory will fade from the earth.

f.w: cut off the remembrance of them
f.g: Their name and legacy will be forgotten.

chapters.n: When the righteous cry out, the Lord hears and rescues them.
God draws close to the broken-hearted and saves the crushed in spirit. A broken heart and contrite spirit is the offering Christ asks of his disciples.

f.g: Crushed, humbled; deeply sorry for sin.

chapters.n: Being righteous doesn’t mean having no trials — the righteous have many. But God brings them through all of them.

f.w: Many are the afflictions of the righteous

chapters.n: God protects even the bones of the righteous. John saw this fulfilled when the soldiers did not break Jesus’ legs at the cross.

f.w: not one of them is broken

chapters.n: Evil itself destroys the wicked, and those who hate the righteous will be held guilty.

f.g: Here, condemned or held guilty.

chapters.n: The final promise: the Lord ransoms his servants, and none who trust him will be condemned.

f.g: Buys back, rescues — fulfilled in Christ’s Atonement.

chapters.n: David uses courtroom and battlefield language at once: be my lawyer against those who accuse me, and my warrior against those who attack me.

f.g: Argue my case, as an advocate in court.

chapters.n: He pictures God arming himself like a soldier and rising to defend him.

f.g: A small round shield (or a large body shield); paired with “shield” for full protection.

chapters.n: David asks God to block the pursuers’ road with a spear — and, most of all, to reassure his soul: “I am your salvation.”

f.w: say unto my soul, I am thy salvation
f.g: What David wants most is a personal word of assurance from God.

chapters.n: He prays that his would-be killers will be frustrated and forced to retreat in disgrace.

f.g: Confused, thrown into disarray.

chapters.n: May they be blown away like chaff — the light husks separated from grain in the wind — with the angel of the Lord driving them.

f.g: The dry husks blown away when grain is winnowed.

chapters.n: He asks that their road become dark and slick as they flee, with God’s angel in pursuit.

f.g: Here simply “pursue, chase.”

chapters.n: His enemies had no reason to attack him, yet they dug a hidden pit and spread a net to catch him, like hunters trapping an animal.
David asks that their own trap catch them by surprise. The Psalms often teach that evil boomerangs on those who plot it.

f.w: let his net that he hath hid catch himself

f.g: Without warning, suddenly.

chapters.n: When God rescues him, David’s whole soul will rejoice in that salvation.
Even his bones — his whole being — will cry out: no one is like the Lord, who rescues the weak from the strong and the poor from those who rob them.

f.g: Plunders, robs.

f.w: LORD, who is like unto thee

chapters.n: Lying witnesses accused him of crimes he knew nothing about — a situation Jesus would also face.
They repaid his kindness with harm, leaving him feeling bereaved and desolate.

f.w: to the spoiling of my soul
f.g: Leaving my soul bereft, like one who has lost a child.

chapters.n: David contrasts his behavior: when they were ill, he wore mourning clothes and fasted for them. His prayer “returned into his bosom” — he prayed with head bowed to his chest, or the blessing came back to him.

f.g: Coarse cloth worn in mourning or humility.

f.w: my prayer returned into mine own bosom
f.g: Either “I prayed with head bowed on my chest,” or “my prayer came back unanswered for them, but blessed me.”

chapters.n: He grieved for them like a brother, like a son mourning his mother. That is how deeply he cared.

f.g: Bent low in deep sorrow.

chapters.n: Yet when David stumbled, they celebrated and ganged up on him — even lowlifes and strangers joined in, tearing at him nonstop.

f.g: Outcasts, lowly people; possibly “smiters” or slanderers.

chapters.n: Like freeloading mockers at a feast, they ground their teeth at him in hatred.

f.w: gnashed upon me with their teeth

chapters.n: “How long will you just watch?” David pleads with God to rescue his precious life from these lion-like enemies.

f.g: My only one — my precious, solitary life.

chapters.n: He vows to praise God publicly in the great congregation once he is rescued.
He asks that those who hate him for no reason won’t smirk and wink at his downfall.

f.g: A gesture of malicious scheming or gloating.

chapters.n: They don’t speak peace; they cook up lies against peaceful, quiet people who mind their own business.

f.w: them that are quiet in the land
f.g: Peaceable, defenseless people.

chapters.n: They open their mouths wide in mockery: “Aha! We saw it with our own eyes!” — gloating over his troubles.
David answers: but you, Lord, have seen it too. Don’t stay silent or distant.
“Wake up and take my case!” David speaks boldly, as if God were asleep — honest language that the Psalms allow in prayer.
He asks God to judge by God’s own justice, so his enemies won’t get to celebrate.
Don’t let them say, “Just what we wanted — we swallowed him whole!”

f.g: We have destroyed him completely.

chapters.n: May those who delight in his harm be wrapped in shame instead, like wearing a garment of disgrace.
In contrast, let David’s supporters shout for joy and keep saying, “The Lord is great — he delights in his servant’s well-being.”

f.g: Hebrew shalom — peace, wholeness, well-being.

chapters.n: The psalm ends with a vow: David’s tongue will talk about God’s justice and praise all day long.
David describes the inner voice of a wicked person: sin speaks to him like an oracle, and he has no reverence for God at all. Paul quotes this line in Romans.

f.w: there is no fear of God before his eyes

chapters.n: The wicked man flatters himself, thinking his sin will never be discovered or hated — self-deception at its worst.

f.w: flattereth himself in his own eyes

chapters.n: His words are full of wrong and deceit, and he has stopped trying to be wise or do good.

f.g: Stopped, given up.

chapters.n: Even lying in bed he plots harm. He chooses a bad path on purpose and never rejects evil.

f.w: He deviseth mischief upon his bed

f.g: Does not hate or reject.

chapters.n: Suddenly the psalm lifts its eyes: God’s loyal love is as high as the heavens, his faithfulness reaches the clouds. The contrast with the wicked could not be sharper.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — steadfast, covenant love.

f.w: Thy mercy, O LORD, is in the heavens

chapters.n: God’s righteousness stands like massive mountains, and his judgments go as deep as the ocean. He cares for both humans and animals.

f.g: The vast ocean depths — beyond human measuring.

chapters.n: God’s loyal love is precious, so people take refuge under his wings like chicks under a mother bird — or under the cherubim’s wings over the ark.
Those who come to God feast at a rich banquet in his house and drink from a river of delights.

f.g: Richness, abundance — the best food.
“Pleasures” is Hebrew ʿedenim, related to Eden — a river of delights.

chapters.n: God is the source of life itself, and only by his light can we see truly. Latter-day revelation teaches that the light of Christ fills all things and gives life.

f.w: in thy light shall we see light

chapters.n: David asks God to keep showing his loyal love to those who know him and his justice to the honest-hearted.

f.g: Knowing God in Hebrew implies a close, covenant relationship.

chapters.n: He asks protection from proud people who would trample him and wicked hands that would drive him away.

f.g: The arrogant who would stamp on him.

chapters.n: As if seeing it already happen, David points: there the evildoers lie fallen, thrown down and unable to rise.

f.g: As if pointing to the very spot where they fall.

chapters.n: This wisdom psalm opens with counsel: don’t get worked up or jealous when wicked people seem to succeed. Like Psalms 25 and 34, it is an acrostic in Hebrew.

f.g: “Fret” means to burn or get heated — don’t let anger or worry eat at you.

chapters.n: Their success is temporary, like grass that withers in the heat.
Instead, trust God and do good. Stay where God has placed you and find safety and nourishment there.

f.g: Possibly “feed on faithfulness” or “dwell securely.”

chapters.n: When we delight in God, our desires begin to match his — and he grants them. Delight shapes desire.

f.w: Delight thyself also in the LORD

chapters.n: Roll your path onto the Lord like handing over a heavy load. Trust him, and he will act.

f.g: Literally “roll” — roll your burden onto him.

chapters.n: God will make your integrity shine like dawn and your just cause blaze like noon. Truth comes to light eventually.
Be still before the Lord and wait patiently. Don’t fume when schemers seem to get ahead.

f.g: Be silent, be still before him.

chapters.n: Let go of anger; it only leads toward doing evil yourself.

f.g: In any way at all.

chapters.n: Evildoers will be removed, but those who wait on the Lord will inherit the land.
Just a little longer and the wicked will be gone. Look for where he used to be — and he won’t be there.
Jesus quoted this verse in the Beatitudes. The humble and gentle will inherit the earth and enjoy abundant peace — a promise Latter-day Saints connect to the earth’s future celestial glory.

f.w: the meek shall inherit the earth

chapters.n: The wicked plot against the righteous and grind their teeth in hatred.

f.g: Grinds his teeth — a sign of rage.

chapters.n: God laughs — not cruelly, but because he sees their day of reckoning approaching.

f.w: The Lord shall laugh at him

chapters.n: They draw swords and string bows against the poor and those who live upright lives.

f.g: In KJV English, “conversation” means conduct or way of life.

chapters.n: But their weapons will turn on themselves, and their bows will snap.

f.w: Their sword shall enter into their own heart

chapters.n: A little gained honestly is worth more than great wealth gained wickedly.

f.w: A little that a righteous man hath

chapters.n: The power of the wicked will be broken, but God holds up the righteous.

f.g: Strength, power.

chapters.n: God knows every day of the upright, and their inheritance lasts forever.
In hard times they won’t be put to shame; even in famine they will have enough.
The wicked will vanish like the fat of sacrificed lambs burned up into smoke on the altar.

f.g: Burned on the altar until gone — or, in another reading, like the beauty of meadows that fades.

chapters.n: The wicked borrow and don’t repay, while the righteous are generous and give freely.

f.w: the righteous sheweth mercy, and giveth

chapters.n: Those God blesses will inherit the land; those under his curse will be cut off.
God directs and firms up each step of a good person, and he takes pleasure in their journey.

f.w: The steps of a good man are ordered by the LORD

chapters.n: A precious promise: a good person may stumble, but won’t be thrown down for good, because God holds his hand.
The voice of experience: in a long life, David has not seen the righteous abandoned or their children begging. This is a general wisdom observation rather than a guarantee against every hardship.

f.w: I have been young, and now am old
f.g: A sign that this is the reflection of an aged teacher.

chapters.n: The righteous are always generous and lend to others, and their children are blessed.
Turn from evil, do good, and live securely forever.

f.w: Depart from evil, and do good

chapters.n: The Lord loves justice and won’t abandon his faithful ones; they are kept safe forever.

f.g: Hebrew ḥasidim — the faithful, devoted ones.

chapters.n: The righteous will inherit the land and live in it permanently.
The righteous speak wisdom and talk about what is just.

f.g: Justice, what is right.

chapters.n: God’s law is written in his heart, so his steps stay firm. Obedience from the heart gives stability.

f.w: The law of his God is in his heart

chapters.n: The wicked lie in wait for the righteous, hoping to kill him.
But God won’t leave him in their power or let him be condemned when tried.
Wait on the Lord and keep his way; he will lift you up to inherit the land, and you will see the wicked removed.
David saw a ruthless man flourishing like a lush tree in its native soil.

f.g: A luxuriant native tree in its home soil — a picture of thriving.

chapters.n: But soon he was gone. David looked for him and he was nowhere to be found.
Watch the person of integrity — his future is peace.

f.g: Whole, blameless, complete — not flawless.

f.w: the end of that man is peace
f.g: Possibly “there is a future (posterity) for the man of peace.”

chapters.n: But sinners will be destroyed together, and the wicked will have no future.
The salvation of the righteous comes from the Lord, who is their stronghold in trouble.

f.g: Hebrew maʿoz — a fortress or refuge.

chapters.n: The psalm ends with assurance: God helps, rescues, and saves those who take refuge in him.
David doesn’t ask to escape correction, but asks God not to correct him in anger. He knows he needs discipline, yet longs for it to come with mercy.

f.w: rebuke me not in thy wrath

f.g: Discipline, correct.

chapters.n: He feels God’s correction like arrows lodged in his body and a hand pressing hard on him.

f.w: thine arrows stick fast in me

f.g: Heavily, severely.

chapters.n: His body has no health and his bones no rest because of his sin. David sees a close link between spiritual guilt and physical suffering.

f.g: Health, wholeness.

chapters.n: His sins have risen over his head like floodwater, and they press on him like a load too heavy to carry.

f.w: as an heavy burden they are too heavy for me

chapters.n: He describes festering wounds — a raw picture of how sin, left untreated, rots and spreads. He owns that it came from his foolishness.

f.g: Festering, infected.
In Hebrew wisdom writing, folly means moral rebellion, not just a lack of intelligence.

chapters.n: He is bent over with grief, walking around in mourning all day.

f.g: Literally “I go about in black,” as one dressed for mourning.

chapters.n: His body burns with sickness; nothing in him feels healthy.

f.g: The lower back and sides; the seat of strength.
Literally “burning” — inflammation or fever.

chapters.n: Weak and crushed, he groans aloud from the turmoil inside.

f.g: Groaned or cried out in anguish.
Turmoil, restlessness.

chapters.n: A tender turn: Lord, you already know everything I long for; even my sighs aren’t hidden from you.

f.w: my groaning is not hid from thee

chapters.n: His heart races, his strength is gone, and even the light in his eyes has faded.

f.g: Throbs, pounds.

chapters.n: Loved ones and friends keep their distance from his suffering; even relatives stay far off. Suffering can be lonely.

f.g: Keep their distance.

chapters.n: Meanwhile, enemies set traps for him and plot against him with lies all day long.

f.g: Plan treachery, scheme lies.

chapters.n: David responds by not responding: like a deaf and mute man, he doesn’t answer their attacks.

f.g: Unable to speak, mute — not a comment on intelligence.

f.w: as a dumb man that openeth not his mouth

chapters.n: He has no rebuttal in his mouth. He leaves his defense to God.

f.g: Arguments, replies, counter-charges.

chapters.n: Here is why he stays silent: his hope is in the Lord, who will answer for him.
He asks God to hear him so his enemies don’t gloat — they puff themselves up the moment he slips.
David feels ready to collapse, and his pain never leaves his sight.

f.g: About to stumble or fall; “halt” means limp or be lame.

chapters.n: He confesses openly and feels true sorrow for his sin — the heart of repentance.

f.w: I will be sorry for my sin

chapters.n: Meanwhile, his enemies are healthy and strong and grow in number, though they hate him without reason.

f.g: Vigorous, full of life.

chapters.n: They repay his good with evil, opposing him precisely because he follows what is good.
Two final cries: don’t abandon me; don’t stay far away.
The psalm ends with an urgent plea: hurry to help me, Lord, my salvation. The answer isn’t yet given, but hope is still voiced.
David had resolved to guard his speech so he wouldn’t sin in front of the wicked, keeping his mouth muzzled like an animal with a bridle. The heading names Jeduthun, one of David’s temple musicians.

f.w: keep my mouth with a bridle
f.g: A muzzle; holding back words.

chapters.n: He stayed completely silent, saying nothing at all — not even good things. But keeping it all in only stirred up his pain.

f.g: Silent, mute.

chapters.n: His heart grew hot like a fire as he brooded, until finally the words burst out — in prayer to God rather than in complaints to people.

f.w: while I was musing the fire burned

f.g: Meditating, brooding.

chapters.n: His request: help me understand how short and fragile my life is. Recognizing our mortality helps us live wisely.

f.w: make me to know mine end

chapters.n: Life is only a few fingers wide in God’s sight. Even at our strongest, we are a passing breath.

f.g: The width of a hand — one of the smallest measures.
Hebrew hevel — a breath or vapor, the key word of Ecclesiastes.

chapters.n: People walk around like shadows, fussing over nothing. They pile up wealth without knowing who will end up with it.

f.g: A mere shadow or image.

f.w: knoweth not who shall gather them

chapters.n: The turning point: if life is so brief, what am I really hoping for? Only you, Lord.
He asks to be freed from all his sins and not to become a laughingstock for fools.

f.g: An object of scorn.

chapters.n: He fell silent because he recognized God’s hand in his trial — not to sulk, but in submission.
Still, he pleads: take your hand of discipline off me; I am worn out by it.

f.g: Plague, blow — affliction.

chapters.n: When God corrects sin, the things people treasure fade away like cloth eaten by a moth. Every human being is but a breath.

f.g: As a moth eats away a garment — quietly and completely.

chapters.n: A moving plea: don’t ignore my tears. David calls himself a guest and a traveler passing through God’s land, as his ancestors were.

f.g: A resident foreigner, a guest without permanent rights.
A temporary resident.

chapters.n: He asks for a little relief so he can smile again before he dies. The psalm ends raw and honest, without a tidy resolution.

f.g: Literally “look cheerful again,” brighten up.
Before I depart — before death.

chapters.n: David waited and waited — and then God bent down and heard his cry. Patient waiting is rewarded.

f.g: Literally “waiting I waited” — a Hebrew way of stressing long, steady waiting.
Bent down, leaned toward.

chapters.n: God pulled him out of a muddy pit where he was sinking and set him on solid rock. Many see this as a picture of rescue from sin and death through Christ.

f.g: Thick, sucking mud — like the bottom of a cistern.

f.w: set my feet upon a rock

chapters.n: Deliverance gives him a new song of praise. When others see what God did, they too will reverence and trust him.
Blessed is the one who trusts the Lord rather than looking up to arrogant people or those who follow lies.

f.g: Go after false gods or falsehoods.

chapters.n: God’s wonders and his thoughtful plans for us are so many that no one could ever list them all.

f.g: Toward us.

chapters.n: God isn’t ultimately after animal sacrifices; he wants an obedient, listening heart. “Mine ears hast thou opened” means God has made him able to hear and obey.

f.w: Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire

f.g: Literally “ears you have dug for me.” The Greek Old Testament reads “a body you have prepared me,” which Hebrews 10:5 quotes.

chapters.n: “Here I am; I have come.” Hebrews applies these words to Jesus, who came to do the Father’s will, as written of him in the scroll.

f.g: The scroll — the written law or scripture.

chapters.n: True obedience is joyful and inward: God’s law lives in the heart. This perfectly describes Christ, who always did his Father’s will.

f.w: I delight to do thy will
thy law is within my heart

chapters.n: David has openly proclaimed God’s goodness before the gathered people, not keeping quiet.

f.g: Proclaimed good news.

chapters.n: He hasn’t kept God’s faithfulness and loyal love a private secret but shared it with everyone. Testimony is meant to be borne.

f.w: I have not hid thy righteousness within my heart

chapters.n: Since David hasn’t held back praise, he asks God not to hold back mercy. May God’s love and faithfulness guard him always.
Without warning, the psalm turns to distress: countless troubles and his own sins surround him, more than the hairs on his head. Even after deliverance, new trials come.

f.w: I am not able to look up
f.g: Overwhelmed with shame and trouble.

chapters.n: Verses 13–17 appear again, almost word for word, as Psalm 70. David pleads for God to hurry.
He asks that those trying to destroy him be driven back in confusion.

f.g: Confused, defeated.

chapters.n: May the mockers who taunt him with “Aha, aha!” be stunned by their own shame.

f.g: Appalled, stunned.

chapters.n: In contrast, may all who seek God rejoice and keep saying, “The Lord is great!”

f.g: Made great, honored.

chapters.n: David admits he is poor and needy — yet the Lord is thinking about him. The closing plea: don’t delay.

f.g: Do not delay.

chapters.n: Blessed is the person who pays attention to the weak and helps them; God will rescue that person in his own trouble. Compassion is returned.

f.g: Pays thoughtful attention to, acts wisely toward.
The weak, helpless or sick.

chapters.n: God will protect such a person, keep him alive, and bless him, never handing him over to his enemies.
When this person is sick in bed, God will sustain him and tend to him like a caregiver changing his bed.

f.g: Sickness, weakness.
Turn or change his bed — care for him through his illness.

chapters.n: Now David speaks from his own sickbed, asking for healing of his soul and confessing his sin.
His enemies speak cruelly: “When will he die and be forgotten?”
A visitor comes pretending sympathy, but collects gossip to spread once he leaves.

f.g: Empty, insincere words.
Goes outside.

chapters.n: Everyone who hates him whispers together and plans the worst for him.
They say a deadly disease has gripped him: “He’s down and won’t get up again.”

f.g: Literally “a thing of Belial” — something wicked or deadly.
Sticks tight.

chapters.n: Worst of all, a close friend who shared his table turned against him. Jesus quoted this verse about Judas, who ate with him and then betrayed him.

f.w: lifted up his heel against me
f.g: An image of kicking or turning on someone — treacherous betrayal.
Literally “man of my peace” — a trusted companion.

chapters.n: David asks God to raise him up so he can set things right with his enemies. As king, restoring justice was his duty.

f.g: Repay, give back what is due.

chapters.n: Proof of God’s favor: his enemy hasn’t been allowed to shout in victory over him.
God supports David because of his integrity and places him in his presence forever — the greatest of blessings.

f.w: settest me before thy face for ever

chapters.n: This doxology closes the first of the five “books” of the Psalms (Psalms 1–41). Each book ends with a burst of praise like this one.

f.g: “So be it” — a word of firm agreement.

chapters.n: Book Two of the Psalms begins here. The writer, from the temple singers called the sons of Korah, longs for God the way a thirsty deer longs for flowing streams in a dry land.

f.g: A deer.
Stream beds that run with water — precious in a dry country.

chapters.n: His thirst is not for religion in general but for the living God himself. He aches to come again into God’s presence at the sanctuary.
He has cried so much that tears have been his only food. Meanwhile scoffers keep taunting, “So where is your God?”

f.g: In KJV English, “meat” means food in general.

chapters.n: He remembers happier days leading joyful crowds to the temple at festival time. The memory both comforts and hurts.

f.g: Celebrated a sacred festival, such as Passover or Tabernacles.
Express my deepest feelings openly.

chapters.n: A refrain repeated in verse 11 and in Psalm 43: the psalmist speaks to his own soul, challenging despair with hope. This is a model of honest self-encouragement.

f.g: Bowed low, depressed.
Restless, in turmoil.
The saving help of his presence (literally, his face).

chapters.n: Far from Jerusalem, in the north near the Jordan’s headwaters and Mount Hermon, he chooses to remember God from where he is.

f.g: The peaks of Mount Hermon, at Israel’s northern border.
“Little mountain” — an unknown peak, perhaps near Hermon.

chapters.n: The roaring waterfalls of the north become a picture of his distress: wave upon wave of trouble crashing over him. Jonah later used this same language from inside the fish.

f.g: One roaring depth answers another — overwhelming, endless waters.

f.w: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me

chapters.n: Yet even in this flood, God’s loyal love will come by day and his song will fill the night. Faith holds onto God through both light and dark.

f.w: in the night his song shall be with me

chapters.n: He brings his honest question to God, his rock: why have you forgotten me? The Psalms show that faithful people can ask hard questions.
The enemies’ daily taunt cuts like a sword into his bones.

f.g: Taunt, mock.

chapters.n: The refrain returns, now calling God “the health of my countenance” — the one who will bring the light back to his face. Hope has the last word.

f.g: The salvation of my face — the one who will make me look up again.

chapters.n: Psalm 43 continues Psalm 42 — it has no title and repeats the same refrain, so many think they were once a single song. The psalmist asks God to defend him against a faithless people and a lying man.

f.g: Vindicate me; defend my cause.
A people without ḥesed (covenant loyalty) — faithless.

chapters.n: He knows God is his fortress, yet he feels rejected. He repeats the question from Psalm 42: why must I go around mourning?

He asks God to send light and truth as guides, like messengers that will lead him home to the holy mountain and the temple. Latter-day revelation connects light and truth with intelligence and the Spirit.

f.g: Mount Zion in Jerusalem, where the temple stood.

chapters.n: Once there, he will go to the altar and praise God — his greatest joy — with music. The longing of Psalm 42 turns to anticipation.

f.g: Literally “God, the gladness of my joy.”

chapters.n: For the third time the refrain sounds. The questions remain, but the answer is firm: hope in God, for I will praise him again.
A national lament begins with memory. The people recall stories their ancestors passed down about God’s mighty acts long ago.
God drove out the Canaanite nations and planted Israel in the land like a gardener planting a vine.

f.g: The nations — here the Canaanite peoples.

chapters.n: Israel didn’t win the land by their own weapons. It was God’s power and the light of his face — his favor — that gave it to them.

f.w: not the land in possession by their own sword

f.g: God’s smiling favor and presence.

chapters.n: Speaking for the nation, the leader declares God his king and asks him to order victories for Jacob, that is, Israel.

f.g: Another name for the nation of Israel, descended from Jacob.

chapters.n: With God’s power and name, Israel can push back any enemy.
The speaker refuses to rely on his own bow or sword.
It has always been God who saved them and embarrassed their enemies.
So their boast is in God all day long. A “Selah” marks a pause before everything changes.

f.g: A musical or liturgical marker, possibly a pause.

chapters.n: “But now” — the shock: God seems to have abandoned them and no longer marches with their armies.

f.w: goest not forth with our armies

chapters.n: They retreat before enemies, who plunder them freely.

f.g: Plunder, take as loot.

chapters.n: They feel like sheep set aside for slaughter and scattered among foreign nations. This may reflect a time of military defeat or exile.
It feels as if God sold his people for nothing — as if they were worthless to him.

f.w: Thou sellest thy people for nought

chapters.n: Neighboring nations mock and laugh at them.

f.g: Ridicule, contempt.

chapters.n: Israel’s name has become a proverb of failure, and people shake their heads at them in contempt.

f.g: A saying used to mock someone.

chapters.n: The speaker can’t escape his disgrace; shame covers his face all the time.

f.g: Disgrace, dishonor.

chapters.n: It comes from the insults of those who mock God and from enemies bent on revenge.
The heart of the lament: this happened even though we have stayed faithful to your covenant. Their suffering is not punishment for unfaithfulness, which makes it so hard to understand.

f.w: neither have we dealt falsely in thy covenant
f.g: Unlike many laments, this one claims innocence — the problem of righteous suffering.

chapters.n: They haven’t turned away in heart or strayed from God’s path.

f.g: Turned aside.

chapters.n: Even when God crushed them in a desolate place haunted by wild animals and covered them in deep darkness, they stayed loyal.

f.g: Jackals — animals of desolate ruins.
Deep darkness.

chapters.n: If they had forgotten God or prayed to foreign gods...

f.g: Raised hands in prayer.

chapters.n: ...wouldn’t God know? He sees the secrets of every heart. They are confident in their sincerity.

f.w: he knoweth the secrets of the heart

chapters.n: Their suffering comes because of their loyalty to God. Paul quoted this verse to say that nothing — not even such suffering — can separate us from Christ’s love.

f.w: we are counted as sheep for the slaughter

chapters.n: A bold cry: “Wake up, Lord! Why are you sleeping?” The Psalms let God’s people speak this honestly.
Why do you hide your face and forget our suffering?
They lie flat on the ground, utterly humbled.

f.w: our belly cleaveth unto the earth
f.g: Lying face down in the dust — total defeat and grief.

chapters.n: The final plea rests not on their merit but on God’s loyal love: rise up and redeem us.

f.g: Because of your ḥesed — your faithful covenant love.

chapters.n: This is a royal wedding song. The poet’s heart overflows with a beautiful theme, and his tongue moves as fast as a skilled scribe’s pen.

f.g: Overflowing, bubbling up.
A skilled, quick scribe.

chapters.n: The king is praised as the most handsome of men, with gracious speech. Christians have long read this king as a picture of Christ.

f.w: grace is poured into thy lips

chapters.n: The king is called to strap on his sword and appear in splendor as a mighty warrior.

f.g: Fasten on, strap on.

chapters.n: He rides out victoriously for the cause of truth, humility, and righteousness — a king who fights for good things.

f.g: Awe-inspiring deeds.

chapters.n: His arrows strike the hearts of his enemies, and nations fall before him.
Remarkably, the king is addressed as “God,” whose throne lasts forever. Hebrews quotes these verses about Jesus Christ, the eternal King.

f.w: Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever

f.g: A royal staff, the symbol of rule; a “right sceptre” means just rule.

chapters.n: Because he loves righteousness, God has anointed him with joy above all others. “Anointed” is the root of Messiah and Christ.

f.w: anointed thee with the oil of gladness

f.g: Your companions — other kings or the bridegroom’s friends.

chapters.n: His wedding robes are scented with precious spices, and music from ivory-decorated palaces makes him glad.

f.g: Costly fragrant spices; myrrh and aloes were also used at Jesus’ burial.
Palaces inlaid with ivory.

chapters.n: Princesses are among the honored ladies, and the queen stands at his right hand in the finest gold.

f.g: Ophir was a distant land famous for fine gold.

chapters.n: Now the bride is addressed: listen, and leave behind your family and homeland to begin a new life. Many see here a picture of the Church as the bride of Christ, leaving the world behind.
The king will delight in her beauty. Since he is now her lord, she should honor him.

f.g: Bow before him — a gesture of honor to a king.

chapters.n: Even wealthy Tyre will bring gifts, and the rich will seek her favor.

f.g: The people of Tyre, a rich Phoenician trading city.

chapters.n: The princess is radiant in her chamber, dressed in gold-woven clothing.

f.g: Inside the palace chamber — possibly also a hint of inner beauty.
Woven or embroidered with gold thread.

chapters.n: She is led to the king in embroidered robes, followed by her bridesmaids.

f.g: Embroidered garments.

chapters.n: The wedding procession enters the palace with joy and celebration.
The poet turns to the king: your sons will take your ancestors’ place and become princes everywhere. Covenant blessings extend to future generations.
The poet promises to make the king’s name remembered in every generation, so that people will praise him forever.
A song of confidence: God is a safe shelter and source of strength, always ready to help — and he is truly present in trouble, not far away.

f.g: Literally “a help readily found” — easy to find in trouble.

chapters.n: So we won’t be afraid, even if the earth itself gave way and mountains collapsed into the sea. This is the world at its most unstable.
Even if the oceans roar and the mountains tremble, the faithful stay calm. In ancient imagery, the raging sea symbolized chaos, which God controls.

f.g: A musical or liturgical marker, possibly a pause.

chapters.n: In contrast to the raging sea is a peaceful river that brings joy to God’s city. Jerusalem had no great river, so this points to God’s presence as a life-giving stream.

f.g: Jerusalem, Zion — where God dwelt in the temple.

chapters.n: Because God lives in the city, it won’t be shaken. He will help her at the break of dawn.

f.g: At the turning of the morning — at dawn, when attacks often came and rescues happened.

chapters.n: Nations roar and kingdoms totter, but God only has to speak and the earth melts.

f.w: he uttered his voice, the earth melted

chapters.n: The refrain: the Lord of armies is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress.

f.g: The Lord of armies — commander of heaven’s forces.
Here a high, secure fortress.

chapters.n: Come and see what the Lord has done — the devastation he has brought on his enemies.
God puts an end to war across the earth, breaking bows, snapping spears, and burning chariots. This anticipates the Millennium, when war will end.
God speaks directly: “Stop striving and know that I am God.” The Lord repeated this to the Saints during persecution in Missouri.

f.w: Be still, and know that I am God

f.g: Let go, stop fighting, relax your grip.

chapters.n: The refrain returns to close the psalm, sealing its message: God is with us.

f.w: The LORD of hosts is with us

chapters.n: All peoples, not just Israel, are invited to clap and shout to God with joy, as crowds would celebrate a newly crowned king.
The reason: the Most High Lord is awesome, the great King over the whole earth.

f.g: Awe-inspiring, to be reverenced.

chapters.n: He brought nations under Israel’s rule — recalling the conquest of the promised land.
God chose Israel’s land as their inheritance — the pride of Jacob, the people he loves.

f.g: Jacob’s pride — the promised land, or the temple.

chapters.n: God “goes up” with shouting and trumpets — perhaps a procession carrying the ark up to the temple. Many Christians also connect this with Christ’s ascension and coming reign.

f.w: God is gone up with a shout

f.g: Hebrew shofar, a ram’s horn.

chapters.n: Four times in one verse: sing praises! Hebrew poetry repeats to show intensity.
God is King of all the earth, so praise him thoughtfully, with understanding and skill.

f.g: Hebrew maskil — skillfully, with insight.

chapters.n: God rules the nations from his holy throne.
Leaders of the nations gather as one people with Abraham’s descendants — a fulfillment of God’s promise that all nations would be blessed through Abraham.

f.w: the people of the God of Abraham

f.g: Rulers and protectors of the nations.

chapters.n: A song of Zion: the Lord is great and deserves great praise in Jerusalem, his holy mountain. The city is honored because God dwells there.

f.g: Mount Zion, the temple hill in Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Mount Zion is beautiful in its height and a joy to the whole earth. “The sides of the north” borrows a phrase for the sacred mountain where God was said to dwell.

f.g: Beautiful in its elevation — lovely and lofty.
Hebrew Zaphon — a name for the holy mountain of the gods in Canaanite lore, here claimed for the true God.

f.w: the city of the great King

chapters.n: God himself, not the city’s walls, is its true fortress.

f.g: A high, secure stronghold.

chapters.n: Enemy kings joined forces and advanced together against the city.

f.g: Met by agreement, joined forces.

chapters.n: But when they saw it, they were stunned, panicked, and fled. Some connect this with the sudden collapse of the Assyrian siege in Hezekiah’s day.
Terror gripped them like the pains of a woman in labor — sudden and unstoppable.

f.g: Labor in childbirth.

chapters.n: God shatters even the great ocean-going ships with an east wind. Their power is nothing before him.

f.g: Large merchant ships built for long voyages — a symbol of human pride and wealth.
A hot, violent wind from the desert.

chapters.n: What our ancestors told us, we have now seen for ourselves: God protects his city forever. Testimony moves from hearing to seeing.

f.w: As we have heard, so have we seen

chapters.n: Inside the temple, the worshippers reflect on God’s loyal love.

f.g: Meditated on, pictured in our minds.

chapters.n: God’s praise spreads as far as his fame — to the ends of the earth — and his right hand acts with justice.

f.g: As widely as your reputation reaches.

chapters.n: Let Zion and the towns of Judah celebrate God’s just decisions.

f.g: The towns and villages of Judah, or its women.

chapters.n: An invitation to walk around the city and count its towers — to see for yourself how safe it is.

f.g: Count.

chapters.n: Study its defenses and palaces so you can describe them to your children. Faith is meant to be passed on.

f.g: Ramparts, defensive walls.

f.w: tell it to the generation following

chapters.n: The real point: Zion’s true defense is God himself, who will lead us always — even through death.

f.g: Some manuscripts read “forever”; either way, God guides his people to the end.

chapters.n: A wisdom psalm addressed to everyone in the world. Its message about wealth and death applies to all people, not only Israel.

f.g: Listen carefully.

chapters.n: Rich and poor, important and ordinary — all need to hear this, because death treats everyone the same.

f.g: Literally “sons of Adam and sons of man” — common folk and nobles.

chapters.n: The psalmist promises to share wisdom he has thought deeply about.

f.g: Thoughtful reflection.

chapters.n: He will listen for God’s insight and then explain a puzzling riddle to the music of a harp.

f.g: A riddle or puzzle — here, why the wicked rich seem to prosper.
Hebrew mashal — a proverb or comparison.

chapters.n: Why should I be afraid when evil people surround me and plot against me?

f.g: Probably “the iniquity of those who dog my heels” — enemies following close behind.

chapters.n: These are people who trust in their wealth and brag about how much they have...
...but no amount of money can buy another person out of death. No one can pay God a ransom for a life.

f.g: Buy back, ransom.

chapters.n: The price of a soul is far too costly — no human could ever pay it. This points to the need for a Redeemer who could pay what we cannot.

f.w: the redemption of their soul is precious
f.g: The ransom for a life is too costly; one must give up on paying it.

chapters.n: No one can pay enough to live forever and never see the grave.

f.g: The pit, decay of the grave.

chapters.n: Everyone can see that wise people die, as do fools; all leave their wealth to someone else.

f.g: Stupid, senseless — like an animal.

chapters.n: The rich imagine their estates will last forever and name their lands after themselves — yet their only lasting home is the grave.

f.w: they call their lands after their own names
f.g: Some ancient versions read “their graves are their homes forever.”

chapters.n: A refrain repeated in verse 20: even a person of high honor doesn’t last; he dies like the animals.

f.g: Does not remain, cannot spend the night — he is only passing through.

chapters.n: This is the path of the self-confident, yet those who follow them still praise their ideas.

f.g: Foolish self-confidence.

chapters.n: Like sheep herded into a pen, they are led into the grave with death as their shepherd. In the morning — a hint of a future day — the upright will rule over them.

f.g: Death shall shepherd them — a dark reversal of Psalm 23.
Perhaps a hint of resurrection or a coming day of vindication.

chapters.n: The great turn of the psalm: no one can ransom himself — but God will ransom me from the grave and take me to himself. This is one of the clearest hopes beyond death in the Old Testament.

f.w: God will redeem my soul from the power of the grave

f.g: He will take me — the same verb used of Enoch being taken.

chapters.n: So don’t be intimidated when someone gets rich and his house grows grand.

f.g: Don’t be overawed or envious.

chapters.n: When he dies, he takes nothing with him; his splendor stays behind.
While alive he congratulated himself, and people praise those who do well for themselves.

f.g: Congratulated himself, considered himself fortunate.

chapters.n: Yet he will join his ancestors in the darkness and never see light again.
The refrain returns with a key word added: a person in honor who lacks understanding is like the beasts. Wisdom — knowing God — is what makes the difference.

f.g: Lacks insight — the added word that distinguishes this from verse 12.

chapters.n: Asaph, one of David’s chief musicians, pictures a great courtroom. God speaks and summons the whole earth, from east to west, as witnesses.

f.w: The mighty God, even the LORD
f.g: Three divine names in Hebrew: El, Elohim, YHWH — a majestic opening.

f.w: from the rising of the sun unto the going down thereof

chapters.n: God shines out from Zion, the most beautiful place, like the sun rising.
God comes with fire and storm, as he did at Sinai. He will not stay silent any longer.

f.w: a fire shall devour before him

chapters.n: He calls heaven and earth as witnesses in his case against his own people.

f.w: He shall call to the heavens from above

chapters.n: “Gather my faithful ones” — those who entered into covenant with God through sacrifice. Latter-day Saints see in this gathering a theme of the last days.

f.w: Gather my saints together unto me
made a covenant with me by sacrifice

chapters.n: Heaven proclaims that God is just — he is the judge himself.
The case begins. God addresses Israel personally: I am your God, and I am testifying against you.

f.g: Give witness in court.

chapters.n: The problem isn’t that they failed to offer sacrifices — they offered them constantly.

f.g: Correct, rebuke.

chapters.n: God doesn’t need any of their bulls or goats.
Every animal already belongs to him — even the cattle grazing on a thousand hills.

f.w: the cattle upon a thousand hills

chapters.n: He knows every bird and wild creature. Nothing in creation is outside his ownership.
Even if God were hungry — which he is not — he wouldn’t need to ask them. The whole world is his.

f.w: the world is mine, and the fulness thereof

chapters.n: A gently ironic question: do I eat meat and drink blood? Sacrifice was never meant to feed God.
What God really wants is a thankful heart and faithfulness to the promises they’ve made.

f.g: Keep the promises you made to God.

chapters.n: And he wants them to call on him in trouble. He will rescue them, and they will give him glory. Relationship matters more than ritual.

f.w: call upon me in the day of trouble

chapters.n: Now God turns to the wicked: what right do you have to recite my laws and talk about my covenant?

f.w: take my covenant in thy mouth

chapters.n: You hate correction and toss my words behind your back.

f.g: Treat them as worthless, throw them away.

chapters.n: When you see a thief, you join him; you keep company with adulterers. These echo the Ten Commandments.
Your mouth is full of evil and your tongue weaves lies.

f.g: Fashions, harnesses.

chapters.n: You sit around slandering your own brother — your mother’s son.
God was silent, and they assumed he was like them — indifferent to sin. Now he will lay out the evidence before their eyes.

f.w: thou thoughtest that I was altogether such an one as thyself

chapters.n: A solemn warning to those who forget God: consider this now, before judgment comes and no one can save you.
The final word: anyone who offers thanks honors God, and anyone who walks the right path will see God’s salvation.

f.g: Sets his way of life in order; “conversation” means conduct.

chapters.n: The heading ties this psalm to David’s repentance after the prophet Nathan confronted him about Bathsheba and Uriah. He appeals not to his own goodness but to God’s loyal love and great mercy.

f.w: Have mercy upon me, O God

f.g: Wipe out, erase — as writing is wiped from a scroll.
Hebrew ḥesed — steadfast, covenant love.

chapters.n: He asks to be washed thoroughly, like scrubbing a stained garment, and cleansed from sin.

f.g: Thoroughly.

chapters.n: David honestly admits what he did; he can’t stop seeing it. Facing sin is the first step of repentance.
David had wronged Bathsheba, Uriah and the nation, yet he sees that every sin is ultimately against God. God is entirely right to judge him.

f.w: Against thee, thee only, have I sinned
that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest

chapters.n: David confesses that sin has been part of his life from the very beginning. Latter-day Saint teaching holds that children are born innocent, so this is best read as a poetic confession of how deep human weakness runs, not a statement that birth itself is sinful.

f.g: Poetic language for the fallen world each person is born into.

chapters.n: God wants honesty deep inside, not just outward appearances, and he can teach wisdom in the hidden heart.
Hyssop was a plant used to sprinkle blood or water in purification rites. David asks to be cleansed as completely as a healed leper — made whiter than snow.

f.g: A small bushy plant used as a sprinkler in cleansing rituals.

chapters.n: Guilt has felt like broken bones. He longs to hear joy again and be healed.

f.w: the bones which thou hast broken
f.g: A picture of the crushing weight of conviction.

chapters.n: He asks God to turn his face away from the sins — not from David himself — and erase them completely.

f.w: Hide thy face from my sins

chapters.n: One of the great prayers of scripture: not just “forgive me,” but “make me new.” The word “create” is the same verb used for God’s creation in Genesis 1 — only God can do this.

f.w: Create in me a clean heart
f.g: Hebrew bara — create — used only of God’s action.
A steadfast, firm spirit.

chapters.n: David fears losing God’s presence and his Holy Spirit. Latter-day revelation teaches that because of the murder of Uriah, David did lose some eternal blessings, which makes this plea especially poignant.

f.w: take not thy holy spirit from me

chapters.n: He longs for the joy he once felt and asks God to hold him up with a willing, generous spirit.

f.w: Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation

f.g: A willing or generous spirit.

chapters.n: Once forgiven, he will help other sinners find their way back. The repentant often become the best teachers of repentance.

f.w: sinners shall be converted unto thee

chapters.n: David names his sin precisely: bloodguilt, the guilt of Uriah’s death. If delivered, he will sing of God’s righteousness.

f.g: Guilt for shedding innocent blood.

chapters.n: Shame had closed his lips. He asks God to open them so he can praise again.
Animal sacrifice alone can’t fix what is broken in him. Something deeper is needed.
What God truly wants is a broken spirit and contrite heart. The risen Christ taught the Nephites that this would replace animal sacrifice.

f.w: a broken and a contrite heart

f.g: Crushed, deeply humbled.

chapters.n: Personal repentance widens into prayer for the whole community: bless Zion and build up Jerusalem’s walls.

f.w: build thou the walls of Jerusalem
f.g: Some think these final verses were added during or after the exile.

chapters.n: When hearts are right, sacrifices offered at the altar become pleasing to God again. Outward worship matters when it flows from inward change.

The heading links this psalm to Doeg the Edomite, who informed Saul that the priests of Nob had helped David, then killed them. David asks the “mighty man” why he brags about evil, when God’s loyal love outlasts it all.

f.g: Spoken with irony — a so-called hero who is really a villain.
Wicked harm, not mere pranks.

chapters.n: His tongue plots destruction and cuts like a razor — slick, sharp and treacherous.
He actually prefers evil to good and lies to truth.

f.w: Thou lovest evil more than good

chapters.n: He loves words that devour and destroy others.

f.g: Words that swallow up and ruin people.

chapters.n: But God will tear him down permanently — snatch him from his tent and uproot him from life, like a tree pulled up by its roots.

f.g: Uproot, as a tree.
This life, the world of the living.

chapters.n: The righteous will see it with awe and laugh — not cruelly, but at how foolish his boasting turned out to be.
Look at the man who wouldn’t make God his fortress, but trusted in his money and grew strong through wickedness.

f.w: trusted in the abundance of his riches

chapters.n: David contrasts himself: the uprooted tree versus a flourishing olive tree planted near God’s house. Olive trees live for centuries and stay green — a picture of lasting life rooted in God’s love.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — covenant love.

chapters.n: He will praise God forever for what he has done and hope in his name among the faithful.

f.g: Hebrew ḥasidim — the faithful, loyal ones.
Hope in your revealed character.

chapters.n: This psalm is nearly identical to Psalm 14; the main difference is that it uses “God” (Elohim) instead of “the LORD.” The fool isn’t unintelligent — he lives as if God doesn’t matter.

f.w: The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God

f.g: Hebrew nabal — morally senseless, not mentally slow.

chapters.n: God looks down from heaven searching for anyone who understands and seeks him.
Everyone has turned back and become corrupt — not a single one does good. Paul quotes these lines to show that all people need God’s grace.

f.w: there is none that doeth good, no, not one

f.g: Corrupt, spoiled like soured milk.

chapters.n: Don’t evildoers understand anything? They devour God’s people as casually as eating bread, and never pray.

f.w: eat up my people as they eat bread

chapters.n: Here this psalm departs most from Psalm 14: it describes enemies terrified even when there was nothing to fear, as God scattered the bones of the army besieging his people.

f.g: Panic without any visible cause — sent by God.
Left their bodies unburied — total defeat.

chapters.n: A longing that salvation would come from Zion. When God restores his people, all Israel will rejoice. Latter-day Saints also see this as a hope fulfilled in the gathering of Israel.

f.g: Restores the fortunes of his people.

chapters.n: According to its heading, David wrote this when the people of Ziph betrayed his hiding place to Saul. He asks God to save him by his name — his revealed character and power.

f.g: By all that God is and has made known of himself.
Vindicate me, defend my cause.

chapters.n: A simple, urgent request to be heard.
Strangers and violent men are hunting for his life; they have no regard for God at all.

f.g: Outsiders — though the Ziphites were Judahites, they acted like foreigners.

f.w: they have not set God before them

chapters.n: The turning point: “Behold!” God is my helper, sustaining my life.
David trusts God to turn the evil back on his enemies and to deal with them in faithfulness.

f.g: In your faithfulness.

chapters.n: He promises a freewill offering — a sacrifice given out of gratitude, not obligation — and praise for God’s good name.

f.g: Offer a freewill offering.

chapters.n: He speaks as if rescue has already happened: God has delivered him, and he has seen his enemies defeated.

f.w: mine eye hath seen his desire upon mine enemies
f.g: I have looked in triumph on my enemies.

f.w: he hath delivered me out of all trouble

chapters.n: David begs God to listen and not to look away from his plea.

f.g: Don’t turn away, don’t ignore me.

chapters.n: He is restless and groaning in his distress.

f.g: I am restless in my troubled thoughts.
Moan, groan aloud.

chapters.n: Enemies are shouting and pressing in, piling trouble on him in their anger.

f.g: Bring trouble down on me, accuse me.

chapters.n: His heart writhes in pain, and the fear of death has fallen on him.
Fear, trembling and horror overwhelm him.
A wish many people share: if only I had wings like a dove, I would fly away and be at peace.

f.w: Oh that I had wings like a dove!

chapters.n: He would flee far off and live in the desert, away from it all.
He’d hurry to a shelter from the raging storm. Escape seems attractive when life feels like a tempest.
He asks God to confuse the enemies’ speech, as at Babel, because the city is full of violence.
Violence and strife patrol the walls day and night like sentries; trouble fills the city.
Ruin is at its center, and fraud never leaves its marketplace.

f.g: The open square or marketplace, where business and justice took place.

chapters.n: The deepest wound: it wasn’t an enemy who insulted him. He could have handled that, or hidden from it.

f.g: Exalt himself, act arrogantly.

chapters.n: It was a peer, a trusted friend and companion. Many connect this with Ahithophel, David’s counselor who joined Absalom’s rebellion.

f.g: My close friend, confidant.

chapters.n: They shared close friendship and even worshipped together, walking to God’s house side by side. That makes the betrayal all the more painful.
In anguish he asks that the traitors go down alive into the grave, as Korah’s rebels did in the wilderness.

f.g: Alive.
Hebrew Sheol, the grave or world of the dead.

chapters.n: “As for me” — David chooses prayer over revenge. He calls on God, confident the Lord will save him.
He prays evening, morning and noon, crying aloud, and God hears. Regular prayer was part of Israel’s devotion.

f.w: Evening, and morning, and at noon

chapters.n: God has rescued him unharmed from the battle, even though many were fighting against him.

f.g: Many were against me — many who fought with me.

chapters.n: God, enthroned from ancient times, will hear and humble them. Because nothing ever changes for them — no trouble ever shakes them — they have no reverence for God.

f.g: God, who has been enthroned from eternity.
They never face setbacks, so they feel no need of God.

chapters.n: The betrayer attacked those at peace with him and broke his solemn promise.

f.g: He violated his pledged word of friendship.

chapters.n: His words were smooth as butter and soft as oil, but war was in his heart — and his words were really swords.
A treasured promise: throw your burden onto the Lord, and he will hold you up. He will never let the righteous be shaken for good. Peter echoed this counsel.

f.w: Cast thy burden upon the LORD

f.g: Literally “what he has given you” — your lot, your load.

chapters.n: God will bring the violent and deceitful down; they won’t live half their days. David ends with a quiet, firm trust.

f.w: shall not live out half their days

chapters.n: The heading places this when the Philistines seized David in Gath. He asks for mercy because enemies keep trampling him day after day.

f.g: Trample or pant after me, eager to destroy.

chapters.n: Many proud enemies attack him every day. He appeals to God Most High.

f.g: Possibly “proudly” — describing how the enemies fight.

chapters.n: A short, honest verse: when I’m afraid, I choose to trust you. Faith doesn’t mean never feeling fear; it means what we do with it.

f.g: Whenever I am afraid.

chapters.n: Here is the refrain (repeated in verses 10–11): trusting God’s word, he won’t fear what mere mortals can do.

f.w: I will not fear what flesh can do unto me

f.g: Mortal, weak humanity.

chapters.n: All day they twist his words and think up ways to hurt him.

f.g: Twist, distort my words.

chapters.n: They band together, lurk in hiding, and watch his every step, waiting to take his life.

f.g: Watch my heels — track my movements.

chapters.n: Will they get away with their evil? David asks God to bring down such nations in his anger.
A beautiful image: God has counted every one of David’s restless wanderings and kept every tear in a bottle. Not one sorrow is forgotten or wasted.

f.w: put thou my tears into thy bottle
f.g: A leather or clay container — God treasures each tear.

f.w: are they not in thy book?

f.g: Count, keep track of.

chapters.n: When he calls, his enemies will retreat. He is sure of one thing: God is on his side.
The refrain returns with both names: in God and in the LORD he praises the word of promise.
Trust replaces fear: what can any human do to him?

f.w: I will not be afraid what man can do unto me

chapters.n: David feels bound by the vows he made to God and will keep them by offering thanks.

f.g: I am obligated by the promises I made to you.

chapters.n: God has rescued him from death and kept his feet from stumbling, so he can walk before God in the light of life.
The heading places David in a cave, hiding from Saul. He takes shelter under God’s wings, like a chick under its mother, until the danger passes.

f.w: in the shadow of thy wings

f.g: Passed by, gone over.

chapters.n: He cries to God Most High, who will complete his purpose for David.

f.g: Fulfills his purpose for me.

chapters.n: God will reach down from heaven and rescue him, sending his loyal love and faithfulness like messengers.

f.g: God’s ḥesed and faithfulness, pictured as two angels sent to help.

chapters.n: David lies down among lion-like men who breathe fire, whose teeth are weapons and whose tongues are sharp swords.

f.g: Ravenous, fiercely eager.

chapters.n: A refrain repeated in verse 11: may God be lifted high above the heavens and his glory fill the earth. In the middle of danger, David thinks of God’s greatness.

f.w: let thy glory be above all the earth

chapters.n: They set a net and dug a pit for him — and fell into it themselves.

f.w: into the midst whereof they are fallen themselves

chapters.n: “My heart is fixed” — steady and firm. Despite everything, he will sing. Verses 7–11 reappear as the opening of Psalm 108.

f.g: Steadfast, firmly established.

chapters.n: He calls his own soul and his instruments to wake up — he will wake the dawn itself with praise.

f.g: My soul, my whole being.
Literally “I will awaken the dawn.”

chapters.n: He will praise God not only in Israel but among all the nations.
God’s loyal love reaches the heavens and his faithfulness the clouds.

f.w: thy mercy is great unto the heavens

chapters.n: The refrain closes the psalm: God be exalted above the heavens, your glory over all the earth.
David challenges the rulers and judges: do you really judge fairly? The word translated “congregation” may instead mean “mighty ones” or “gods” — people in power who should protect justice.

f.g: The Hebrew is uncertain; many read “O gods” or “mighty ones” — rulers acting as judges.

chapters.n: No — in their hearts they plan evil and hand out violence instead of justice, as if weighing it on scales.

f.w: ye weigh the violence of your hands
f.g: Instead of weighing justice on the scales, they deal out violence.

chapters.n: The wicked have gone wrong for as long as anyone can remember, lying from their earliest days. This is poetic exaggeration for deep-rooted corruption.

f.g: A poetic way of saying they have strayed for a long time; scripture also teaches children are born innocent.

chapters.n: Their words are poison like a snake’s — like a cobra that refuses to hear.

f.g: A venomous snake, probably a cobra.

chapters.n: Snake charmers can’t control them, no matter how skilled. These leaders refuse every appeal to conscience.

f.g: Snake charmers, who used music or chants to control snakes.

chapters.n: David asks God to disarm these predators — break the teeth of these young lions so they can’t devour the weak.
May they drain away like water that runs into the ground; may their arrows fall broken.

f.g: Like headless arrows — blunted and useless.

chapters.n: May they vanish like a snail leaving a dissolving trail, or like a stillborn child who never sees daylight. These are vivid images of complete futility.

f.g: Ancient people thought snails melted away as they moved, leaving slime.
A miscarriage or stillbirth.

chapters.n: Faster than a cooking pot can heat over burning thorns, God will sweep them away like a storm. Judgment will come swiftly.

f.w: Before your pots can feel the thorns
f.g: Thorn bushes were quick fuel for cooking fires; this means very suddenly.

chapters.n: The righteous will rejoice when justice comes. The bloody image is battlefield language from the ancient world, expressing total victory of good over evil, not personal cruelty.

f.w: wash his feet in the blood of the wicked
f.g: Ancient war imagery for complete victory.

chapters.n: Then people will say: there really is a reward for the righteous, and there really is a God who judges on earth. Justice vindicates faith.

f.w: there is a reward for the righteous

chapters.n: The heading sets this when Saul sent men to watch David’s house at night to kill him; David escaped through a window with Michal’s help. He asks God to set him safely out of reach.

f.g: Set me on high, out of reach.

chapters.n: He pleads to be saved from evildoers and murderers.

f.g: Men guilty of bloodshed.

chapters.n: Powerful men lie in ambush for him, though he has done nothing to deserve it.

f.g: David protests his innocence toward Saul.

chapters.n: They rush to attack without cause. David asks God to wake up and see what is happening.
He calls on the Lord God of armies to rise up and deal with all the nations and faithless traitors.

f.g: The Lord, commander of heavenly armies.
Here, to come in judgment.

chapters.n: Each evening the attackers return like wild dogs, snarling and prowling around the city. Stray dogs in the ancient Near East were scavengers, not pets.

f.w: make a noise like a dog
f.g: Howl and snarl like pariah dogs.

chapters.n: They spew threats, and their words are swords. They think, “Who will hear us?” — as if God isn’t listening.

f.g: Pour out, spout.

chapters.n: But God laughs at them — their threats are laughable to him.
David waits for God, his strength and his high fortress.

f.g: A high place of safety, a fortress.

chapters.n: God, in his loyal love, will go ahead of him and let him see his enemies defeated.

f.g: In KJV English, “prevent” means go before or meet — not stop.

chapters.n: Surprisingly, David asks God not to kill them quickly, lest the people forget the lesson. Let them wander and fall slowly, as a living reminder.
Let their own proud, lying words trap them.

f.g: Caught by their own arrogance.

chapters.n: Let all the earth know that God rules in Jacob — Israel — and to the ends of the earth.
The image of the prowling dogs returns as a refrain.
Let them roam about for food and growl when they aren’t satisfied.

f.g: Food.
Growl, complain, or stay up all night.

chapters.n: In contrast to the howling dogs at night, David will sing in the morning about God’s strength and love. The night of danger ends in a dawn of praise.
The psalm closes with a refrain of trust, calling God his strength, fortress, and loyal God.

f.g: The God who shows me ḥesed — steadfast love.

chapters.n: The heading ties this psalm to David’s wars with the Arameans and Edom. It opens with national lament: a defeat has made it feel as though God rejected his people. They plead, “Turn back to us.”
The defeat is pictured as an earthquake that split the land. They ask God to repair its cracks.

f.g: Cracks, broken places.

chapters.n: God has given his people hard times, like a drink of wine that makes them stagger.

f.g: Wine that makes one reel — a picture of confusion and judgment.

chapters.n: Yet God has given a banner to his faithful as a rallying point. A banner marked where troops should gather in battle.

f.g: A standard or flag for rallying troops.

chapters.n: So that God’s beloved people may be saved, the psalmist asks God to rescue with his right hand. Verses 5–12 also appear in Psalm 108.
God has spoken from his holy place, like a triumphant warrior dividing up the land. Shechem and Succoth are sites west and east of the Jordan.

f.g: A city in central Canaan where Abraham and Jacob stopped.
A valley east of the Jordan where Jacob built booths.
Measure out, apportion.

chapters.n: God claims Israel’s tribes: Gilead and Manasseh in the east, Ephraim as his helmet, and Judah as his royal scepter.

f.g: My helmet — Ephraim was the strongest northern tribe.
My scepter — the royal tribe of David.

chapters.n: God speaks with scorn of Israel’s enemies: Moab is his washbasin, he throws his sandal onto Edom (claiming ownership), and he shouts over Philistia.

f.g: A washbasin — a lowly household item.
Tossing a sandal onto land was a gesture of claiming it.

chapters.n: Now the king asks: who will lead me into the fortified city of Edom?

f.g: Probably Bozrah or Sela (Petra), Edom’s rocky fortress.

chapters.n: Only God can — the same God who seemed to reject them and didn’t go out with their armies.
Human help is useless; only God can rescue from trouble.

f.w: vain is the help of man

chapters.n: With God we will act bravely, for he will trample our enemies. The psalm moves from defeat to renewed courage.

f.w: Through God we shall do valiantly

chapters.n: David asks God to hear his cry and pay attention to his prayer.

f.g: Pay attention, listen closely.

chapters.n: From far away and with a fainting heart, he asks to be led to a rock higher than himself — a place of safety he can’t climb to on his own. Many see Christ as that rock.

f.w: the rock that is higher than I
From the end of the earth
f.g: From far away — perhaps exile, or the edge of despair.

chapters.n: God has always been his shelter and a strong tower against enemies.
He longs to live in God’s tent forever and find refuge under his wings.

f.g: Shelter, hiding place.
Tent — God’s dwelling place.

chapters.n: God has heard his vows and given him the inheritance promised to those who reverence God.

f.g: Inheritance, possession.

chapters.n: A prayer for the king: may his life be long, spanning many generations. Ultimately this finds fulfillment in Christ, the eternal King.
May the king reign in God’s presence forever, guarded by God’s loyal love and faithfulness.

f.g: God’s ḥesed and faithfulness, pictured as guardians.

chapters.n: Then David will sing praise forever and keep his vows day by day.

f.g: Fulfill my promises.

chapters.n: The heading mentions Jeduthun, a temple musician. David’s soul waits in silence for God alone; his rescue comes only from him. The Hebrew word “only” or “truly” repeats six times in this psalm.

f.g: Literally “is silent” — quietly at rest.
Hebrew ʾak — “only, surely,” a keyword of this psalm.

chapters.n: God alone is his rock, salvation and fortress, so he won’t be badly shaken.
David turns to his attackers: how long will you gang up on one man? You are like a leaning wall or a fence about to collapse.

f.g: A leaning, about-to-fall wall.
Plot harm.

chapters.n: Their only goal is to topple him from his high position. They speak blessings outwardly but curse inside.

f.w: they bless with their mouth, but they curse inwardly

chapters.n: He coaches his own soul: be silent and wait for God alone; your hope comes from him.

f.g: Hope.

chapters.n: The refrain of verse 2 returns, now stronger: not just “not greatly moved” but “not moved” at all.
His salvation and honor rest on God, his mighty rock and refuge.

f.g: My honor, my worth.

chapters.n: He invites everyone to trust God always and pour out their hearts to him. God is a safe place for all of us.

f.w: pour out your heart before him

chapters.n: Humans — whether lowly or important — are just a breath. On a balance scale, they weigh less than air.

f.g: Hebrew hevel — breath, vapor.

f.w: to be laid in the balance

chapters.n: Don’t trust in force or stolen goods. Even if wealth grows honestly, don’t set your heart on it.

f.w: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them

chapters.n: A Hebrew way of saying “I’m certain”: God spoke once, and I heard it twice — power belongs to God.

f.w: God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this
f.g: A numerical saying emphasizing certainty.

chapters.n: Not only power but loyal love belongs to God. He repays everyone according to what they have done.

f.w: thou renderest to every man according to his work

chapters.n: The heading places David in the wilderness of Judah, a dry and desolate region. His physical thirst becomes a picture of his soul’s thirst for God. He seeks God eagerly, at the start of the day.

f.g: I seek you earnestly — the word is related to “dawn.”

chapters.n: He remembers seeing God’s power and glory in the sanctuary and longs to experience it again.

f.g: The holy place — the tabernacle where God’s presence dwelt.

chapters.n: God’s loyal love is better than life itself, so David will praise him. Relationship with God is worth more than survival.

f.w: thy lovingkindness is better than life

chapters.n: For the rest of his life, he will bless God and lift his hands in prayer.

f.g: The ancient posture of prayer and praise.

chapters.n: His soul is satisfied as if after a rich feast. Even in the desert, God feeds him.

f.g: The richest foods — a picture of complete satisfaction.

chapters.n: Lying awake at night, he thinks about God through the night watches.

f.g: The night was divided into watches (shifts) of guard duty.

chapters.n: God has been his help, so he sings for joy in the shelter of his wings.
His soul clings to God, and God’s right hand holds him up — a picture of mutual holding.

f.g: Clings to you, sticks close — the same word as “cleave” in Genesis 2:24.

chapters.n: Those who want to kill him will go down into the depths of the earth — the grave.

f.w: the lower parts of the earth
f.g: The underworld, the realm of the dead.

chapters.n: They will fall in battle and be left for scavengers.

f.g: Jackals, which scavenged battlefields.

chapters.n: The king will rejoice in God, and all who swear by God’s name will celebrate, while liars are silenced.

f.g: Takes oaths in God’s name — that is, is loyal to him.

chapters.n: David asks God to hear his complaint and guard his life from the dread his enemies cause.

f.g: Here, “complaint” — an honest lament poured out to God.

chapters.n: He asks to be hidden from the secret plots and noisy mob of evildoers.

f.g: A tumultuous, scheming crowd.

chapters.n: Their tongues are sharpened like swords, and their cruel words fly like arrows.

f.g: Sharpen.

chapters.n: From hiding they shoot at the innocent without warning and without any fear of consequence.

f.g: The blameless, the person of integrity.

chapters.n: They egg each other on, plan hidden traps, and ask, “Who will ever see?”

f.g: Talk together, conspire.
Secretly.

chapters.n: They work hard devising perfect crimes. Human hearts and minds are deep — and capable of great cunning.
The great reversal: God himself shoots an arrow, and they are suddenly struck — just as they tried to strike the innocent.

f.g: The same words as verse 4, turned back on the attackers.

chapters.n: Their own tongues bring them down, and onlookers shake their heads and back away.

f.w: make their own tongue to fall upon themselves

chapters.n: Everyone will be struck with awe, tell what God has done, and think carefully about it.

f.g: Reflect on with understanding.

chapters.n: The righteous will rejoice, take refuge in the Lord, and celebrate.

f.g: Boast, rejoice.

chapters.n: A harvest thanksgiving. Praise is waiting for God in Zion, ready to be offered, along with vows made in times of need.

f.g: Zion — Jerusalem’s temple mount.
Some render it “praise is fitting for you” or “silence is praise for you.”

chapters.n: God hears prayer, so all people will come to him.

f.g: All humanity.

chapters.n: Sins overwhelm us, but God wipes them away. The word “purge” is related to atonement — covering and cleansing sin.

f.g: Atone for, cover — Hebrew kipper, the root of Yom Kippur (Day of Atonement).

chapters.n: Blessed is the one God invites close to live in his courts. We will be filled with the good things of his holy temple.

f.g: The temple courtyards.

chapters.n: God answers prayers with awesome acts of justice. He is the hope of the whole earth, even distant sailors.

f.g: Awe-inspiring deeds of saving justice.

chapters.n: With his power he set the mountains firmly in place.

f.g: Wearing strength like a belt.

chapters.n: He calms the roaring seas and the uproar of nations alike — Jesus showed this same power on the Sea of Galilee.

f.w: Which stilleth the noise of the seas

chapters.n: People at the ends of the earth stand in awe at God’s signs. From sunrise to sunset, God makes the world sing for joy.

f.g: Signs, wonders.

f.w: the outgoings of the morning and evening
f.g: East and west — where the sun rises and sets.

chapters.n: God visits the earth with rain. The “river of God” — the rains from heaven — waters the grain fields.

f.g: In KJV English, “corn” means grain such as wheat or barley.

chapters.n: He soaks the plowed ridges, levels the furrows, softens the soil with showers, and blesses the sprouts.

f.g: Levels or smooths the plowed rows.

chapters.n: God crowns the year with a bountiful harvest; his cart tracks overflow with abundance as he passes.

f.g: Your wagon tracks drip with richness — as a harvest cart spills grain.

chapters.n: Even desert pastures receive the overflow, and the hills are wrapped in joy.
Meadows are dressed with flocks and valleys draped in grain — the whole landscape shouts and sings. Creation itself joins the praise.

f.w: they shout for joy, they also sing

chapters.n: The whole earth is invited to shout joyfully to God. Praise starts global.
Sing the glory of his name and make his praise splendid.
Tell God how awesome his deeds are. His power is so great his enemies cringe before him.

f.g: Awe-inspiring.
Literally “feign obedience” — cower before him.

chapters.n: All the earth will bow and sing to his name.

f.w: All the earth shall worship thee

chapters.n: “Come and see” — God’s mighty acts on behalf of people are open for all to witness.
He turned the Red Sea into dry ground and the Jordan into a walkway. “There did we rejoice” — later generations share in the joy as if they had been there.

f.w: He turned the sea into dry land

chapters.n: God rules forever and watches over the nations; let no rebel puff himself up.
All peoples are called to bless God and make his praise heard.
He keeps us alive and doesn’t let our feet slip.
God has tested his people, refining them like silver in a furnace. Trials can purify.

f.g: Tested.

chapters.n: He let them be caught in a net and loaded heavy burdens on their backs.

f.g: Backs, hips — the place where loads are carried.

chapters.n: Enemies rode over them; they passed through fire and water — yet God brought them into a place of abundance.

f.w: we went through fire and through water

f.g: A place of abundance, overflowing.

chapters.n: Now one worshipper speaks: I will come to your temple with offerings and keep my vows.
These are the promises he made when he was in trouble — and he means to keep them.
He will bring the best animals, with smoke of rams rising like incense. His gratitude is generous.

f.g: Fattened animals — the best of the flock.
The smoke of burning rams rising like incense.

chapters.n: He invites all who reverence God to come listen to his personal testimony.

f.w: I will declare what he hath done for my soul

chapters.n: He cried out to God, and praise was already on his tongue.

f.g: Highly praised.

chapters.n: If he had cherished sin in his heart, God would not have listened. Sincerity matters in prayer.

f.w: If I regard iniquity in my heart

chapters.n: But God truly heard him and paid attention to his prayer.
Blessed be God, who didn’t reject his prayer or withdraw his loyal love.

f.g: His ḥesed — steadfast, covenant love.

chapters.n: This short psalm echoes the priestly blessing of Aaron: be gracious to us, bless us, make your face shine on us.

f.w: cause his face to shine upon us

chapters.n: Here is the purpose of Israel’s blessing: so that God’s way and saving power become known among all nations. God blesses his people to bless the world.

f.g: Your salvation.

chapters.n: A refrain: let all peoples praise God.
Let the nations sing for joy, because God judges fairly and guides the nations.

f.g: Lead, guide like a shepherd.

chapters.n: The refrain repeats, framing the psalm’s center.
The earth has produced its harvest — a sign of God’s blessing.

f.w: Then shall the earth yield her increase

chapters.n: God will keep blessing us, and the whole world will come to reverence him.

f.w: all the ends of the earth shall fear him

chapters.n: This grand, difficult processional hymn opens with the words Moses spoke whenever the ark set out in the wilderness: let God rise up and scatter his enemies.

f.w: Let God arise, let his enemies be scattered

chapters.n: The wicked vanish before God like smoke in the wind or wax near a flame.

f.w: as wax melteth before the fire

chapters.n: But the righteous rejoice in God’s presence with great gladness.
Sing to the one who rides across the skies — whose name is JAH, a short form of Jehovah.
