f.g: A short form of YHWH (Jehovah), as in “Hallelu-jah” — “praise Jah.”
Hebrew may read “rides through the deserts” or “rides on the clouds.”

chapters.n: Mighty as he is, God cares most tenderly for the vulnerable: he is a father to orphans and defender of widows.

f.g: Defender, champion.

chapters.n: God gives the lonely a family and frees prisoners, but rebels end up in a barren land.

f.w: God setteth the solitary in families
f.g: Gives the lonely a home.

f.w: he bringeth out those which are bound

chapters.n: The psalm recalls God marching ahead of Israel through the wilderness.

f.w: when thou wentest forth before thy people

chapters.n: At his coming the earth quaked and the sky poured rain; Sinai itself shook.
God sent abundant rain to refresh his weary land and people.

f.g: Israel’s land, or the people themselves.

chapters.n: His people settled in the land, and in his goodness God provided for the poor.

f.g: Possibly “your flock” or “your creatures.”

chapters.n: God gave the command, and a great host of women proclaimed the good news of victory. The Hebrew word for “those that published it” is feminine.

f.w: great was the company of those that published it
f.g: The proclaimers are women — like Miriam and the women who celebrated victories.

chapters.n: Enemy kings fled in haste, and women at home divided the loot.

f.g: Quickly.
Plunder from the battle.

chapters.n: A notoriously hard verse. It seems to say that even those who stayed among the sheepfolds will share in rich treasure, pictured as a dove with silver and gold wings.

f.g: Lain among the sheepfolds or hearth-stones — the Hebrew is uncertain.

f.w: wings of a dove covered with silver
f.g: Possibly a prized trophy, or Israel pictured as a dove.

chapters.n: When God scattered the kings, it was like snow falling on Mount Zalmon — perhaps bleached bones, or the glint of scattered weapons.

f.g: Zalmon, a hill near Shechem.

chapters.n: Mount Bashan, the majestic many-peaked range to the northeast, is described as a mountain of God.

f.g: A fertile, high region east of the Sea of Galilee; Mount Hermon’s range.

chapters.n: The great mountains look on in jealousy, because God chose little Mount Zion as his home forever. God’s choice, not size, makes a place holy.

f.g: Why look with envy?

f.w: the LORD will dwell in it for ever

chapters.n: God’s heavenly chariots number in the countless thousands; the Lord comes from Sinai into his sanctuary.

f.w: The chariots of God are twenty thousand

chapters.n: God ascends Zion like a victorious king leading captives and receiving tribute. Paul applied this verse to Christ, who ascended to heaven and gave gifts to his Church.

f.w: Thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive

f.g: Received tribute among people; Ephesians reads “gave gifts unto men.”

chapters.n: Blessed is the Lord who carries our burdens every day — or loads us with blessings. Either way, he is our salvation.

f.g: May also be read “daily bears our burden.”

chapters.n: Our God is a God who saves, and escape from death belongs to him alone.

f.g: The ways of escape from death.

chapters.n: God will crush the heads of enemies who keep walking in their sins.

f.g: Long hair may signal a warrior’s vow or pride.

chapters.n: God says he will bring his enemies back from wherever they flee — from the mountains of Bashan or the depths of the sea — to face justice.

f.w: I will bring again from Bashan

chapters.n: Ancient battlefield language for total victory over evil.
Now a procession appears: everyone watches God, the King, march into the sanctuary.

f.g: Processions.

chapters.n: Singers lead, musicians follow, and young women play tambourines in the middle.

f.g: Hand drums or tambourines.

chapters.n: Bless God in the great assemblies, you who descend from Israel’s fountain — Jacob.

f.g: The source of Israel — Jacob, the ancestor of the tribes.

chapters.n: The tribes march in: little Benjamin first (Israel’s first king, Saul, came from it), then Judah’s leaders, and northern tribes Zebulun and Naphtali.

f.g: The smallest tribe, descended from Jacob’s youngest son.

chapters.n: Your God has ordained your strength; show your power again, O God, as you have before.
Because of the temple in Jerusalem, foreign kings will bring gifts to God.

f.w: shall kings bring presents unto thee

chapters.n: God is asked to rebuke the “beast of the reeds” (perhaps Egypt) and the herds of bull-like nations until they bring silver in tribute. Scatter those who love war.

f.g: Literally “the beast of the reeds” — possibly the crocodile or hippopotamus, a symbol of Egypt.

f.w: scatter thou the people that delight in war

chapters.n: Envoys will come from Egypt, and Ethiopia will reach out its hands to God — a vision of distant nations turning to the Lord.

f.w: Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God

f.g: Hebrew Cush — the land south of Egypt.

chapters.n: All kingdoms of the earth are invited to sing to the Lord.
He rides across the ancient heavens and thunders with a mighty voice.

f.w: he doth send out his voice

chapters.n: Acknowledge God’s power: his majesty is over Israel and his strength is in the skies.

f.g: Give credit, acknowledge.

chapters.n: God is awesome from his sanctuary, and he gives strength to his people. The psalm closes simply: “Blessed be God.”

f.w: giveth strength and power unto his people

chapters.n: After Psalm 22, this is the psalm most often quoted in the New Testament about Jesus’ suffering. David opens drowning in trouble: the water has risen to his neck.

f.w: the waters are come in unto my soul
f.g: “Soul” here can mean neck or throat — the water is up to his neck.

chapters.n: He is sinking in thick mud with no footing, and floods are washing over him.
He has cried until he is exhausted and hoarse, and his eyes grow dim from watching for God to act.

f.g: My eyes grow weak from looking and waiting.

chapters.n: Those who hate him without reason outnumber the hairs on his head. Jesus quoted this line about the hatred he faced. He is forced to pay back what he never stole.

f.w: They that hate me without a cause
then I restored that which I took not away
f.g: He was made to repay for things he hadn’t taken — falsely accused.

chapters.n: David doesn’t claim to be sinless; God knows his foolish moments. This verse reminds us the psalm first belongs to a real, imperfect man before it points to the sinless Christ.

f.w: my sins are not hid from thee

chapters.n: He asks that his troubles not cause other believers to lose faith or be embarrassed.

f.g: Disgraced, discouraged.

chapters.n: He is mocked because of his loyalty to God.

f.w: for thy sake I have borne reproach

chapters.n: Even his own brothers treat him like a stranger. Jesus’ own brothers did not at first believe in him.

f.w: I am become a stranger unto my brethren

chapters.n: His passion for God’s house consumes him. John recalled this verse when Jesus cleansed the temple, and Paul applied the second half to Christ bearing the insults aimed at God.

f.w: the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up
the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me

chapters.n: When he wept and fasted in humility, people mocked him for it.

f.g: Humbled himself by fasting.

chapters.n: When he wore mourning clothes, he became a joke to them.

f.g: A byword, an object of mockery.

chapters.n: Leaders sitting at the city gate gossiped about him, and drunkards sang songs mocking him.

f.w: They that sit in the gate
f.g: Elders and officials — the gate was where business and justice happened.

chapters.n: “But as for me” — he turns to prayer, trusting this is the right time and appealing to God’s abundant loyal love.
He asks to be pulled from the mud and the deep waters.
Don’t let the flood sweep me away or the pit close its mouth over me — like a well capped with a stone.

f.w: let not the pit shut her mouth upon me
f.g: A picture of being sealed in a well or grave.

chapters.n: He bases his appeal on God’s goodness and many tender mercies.

f.g: Deep compassion, like a mother’s love.

chapters.n: Don’t hide from me — I’m in trouble; answer quickly.
Come close to me and redeem my life.

f.g: Ransom, rescue as a near relative would.

chapters.n: God knows all the insults and shame he has endured; every enemy is in full view.
Insults have broken his heart. He looked for sympathy and comfort but found none — words that echo the loneliness of Christ in Gethsemane and on the cross.

f.w: for comforters, but I found none

chapters.n: Instead of food they gave him poison, and for his thirst, sour wine. The Gospels record that at the cross Jesus was offered wine mixed with gall and given vinegar to drink.

f.w: They gave me also gall for my meat
in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink

f.g: A bitter, poisonous herb.

chapters.n: David now prays for justice on his tormentors: let their feasts become traps. Paul quoted verses 22–23 about those in Israel who rejected Christ.

f.w: Let their table become a snare before them

chapters.n: Let them be blinded and weakened — their strength shaking.

f.g: The seat of strength.

chapters.n: He asks God to pour out his anger on them.

f.g: Righteous anger.

chapters.n: May their homes be deserted. Peter applied this verse to Judas after his betrayal.
They pursue someone God has already afflicted and talk mockingly about his pain.
Let them pile guilt upon guilt and never share in God’s righteousness. These angry prayers leave judgment in God’s hands rather than taking revenge personally.
May their names be erased from the book of life and not recorded with the righteous.
“But I am poor and in pain” — he asks God’s salvation to lift him to safety.

f.g: Place me out of reach, on a secure height.

chapters.n: The psalm turns to praise: he will sing and give thanks to God.

f.g: Make great, honor.

chapters.n: Grateful praise pleases God more than offering a full-grown bull.
The humble will see and rejoice; those who seek God will have their hearts revived.
The Lord listens to the needy and doesn’t look down on those imprisoned for his sake.

f.g: Those held captive, perhaps for their faith.

chapters.n: All creation — sky, earth, sea and every creature — is called to praise.
God will rescue Zion and rebuild Judah’s towns so his people can settle there.
The children of God’s servants will inherit it, and those who love his name will live there.

f.w: The seed also of his servants shall inherit it

chapters.n: This short psalm repeats Psalm 40:13–17 almost word for word, as a stand-alone urgent prayer. The heading says it is “to bring to remembrance” — perhaps to remind God, or to accompany a memorial offering.

f.w: Make haste, O God, to deliver me

chapters.n: May those trying to take his life be frustrated, confused and driven back.

f.g: Thrown into confusion.

chapters.n: May the mockers who say “Aha, aha!” be turned back by their own shame.

f.g: A gloating taunt.

chapters.n: In contrast, may all who seek God rejoice and keep saying, “God is great!”
He admits his need and asks God to hurry — don’t delay! The prayer ends without resolution, but with trust.

f.g: Do not delay.

chapters.n: This psalm is the prayer of an older person who has trusted God all his life. It opens much like Psalm 31: may my trust never end in disappointment.

f.w: In thee, O LORD, do I put my trust

f.g: Shame, disgrace.

chapters.n: He asks God, who always does right, to rescue him and lean in to listen.

f.g: Bend down to hear.

chapters.n: He wants God to be a fortress home he can always run to. God has already given the command to save him.

f.g: A rock of refuge, a dwelling of safety.

chapters.n: He asks to be freed from the grip of cruel and unjust people.
God has been his hope and trust since he was young.

f.w: thou art my trust from my youth

chapters.n: Even before birth, God held him. A lifetime of care is reason for a lifetime of praise.

f.w: By thee have I been holden up from the womb

f.g: Womb.

chapters.n: Many people look at his life and see a portent — either a warning of disaster or a wonder of God’s protection. Either way, God is his refuge.

f.g: A sign, a portent — something people stare at.

chapters.n: He wants his mouth to be full of praise all day long.
A heartfelt plea of old age: don’t cast me aside when I’m old and my strength is gone.

f.w: Cast me not off in the time of old age

chapters.n: Enemies talk about him and plot together.
They think he is an easy target now: “God has left him — chase him down; no one will save him.”
He asks God to stay close and hurry to help.

f.w: O God, be not far from me

chapters.n: May his accusers be put to shame and wrapped in disgrace.
Whatever happens, he will keep hoping and praise God more and more. Faith can grow, not shrink, with age.
He will tell of God’s saving acts all day, though they are beyond counting.

f.w: I know not the numbers thereof
f.g: They are too many to count.

chapters.n: He will go forward in God’s strength and speak of God’s righteousness — God’s alone.

f.w: I will go in the strength of the Lord GOD

chapters.n: God has taught him since youth, and he has spent his life proclaiming God’s wonders.
Now, gray-haired, he asks God to stay with him until he can pass his testimony on to the next generation. Older believers have a unique calling to share their faith with the young.

f.w: until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation

chapters.n: God’s righteousness reaches the heavens; he has done great things. Who is like him?
God has let him see many hard troubles, yet he trusts God will revive him and raise him from the depths. Many hear a hint of resurrection here.

f.g: Revive, bring back to life.

f.w: from the depths of the earth

chapters.n: God will restore his honor and comfort him again on every side.
He will praise God with harp and lyre. He calls God “the Holy One of Israel” — a title Isaiah loved and used often.

f.g: A stringed instrument like a lyre.

chapters.n: His lips will shout for joy and his redeemed soul will sing.

f.w: my soul, which thou hast redeemed

chapters.n: All day his tongue will speak of God’s justice, because those who wanted to harm him have been shamed.
Headed “for Solomon,” this is a prayer for the king and his heir: give him your sense of justice, O God. Ancient readers and Christians alike saw in it a portrait of the ideal King, the Messiah.

f.g: The royal heir — traditionally Solomon, son of David.
Just decisions; the wisdom to rule fairly.

chapters.n: May he judge God’s people rightly and treat the poor fairly. A king’s true test is how he treats the weak.

f.w: He shall judge thy people with righteousness

chapters.n: Under a just king, even the mountains and hills seem to yield peace and prosperity.

f.g: Hebrew shalom — wholeness, well-being, prosperity.

chapters.n: He will defend the poor, save the children of the needy, and crush the oppressor.
May people reverence God for as long as the sun and moon last — through every generation.

f.w: as long as the sun and moon endure

chapters.n: A good ruler is like gentle rain on a freshly cut field — refreshing and life-giving.

f.w: He shall come down like rain upon the mown grass

chapters.n: In his reign the righteous will thrive, with peace lasting until the moon is no more.
His rule will stretch from sea to sea and from the river (the Euphrates) to the ends of the earth. Zechariah repeats this of the coming King.

f.g: The Euphrates, Israel’s ideal northeastern border.

chapters.n: Desert tribes will bow before him, and his enemies will lie face down in the dust.

f.g: An image of total submission.

chapters.n: Kings from far-off lands will bring tribute. Tarshish lay far to the west; Sheba and Seba to the south. The visit of the Queen of Sheba and the wise men’s gifts to Jesus echo this.

f.g: A wealthy kingdom in southern Arabia.

chapters.n: All kings will bow before him and all nations serve him — a promise fully realized only in Christ’s reign.

f.w: all kings shall fall down before him

chapters.n: Why he deserves this honor: he rescues the needy who cry for help and the poor who have no one else.
He has compassion on the weak and saves their lives.
He redeems them from oppression and violence, and their lives are precious to him. To this king, no poor person is expendable.

f.w: precious shall their blood be in his sight

chapters.n: Long live the king! May he receive gold from Sheba, be prayed for always, and blessed every day.

f.g: Like “Long live the king!”

chapters.n: Grain will grow abundantly even on mountaintops, waving like the forests of Lebanon, and cities will thrive like grass.

f.g: Grain.
Rustle like Lebanon’s cedar forests.

chapters.n: His name will last forever, and all nations will be blessed through him — fulfilling God’s promise to Abraham.

f.w: men shall be blessed in him

chapters.n: Verses 18–19 are a doxology closing Book Two of the Psalms (42–72). Only God does truly wondrous things.
May his glorious name be blessed forever and his glory fill the whole earth. Amen and Amen.

f.w: let the whole earth be filled with his glory

chapters.n: An editor’s note: “The prayers of David son of Jesse are ended.” It marks the end of an earlier collection, though more Davidic psalms appear later in the book.

f.g: David’s father, from Bethlehem.

chapters.n: Book Three of the Psalms opens with Asaph, a chief musician of David’s time, stating the truth he nearly lost hold of: God really is good to the pure in heart.

f.w: such as are of a clean heart

f.g: Surely, indeed — a conclusion reached after struggle.

chapters.n: “But as for me” — he confesses that his faith almost slipped out from under him.

f.w: my steps had well nigh slipped
f.g: My feet almost lost their footing.

chapters.n: The cause: he grew envious when he saw arrogant, wicked people doing well. This is one of scripture’s most honest treatments of a common struggle.

f.w: I was envious at the foolish

f.g: The boastful, arrogant.

chapters.n: They seemed to live without pain and die without struggle; their bodies were healthy and strong.

f.w: there are no bands in their death
f.g: They have no pangs — no struggles, even at death.

chapters.n: They didn’t seem to have the troubles everyone else has.
So they wear pride like a necklace and violence like clothing — proudly displayed.

f.w: pride compasseth them about as a chain
f.g: Pride is their necklace.

chapters.n: Their eyes bulge from overeating; they have more than they could ever imagine wanting.

f.g: Excess, luxury.

chapters.n: They mock and speak with malice, threatening oppression from their lofty position.

f.g: Talk down arrogantly from on high.

chapters.n: Their mouths claim heaven and their tongues swagger across the earth — no limit to their arrogance.
Even God’s own people turn toward them and drink in their words as if from an overflowing cup. The Hebrew is difficult here.

f.w: waters of a full cup are wrung out to them
f.g: They soak up abundant water — likely, they eagerly accept the arrogant’s message.

chapters.n: The arrogant say, “How could God know? Does the Most High even notice?”
Here they are: wicked, always comfortable, always getting richer.
The low point: Asaph wonders if keeping his heart pure and his hands clean has been pointless.

f.w: I have cleansed my heart in vain

chapters.n: Meanwhile he suffers all day and is disciplined every morning.

f.g: Disciplined, corrected.

chapters.n: Yet he realizes that if he spoke this way openly, he would betray the community of believers. He keeps his doubts from harming others.

f.w: offend against the generation of thy children
f.g: Betray or mislead God’s people.

chapters.n: When he tried to figure it out on his own, it only wore him out.

f.g: A weary burden, too hard.

chapters.n: The turning point of the psalm: in God’s sanctuary, he finally understood how the story ends for the wicked. Perspective often comes in the house of the Lord.

f.w: Until I went into the sanctuary of God

chapters.n: God has set the wicked on slippery ground; they are headed for ruin. Asaph’s feet nearly slipped (verse 2), but theirs certainly will.
How suddenly they are ruined, swept away by terrors!
Their success is like a dream that vanishes when one wakes. When God rises up, their image dissolves.

f.w: As a dream when one awaketh

chapters.n: Looking back, Asaph admits his bitterness had soured his heart and stung his inner self.

f.g: Kidneys — the seat of deep emotions.
Pierced, stung.

chapters.n: He was senseless, acting like a dumb animal before God.

f.g: Like a brute animal without understanding.

chapters.n: “Nevertheless” — even then, God never let go. Asaph realizes God had been holding his right hand all along.

f.w: thou hast holden me by my right hand

chapters.n: God will guide him with counsel in this life and afterward receive him into glory — one of the Old Testament’s clearest hopes of life with God after death.
The heart of the psalm: whom do I have in heaven but you? And on earth, there is nothing I desire besides you. Wealth no longer looks so appealing.

f.w: Whom have I in heaven but thee?

chapters.n: His body and heart may fail, but God is his strength and his inheritance forever.

f.g: My share, inheritance — as the Levites had God instead of land.

chapters.n: Those who wander far from God will perish; those who are unfaithful to him will be destroyed.

f.g: Be unfaithful — scripture often pictures idolatry as betraying a marriage covenant.

chapters.n: His conclusion: for me, it is good to be near God. He has made the Lord his refuge so he can tell of all God’s works.

f.w: it is good for me to draw near to God

chapters.n: A lament after the temple’s destruction — most likely by Babylon in 587 BC. Why has God rejected his flock forever? Why is his anger smoking against them?

f.g: Fume — an image of burning anger.

chapters.n: Remember your people, bought long ago and redeemed as your own tribe, and Mount Zion, where you lived.

f.g: The tribe that is your own possession.

chapters.n: Come walk through the endless ruins; see what the enemy did to the sanctuary.

f.g: Hurry, come and look.

chapters.n: The enemies roared in the place where God met his people, and set up their own banners as symbols of victory.

f.g: Military standards or banners.
Meeting place — the temple.

chapters.n: They hacked like woodsmen swinging axes in a thick forest.
The beautiful carved wood of the temple was smashed with axes and hammers.

f.g: The temple’s carved wood paneling.

chapters.n: They set fire to the sanctuary and leveled the place where God’s name dwelt.

f.w: They have cast fire into thy sanctuary
the dwelling place of thy name

chapters.n: Their plan was to crush everything; they burned all of God’s meeting places throughout the land.

f.g: Meeting places — not the later synagogues, but sites where God was worshipped.

chapters.n: Worst of all: no signs, no prophet, no one who knows how long this will last. Spiritual silence is its own kind of loss.

f.w: there is no more any prophet

chapters.n: How long, O God, will the enemy mock you and insult your name?

f.g: Speak contemptuously of.

chapters.n: Why do you keep your hand tucked in your robe? Take it out and act!

f.w: pluck it out of thy bosom
f.g: Draw your hand out of the fold of your garment — stop holding back.

chapters.n: The prayer turns to remembrance: God has been King from ancient times, bringing salvation throughout the earth.
God split the sea and crushed the sea monsters — recalling both the Exodus and the ancient picture of God taming the chaotic waters at creation.

f.g: Sea monsters — symbols of chaos and of Egypt.

chapters.n: He crushed the heads of Leviathan, the great sea monster, and gave it as food to desert creatures.

f.g: A legendary sea monster, symbol of chaos and evil powers.

chapters.n: God opened springs and streams and dried up rivers — as at the rock in the wilderness and the crossing of the Jordan.
Day and night both belong to God; he made the sun and the light.

f.w: The day is thine, the night also is thine

chapters.n: He set the boundaries of the earth and made the seasons.
So, Lord, remember how the enemy has mocked you and foolish people have insulted your name.
Don’t hand your helpless dove over to wild beasts; don’t forget your afflicted people forever.

f.g: A gentle, defenseless bird — an image of Israel.

chapters.n: Remember your covenant, for the dark corners of the land are full of violence. The covenant is the basis of their hope.
Don’t let the oppressed go away disappointed; let the poor and needy praise you.
Rise up, O God, and defend your own cause — it is your name being mocked.

f.g: Take up your own case in court.

chapters.n: Don’t ignore the uproar of your enemies, which keeps getting louder. The psalm ends without an answer — a lament still waiting.

f.g: Uproar, noise.

chapters.n: The congregation gives thanks twice over, because God’s name — his presence — is near, as his wonderful deeds show.
Now God himself speaks: when the time I have set arrives, I will judge with perfect fairness. God, not humans, chooses the moment of justice.

f.w: When I shall receive the congregation
f.g: Better, “When I choose the appointed time.”

chapters.n: Even if the earth and its people seem to melt and totter, God holds its pillars steady.

f.w: I bear up the pillars of it

chapters.n: God warns the boastful: stop bragging. To the wicked: don’t raise your horn.

f.g: An animal’s horn — a symbol of strength and pride.

chapters.n: Don’t lift your horn so high or speak with stubborn arrogance.

f.g: Stubborn pride, like an ox that won’t bend to the yoke.

chapters.n: Lifting up — success and honor — doesn’t come from any direction on earth. (The north isn’t mentioned; some think it is left for God’s own dwelling.)

f.g: Lifting up, exaltation.

chapters.n: God is the judge: he lowers one person and raises another. True honor comes from him.

f.w: he putteth down one, and setteth up another

chapters.n: God holds a cup of foaming, spiced wine — the cup of his judgment. The wicked will have to drink it to the last bitter drop.

f.g: The cup of God’s wrath — a common image of judgment.
The thick sediment at the bottom of a cup.

chapters.n: “But I” — the psalmist will declare God’s deeds forever and sing to the God of Jacob.
God will cut off the proud strength of the wicked and lift up the strength of the righteous.

f.w: the horns of the righteous shall be exalted

chapters.n: A song of Zion celebrating God’s victory over an enemy army. God has made himself known in Judah, and his name is great in Israel. Many link it with the defeat of Assyria in Hezekiah’s day.
His tent is in Salem — an old name for Jerusalem — and his dwelling in Zion.

f.g: An ancient name for Jerusalem, where Melchizedek was king.
Literally “lair” or “booth” — continuing the lion imagery.

chapters.n: There God shattered the enemy’s flaming arrows, shields and swords — he ended the war itself.

f.g: Literally “the flashes of the bow” — fiery arrows.

chapters.n: God is radiant and majestic — greater than the mountains where predators hunt their prey.

f.g: Mountains full of game — or the enemy’s mountain strongholds.

chapters.n: The bravest warriors were plundered; they fell into the sleep of death and couldn’t lift a hand.

f.g: Plundered, stripped.
They have died.

chapters.n: At God’s rebuke, horses and chariot riders were stunned into deathly sleep.
God alone is to be reverenced. Who can stand before him when he is angry?

f.w: who may stand in thy sight

chapters.n: God pronounced judgment from heaven, and the earth fell silent in awe.
He rose to judge in order to save all the humble of the earth. God’s judgment is for rescue.

f.g: The humble, the oppressed.

chapters.n: Even human fury ends up bringing God praise, and he restrains whatever wrath remains. God can turn even opposition to his purposes.

f.w: the wrath of man shall praise thee

chapters.n: Make vows to the Lord and keep them; let the surrounding nations bring gifts to the one who deserves reverence.
God humbles the pride of princes and is awesome to the kings of the earth.

f.w: cut off the spirit of princes
f.g: Breaks the arrogance of rulers.

chapters.n: Asaph cried out to God aloud, and God listened. The psalm then explains the long night that led to this point.
In trouble he sought the Lord; all night his hands were stretched out in prayer, and nothing could comfort him.

f.w: my sore ran in the night
f.g: Literally “my hand was stretched out in the night” — continual prayer.

f.w: my soul refused to be comforted

chapters.n: Strangely, thinking of God made him groan; his meditation only left him faint. Sometimes faith feels like a struggle before it brings peace.

f.g: I mused, meditated with sighs.

chapters.n: God kept him from sleeping, and he was too upset even to talk.

f.g: You keep my eyelids open.

chapters.n: He thought about the past — the old days, years long gone.
He remembered the songs he once sang at night, and searched his own heart for answers.

f.g: Talk, reason.

chapters.n: Then come six painful questions. First: has the Lord rejected us forever? Will he never again show favor?
Has his loyal love vanished? Has his promise failed for all time?

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — steadfast covenant love.
Completely gone.

chapters.n: Has God forgotten how to be gracious? Has anger shut off his compassion? The questions themselves imply the answer — no, he hasn’t.

f.w: Hath God forgotten to be gracious?

chapters.n: The turning point: “This is my weakness” — or, “this is my grief.” Then he chooses to remember the years when God’s right hand acted for his people.

f.g: This is my sickness — or, “my grief is that God’s right hand has changed.” The Hebrew can be read both ways.

chapters.n: He resolves to remember God’s deeds and ancient wonders. Memory becomes medicine for despair.

f.w: I will remember the works of the LORD

chapters.n: He will meditate on all God has done and talk about it.
God’s way is holy. No god is as great as ours.

f.g: Or “in holiness.”

chapters.n: God works wonders and has shown his power among the nations.
With his strong arm he redeemed the descendants of Jacob and Joseph — all Israel — from Egypt.

f.w: the sons of Jacob and Joseph
f.g: Joseph is mentioned because his sons Ephraim and Manasseh became major tribes.

f.w: Thou hast with thine arm redeemed thy people

chapters.n: Now the Red Sea crossing is retold: the waters saw God and writhed in fear; the depths shook.
Clouds poured rain, thunder rolled, and lightning arrows flashed.

f.g: Lightning bolts.

chapters.n: Thunder rumbled in the whirlwind, lightning lit the world, and the earth trembled.
God’s path went straight through the sea, yet no one could see his footprints. He was at work even when unseen — a comfort for anyone who feels God is absent.

f.g: His footprints were unseen, though he was truly present.

chapters.n: The psalm ends quietly: God led his people like a flock through Moses and Aaron. The great God of storms is also a gentle shepherd who works through his servants.

f.w: by the hand of Moses and Aaron

chapters.n: Asaph speaks like a teacher gathering his people for a history lesson. This long psalm retells Israel’s story so the next generation won’t repeat their ancestors’ mistakes.

f.g: Hebrew torah — teaching or instruction, not only legal code.

chapters.n: He will speak in a parable and explain puzzling lessons from the past. Matthew saw Jesus’ teaching in parables as fulfilling this verse.

f.w: I will open my mouth in a parable

f.g: Riddles, lessons that need explaining.

chapters.n: These are stories they had heard and learned from their own parents.
We won’t hide them from our children, but will tell the next generation of the Lord’s power and wonders. Passing on faith is a sacred duty.

f.w: We will not hide them from their children

chapters.n: God gave Israel his testimony and law, commanding parents to teach them to their children.

f.g: God’s solemn decrees or witness.

f.w: make them known to their children

chapters.n: Then children not yet born would learn them and teach them to their own children — a chain of faith across generations.
The goal: that each generation would trust God, remember his works, and keep his commandments.
And so they wouldn’t be like their ancestors — stubborn, rebellious, unsteady in heart and spirit.
Ephraim, the leading northern tribe, is the first example: though well armed, they turned and ran in battle — a picture of spiritual retreat.

f.g: The largest northern tribe, often standing for the whole northern kingdom.

chapters.n: They broke God’s covenant and refused to live by his law.
They forgot the miracles God had shown them. Forgetting is the root problem in this whole psalm.
God did marvels in Egypt, in the region of Zoan, before their very eyes.

f.g: An important city in the Nile delta (Greek Tanis).

chapters.n: He split the sea, led them through, and piled the waters up like walls.
He guided them with a cloud by day and fire by night.
He split rocks in the desert and gave them water as abundant as the ocean depths.

f.w: He clave the rocks in the wilderness

chapters.n: He brought streams out of rock, flowing like rivers.
Yet they kept sinning, rebelling against the Most High in the desert.

f.g: Rebelling against, defying.

chapters.n: They tested God by demanding the food they craved.

f.g: Put God to the test, challenged him.
Food.

chapters.n: They spoke against God: “Can God really set a table in the wilderness?” Doubt dressed up as a question.

f.w: Can God furnish a table in the wilderness?

chapters.n: “Sure, he struck the rock and water gushed out — but can he give bread and meat too?” Past miracles didn’t produce trust.
The Lord heard and was angry; his anger burned like fire against Israel.

f.w: a fire was kindled against Jacob

chapters.n: The reason: they didn’t believe God or trust his power to save. Unbelief is the core sin here.
Even though he had commanded the skies and opened heaven’s doors...
...and rained down manna for them to eat — grain from heaven. Jesus said he himself is the true bread from heaven.

f.g: Grain from heaven.

chapters.n: People ate the bread of angels — food sent from heaven — and he gave them plenty.

f.g: Bread of the mighty ones — heavenly food.

chapters.n: God stirred the east and south winds...
...and rained down meat on them like dust — birds as countless as sand on the seashore.

f.g: The quail God sent in the wilderness.

chapters.n: He dropped them right in the middle of the camp, all around their tents.
They ate until stuffed; God gave them what they craved.
But they didn’t turn from their craving. While the meat was still in their mouths...

f.g: Separated from their craving.

chapters.n: ...God’s anger struck and killed their strongest young men. The place was later named “graves of craving.”

f.w: The wrath of God came upon them

chapters.n: Even so, they kept sinning and didn’t believe despite all his wonders.
So God let their days vanish like a breath and their years end in sudden terror — the wilderness generation died without entering the land.

f.g: A breath, vapor.

chapters.n: Whenever God struck them, they came looking for him again, eager to return.

f.g: Sought earnestly.

f.w: When he slew them, then they sought him

chapters.n: They remembered that God was their rock and their Redeemer.

f.g: Hebrew goʾel — kinsman-redeemer who rescues family.

chapters.n: But their return was mostly talk — flattering words and lies.
Their hearts weren’t truly loyal, and they didn’t stay faithful to his covenant.

f.w: their heart was not right with him

chapters.n: Yet God, full of compassion, forgave them and didn’t destroy them. Again and again he held back his anger. Mercy keeps winning in this story.

f.w: being full of compassion, forgave their iniquity

chapters.n: He remembered they were only mortal — like a breeze that blows by and doesn’t return.

f.w: he remembered that they were but flesh

chapters.n: How often they rebelled in the wilderness and grieved him!
Again and again they tested God and pained the Holy One of Israel.

f.g: Provoked, pained; some translate “set limits on.”

chapters.n: They forgot his power and the day he rescued them from the enemy.
Now the psalm recalls the plagues of Egypt — the signs God worked in the region of Zoan.
He turned the Nile and its canals to blood so the Egyptians couldn’t drink.
He sent swarms of flies to devour them and frogs to ruin them.

f.g: Various.

chapters.n: He handed their crops over to caterpillars and locusts.
He destroyed their vines with hail and their sycamore-fig trees with frost.

f.g: Sycamore-figs, an important food tree in Egypt.

chapters.n: He gave their cattle to the hail and their flocks to lightning.
He unleashed his fierce anger on them — a band of destroying angels.

f.g: Messengers of disaster — angels bringing calamity, not wicked spirits.

chapters.n: He cleared a path for his anger and gave them over to plague.

f.g: Plague, deadly disease.

chapters.n: He struck every firstborn in Egypt, the pride of their strength in the tents of Ham.

f.w: smote all the firstborn in Egypt

f.g: Son of Noah, regarded as ancestor of Egypt.

chapters.n: But he led his own people out like a shepherd guiding sheep through the wilderness.
He led them safely so they had nothing to fear, while the sea swallowed their enemies.
He brought them to his holy land, to the hill country his power had won.

f.g: The hill country of Canaan, or Mount Zion.

chapters.n: He drove out nations before them, measured out their inheritance, and settled the tribes in their homes.

f.w: divided them an inheritance by line
f.g: Measured out land with a surveying cord.

chapters.n: Yet in the land they again tested and rebelled against God, and didn’t keep his decrees.

f.g: God’s solemn decrees.

chapters.n: They turned away like their fathers, as unreliable as a warped bow that misses its mark.

f.g: A slack or warped bow that won’t shoot straight.

chapters.n: They angered him with their hilltop shrines and stirred his jealousy with carved idols.

f.g: Hilltop shrines, often used for idol worship.

chapters.n: God heard and was angry, and strongly rejected Israel.
He abandoned the tabernacle at Shiloh, where he had dwelt among people. Jeremiah later warned Jerusalem to remember Shiloh.

f.g: Shiloh was Israel’s worship center in the days of Eli and young Samuel.

chapters.n: He allowed the ark — symbol of his strength and glory — to be captured by the Philistines.

f.w: his glory into the enemy's hand

chapters.n: He gave his people over to the sword and was angry with his inheritance.
Fire consumed the young men, and the young women had no wedding songs.

f.w: their maidens were not given to marriage
f.g: Literally “had no wedding song” — there were no grooms left.

chapters.n: Their priests fell in battle, and their widows couldn’t even mourn. Eli’s sons were killed, and Phinehas’s widow died in childbirth.

f.w: Their priests fell by the sword

chapters.n: Then the Lord woke as if from sleep, like a warrior roused and shouting. A bold image: God was never really asleep, but it felt that way.
He drove his enemies back and put them to lasting shame — perhaps recalling the plagues that struck the Philistines while they held the ark.

f.w: smote his enemies in the hinder parts

chapters.n: He passed over Joseph’s tribe — Ephraim, where Shiloh lay — as the site of his sanctuary.

f.g: Shiloh, in Ephraim’s territory.

chapters.n: Instead he chose Judah and Mount Zion, which he loved. Latter-day Saints honor both tribes’ roles: Judah bearing the Bible and Ephraim the latter-day gathering.
He built his sanctuary high like the heavens and firm like the earth he founded forever.

f.g: The heights — the heavens.

chapters.n: He chose his servant David, taking him from tending sheep.
From caring for nursing ewes, God brought him to shepherd Jacob and Israel. A gentle shepherd became a king.

f.g: Mother sheep nursing lambs — needing careful handling.

chapters.n: David shepherded them with an honest heart and skillful hands. The long, painful history ends with hope in a faithful shepherd-king — pointing toward Christ, the Good Shepherd and Son of David.

f.g: With understanding hands — skilled leadership.

chapters.n: Like Psalm 74, this lament mourns Jerusalem’s fall, probably to Babylon in 587 BC. Foreign nations have invaded God’s own land, defiled his temple, and left Jerusalem in rubble.

f.g: The nations — foreign peoples.

chapters.n: The bodies of God’s faithful were left for birds and wild animals — a terrible disgrace in a culture that honored burial.

f.w: meat unto the fowls of the heaven

f.g: Hebrew ḥasidim — faithful ones.

chapters.n: Blood was poured out like water around Jerusalem, and no one was left to bury the dead.
Israel has become a joke to the surrounding nations.

f.g: Mockery.

chapters.n: How long, Lord? Will your jealous anger burn forever? God’s jealousy is his fierce, protective love for his covenant people, which they had betrayed.

f.g: God’s passionate zeal for an exclusive covenant relationship.

chapters.n: The people ask God to turn his anger instead on nations that don’t know or call on him. Jeremiah used nearly the same words.

f.w: Pour out thy wrath upon the heathen

chapters.n: For those nations have devoured Jacob and ruined his homeland.

f.g: Destroyed Israel.

chapters.n: Don’t hold our ancestors’ sins against us. Let your compassion come quickly to meet us, for we are crushed.

f.g: Come before, go to meet.
Possibly “the sins of our ancestors.”

chapters.n: Help us for the honor of your name; rescue us and cover our sins. Their hope rests on God’s character, not their merit.

f.g: Atone for, cover our sins.

chapters.n: Why let the nations sneer, “Where is their God?” Show your justice openly by avenging your servants’ blood.
Let the groans of prisoners reach you; by your great power, keep alive those condemned to die.

f.w: those that are appointed to die
f.g: Literally “sons of death.”

chapters.n: Pay back our neighbors seven times over for the insults they hurled at you. Seven symbolizes completeness — full justice.

f.g: Completely, in full measure.
Into the fold of their robe, as grain poured into a lap.

chapters.n: Then we, your people and the sheep of your pasture, will thank you forever and tell your praise to every generation. Lament ends in a promise of praise.
Asaph calls on God as the Shepherd of Israel, who leads Joseph’s tribes like a flock and sits enthroned above the cherubim on the ark. “Shine forth” — show yourself!

f.g: Enthroned above the winged cherubim on the ark’s lid.

chapters.n: Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh were the tribes of Rachel — Joseph and Benjamin’s families — who camped around the ark. The psalm likely reflects the northern kingdom’s crisis under Assyria.
The refrain (repeated in verses 7 and 19, growing stronger each time): restore us, let your face shine, and we will be saved.

f.g: Restore us, bring us back.

chapters.n: Lord God of armies, how long will you be angry even when your people pray?

f.w: how long wilt thou be angry
f.g: Literally “how long will you smoke” — fuming anger.

chapters.n: Tears have become their daily bread and drink — sorrow in heaping portions.

f.g: By the bowlful; literally “a third” — a large measure.

chapters.n: Israel has become something neighbors fight over, and enemies laugh at them.
The refrain returns, now addressing the “God of hosts.”
An extended parable: Israel is a vine God brought out of Egypt and replanted in Canaan after clearing out the nations.

f.w: Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt

chapters.n: God cleared the ground, and the vine took deep root and filled the land.
It grew so large its shade covered the hills and its branches were like mighty cedars.

f.g: Literally “cedars of God” — the mightiest cedars.

chapters.n: Its branches reached to the Mediterranean Sea and its shoots to the Euphrates River — the full extent of David and Solomon’s kingdom.

f.g: The Euphrates.

chapters.n: Then why have you torn down its protective walls so every passerby can pick its fruit?

f.g: Stone walls or thorn hedges that protected a vineyard.

chapters.n: Wild boars ravage it and wild creatures feed on it — invading armies devouring the land.

f.w: The boar out of the wood
f.g: A wild boar — destructive in vineyards.

chapters.n: Turn back, God of armies! Look down from heaven and tend this vine again.

f.g: Come and care for.

chapters.n: Care for the vine your own hand planted, the son you made strong for yourself.

f.g: Literally “son” — Israel as God’s son.

chapters.n: It has been burned and cut down; its people perish under God’s rebuke.

May God’s hand rest on the man at his right hand, the son of man he strengthened. Originally this likely meant Israel or its king; Christians also hear a hint of Christ, the Son of Man at God’s right hand.

f.w: the man of thy right hand
f.g: A wordplay on Benjamin, whose name means “son of the right hand.”

chapters.n: Then we will never turn away from you again; give us life, and we will call on your name.

f.g: Revive, give life.

chapters.n: The refrain reaches its fullest form, using God’s covenant name: LORD God of hosts, restore us; shine on us, and we will be saved.
A festival song: sing loudly to God our strength; shout for joy to the God of Jacob.
Strike up the music — tambourine, sweet harp and lyre.

f.g: A hand drum or tambourine.
A stringed instrument like a lyre.

chapters.n: Blow the ram’s horn at the new moon and the full moon, on the feast day. This likely refers to the Feast of Trumpets and Tabernacles in the autumn.

f.g: Hebrew shofar, a ram’s horn.
At the full moon — when the great festivals began.

chapters.n: These festivals were commanded by God as part of Israel’s law.

f.g: A fixed decree.

chapters.n: God established this as a witness when he went out against Egypt. Then a new voice speaks: “I heard a language I didn’t know” — the psalmist receiving a prophetic word.

f.g: Here standing for all Israel.

f.w: I heard a language that I understood not
f.g: Perhaps an unfamiliar voice — God’s — speaking an unexpected message.

chapters.n: Now God speaks: I lifted the heavy load from Israel’s shoulders and freed their hands from carrying baskets of clay in Egypt.

f.w: I removed his shoulder from the burden

f.g: Baskets used to carry bricks or clay.

chapters.n: You called in trouble and I rescued you. I answered you from the hidden thundercloud at Sinai, and tested you at the waters of Meribah.

f.g: “Quarreling” — where Israel complained about water.

chapters.n: Listen, my people, while I warn you — if only you would listen!
You shall have no foreign god among you or bow to any foreign god. This echoes the first commandment.

f.w: There shall no strange god be in thee

chapters.n: I am the Lord who brought you out of Egypt. Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it — God longs to give generously.

f.w: I am the LORD thy God
open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it

chapters.n: But my people wouldn’t listen; Israel wanted nothing to do with me.
So I let them follow their stubborn hearts and their own plans. Sometimes God’s judgment is simply letting people have their way.

f.w: I gave them up unto their own hearts' lust

chapters.n: A heartbreaking cry from God himself: “Oh, if only my people would listen and walk in my ways!”

f.w: Oh that my people had hearkened unto me

chapters.n: I would quickly have defeated their enemies.
Those who hate the Lord would cringe before him, and Israel’s blessing would last forever.

f.g: Israel’s time of prosperity — or the enemies’ time of punishment.

chapters.n: God would have fed them with the finest wheat and satisfied them with honey from the rock. The psalm ends with what could be — an open invitation still waiting.
A courtroom scene: God takes his place in the divine council and judges among the “gods.” Interpreters differ on whether these are heavenly beings or human judges given divine authority.

f.g: Literally “the council of God” — a heavenly assembly.
Hebrew elohim — mighty ones; possibly human judges who act in God’s name.

chapters.n: God’s charge: how long will you judge unjustly and show favor to the wicked?

f.w: accept the persons of the wicked
f.g: Show favoritism toward the wicked.

chapters.n: Their job is to defend the weak and orphans and to uphold the rights of the poor and oppressed.
Rescue the weak and needy from the grip of the wicked. Justice is measured by how the vulnerable are treated.
These judges don’t understand and walk in darkness, so the very foundations of the world are shaken. Injustice unsettles the moral order of creation.

f.g: Shaken, tottering.

chapters.n: God says, “You are gods, children of the Most High.” Jesus quoted this when he was accused of blasphemy. Latter-day Saints see in it a witness of humanity’s divine parentage and potential.
Yet despite their high calling, they will die like ordinary mortals and fall like any ruler. Divine potential doesn’t excuse unrighteousness.
The psalm ends in prayer: rise up, O God, and judge the earth yourself, for all nations belong to you.

f.w: Arise, O God, judge the earth

chapters.n: The last of Asaph’s psalms opens with an urgent plea: God, don’t stay silent or still while your people are threatened.

f.g: Don’t remain quiet; act.

chapters.n: God’s enemies are in an uproar and raising their heads in defiance.

f.g: Acted proudly, rebelled.

chapters.n: They plot craftily against God’s people — those he treasures and protects.

f.g: Those God shelters and treasures.

chapters.n: Their goal is total destruction: wipe Israel off the map so its name is forgotten.

f.w: let us cut them off from being a nation

chapters.n: They have united in one mind, forming an alliance — not just against Israel but against God himself.

f.g: Allied, joined in a covenant.

chapters.n: The list of enemies surrounds Israel: Edom, the desert Ishmaelites, Moab, and the Hagrites east of the Jordan.

f.g: Hagrites, a tribe east of the Jordan, possibly descended from Hagar.
Desert tribes descended from Ishmael.

chapters.n: More foes: Gebal (Byblos or a region near Edom), Ammon, Amalek, the Philistines and Tyre.

f.g: Either Byblos on the coast of Lebanon or a region south of the Dead Sea.
Israel’s ancient enemy from the Exodus.

chapters.n: Even Assyria has joined, lending strength to Moab and Ammon, Lot’s descendants. No single historical alliance matches this list exactly; it may gather Israel’s enemies from many eras.

f.g: Assyria.
Moab and Ammon.
Helped.

chapters.n: Do to them what you did in the days of the judges — to Midian under Gideon, and to Sisera and Jabin at the Kishon River under Deborah and Barak.

f.g: The Kishon River in the Jezreel Valley.

chapters.n: They died at En-dor and lay on the ground like manure.

f.g: A town near Mount Tabor, close to where Sisera’s army fell.

chapters.n: Treat their leaders like the Midianite princes Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah and Zalmunna, whom Gideon defeated.
These are the ones who said, “Let’s take God’s pastures for ourselves.”

f.g: God’s pasturelands — the land of Israel.

chapters.n: Make them like tumbleweed blown by the wind, like straw in a gale.

f.g: Whirling dust or tumbleweed.
Leftover dry stalks — light and worthless.

chapters.n: As fire sweeps through a forest and flames set mountains ablaze...
...so pursue them with your storm and terrify them with your hurricane.

f.g: Pursue, chase.

chapters.n: An important twist: cover them with shame “that they may seek thy name.” The deeper goal is not destruction but repentance.

f.w: that they may seek thy name

chapters.n: Let them be disgraced and dismayed forever if they won’t turn.

The purpose of it all: that the world will know that you alone, whose name is Jehovah, are Most High over the earth. This is one of the few places the KJV spells out the divine name. Latter-day Saints understand Jehovah as the premortal Christ.

f.g: An English form of YHWH, God’s covenant name, usually printed “LORD” in the KJV.

chapters.n: A pilgrim’s love song for the temple, by the sons of Korah. How lovely are your dwelling places, Lord of armies!

f.g: Lovely, beloved — not merely “friendly.”
Dwelling places — the temple and its courts.

chapters.n: The psalmist longs so much for God’s courts that he feels faint; his whole being cries out for the living God. Many Latter-day Saints feel this same longing for the temple.

f.w: My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth

f.g: The open courtyards of the temple where worshippers gathered.

chapters.n: He envies even the little birds that nest near God’s altars. If a sparrow can find a home in God’s house, surely there is room for him.

f.w: the sparrow hath found an house

chapters.n: How happy are those who live in God’s house — the priests and Levites — always praising him.

f.w: they will be still praising thee
f.g: They will always be praising you.

chapters.n: Blessed is the one who finds strength in God and whose heart is set on the pilgrim roads to Zion.

f.g: The highways — the pilgrim roads to Jerusalem.

chapters.n: As pilgrims pass through a dry “valley of weeping,” they turn it into a place of springs, and autumn rains fill it with pools. Faith can turn hard places into blessings.

f.g: Possibly “valley of balsam trees” or “valley of weeping” — a dry stretch on the journey.

chapters.n: Rather than growing weary, the pilgrims grow stronger the closer they get, until each one appears before God in Zion.

f.w: They go from strength to strength

chapters.n: A prayer from the temple: Lord God of armies, God of Jacob, hear me.
He prays for the king, God’s anointed, calling God “our shield.”

f.g: The king — Hebrew mashiaḥ (Messiah).

chapters.n: One day in God’s courts is better than a thousand anywhere else. He would rather stand at the threshold of God’s house than live comfortably among the wicked.

f.w: a day in thy courts is better than a thousand

f.g: One who stands at the threshold — a humble position. The Korahites served as temple gatekeepers.

chapters.n: God is both sun and shield — light and protection. He gives grace and honor and withholds nothing good from those who live with integrity.

f.w: no good thing will he withhold

chapters.n: The final beatitude: happy is the one who trusts in you, Lord of armies.

f.w: blessed is the man that trusteth in thee

chapters.n: The psalm opens by remembering a past blessing: God showed favor to his land and restored Israel’s fortunes. Many think this refers to the return from Babylonian exile.

f.g: Restored the fortunes; brought back the exiles.

chapters.n: God forgave his people and covered every sin.
He withdrew all his anger and turned from his fury.
Now a new plea: restore us again, God of our salvation, and end your displeasure with us. The return from exile was hard, and they need renewal again.

f.g: Restore us, bring us back.

chapters.n: Will you be angry with us forever, across every generation?
Won’t you revive us again so your people can rejoice in you? Revival leads to joy.
Show us your loyal love, Lord, and give us your salvation.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — steadfast love.

chapters.n: Now the psalmist listens for God’s answer: God speaks peace to his faithful people — but they must not go back to foolishness.

f.w: I will hear what God the LORD will speak
he will speak peace unto his people

chapters.n: God’s salvation is close to those who reverence him, so that his glory may dwell in the land again — as it did in the temple.

f.w: that glory may dwell in our land

chapters.n: A beautiful image: God’s loyal love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss. Qualities that might seem opposed — mercy and justice — embrace. Many see this fulfilled in Christ’s Atonement.

f.w: Mercy and truth are met together
righteousness and peace have kissed each other

chapters.n: Truth springs up from the earth, and righteousness looks down from heaven. Latter-day Saints often connect this verse with the coming forth of the Book of Mormon from the ground and revelation from heaven in the Restoration.

f.w: Truth shall spring out of the earth
righteousness shall look down from heaven

chapters.n: The Lord will give what is good, and the land will produce its harvest.

f.w: our land shall yield her increase

chapters.n: Righteousness will walk ahead of God like a herald, preparing a path for his steps.

The only psalm in Book Three credited to David. It is woven from phrases found elsewhere in scripture, like a prayer built from beloved lines. David begins by asking God to bend down and listen, for he is poor and needy.
Protect my life, for I am devoted to you. “Holy” here means faithful and loyal, not sinless.

f.g: Hebrew ḥasid — devoted, faithful, a covenant-keeper.

chapters.n: Be gracious to me, Lord, because I call to you all day long.
Make your servant glad, for I lift my soul to you.

f.w: unto thee, O Lord, do I lift up my soul

chapters.n: Here is why he can pray with confidence: God is good, quick to forgive, and overflowing with loyal love toward all who call on him.
Listen to my prayer, Lord, and pay attention to my pleas.

f.g: Humble, earnest requests.

chapters.n: In trouble he will call, because he is confident God will answer.
No so-called god compares to the Lord, and no works match his.

f.w: Among the gods there is none like unto thee

chapters.n: All the nations God made will come and bow before him and honor his name — a vision of worldwide worship.

f.w: All nations whom thou hast made shall come and worship

chapters.n: For he is great, does wonders, and is God alone.
A beautiful prayer: teach me your way so I can walk in your truth; unite my heart — gather my scattered loyalties into one — to reverence you.

f.g: Make my heart undivided, single-minded.

chapters.n: With his whole heart he will praise God and honor his name forever. A united heart can praise wholeheartedly.
God’s love for him is great — he has rescued him from the depths of the grave.

f.g: The depths of Sheol — the realm of the dead; near death.

chapters.n: Arrogant and violent men have risen against him, seeking his life with no regard for God.

f.w: have not set thee before them

chapters.n: But God is the opposite of these violent men: compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, abounding in love and faithfulness. This quotes God’s self-description to Moses on Sinai.

f.w: a God full of compassion, and gracious, longsuffering

f.g: Slow to anger, patient.

chapters.n: Turn to me and be gracious; give your strength to your servant and save the son of your maidservant — one born into your household and service.

f.g: A servant born in the household — one who belongs to God from birth.

chapters.n: He asks for a sign of God’s favor, so his enemies will see that the Lord has helped and comforted him — and be ashamed.

f.g: A sign of your goodness and favor.
Helped.

chapters.n: The psalm opens abruptly, as if mid-thought: God himself laid the foundation of his city, Zion, upon the holy hills of Jerusalem. Its security rests on him, not on walls.
The Lord treasures Zion, the place of his temple, above every other town in Israel. The ‘gates’ stand for the whole city and the people who gather there to worship.

f.g: The towns and homes of Israel, Jacob’s descendants.

chapters.n: The psalmist turns to address the city directly. Wonderful promises have been made about Zion — that God would dwell there and draw the nations to it.

f.g: A Hebrew musical or liturgical marker of uncertain meaning; possibly a pause or a signal to lift the voice.

chapters.n: God speaks, listing Israel’s old rivals and neighbors — Egypt, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, and Ethiopia — and says of each, ‘this one was born there,’ as if counting foreigners among Zion’s own citizens. It is a striking vision of the nations coming to know the Lord.

f.g: Here a poetic name for Egypt (meaning ‘arrogance’ or ‘storm’), not Rahab of Jericho.
Hebrew Cush, the land south of Egypt.

chapters.n: People from everywhere will be spoken of as Zion’s children, and the Most High himself will make the city firm. Belonging to Zion becomes a matter of new birth and covenant, not ancestry.

f.w: This and that man was born in her

f.g: Hebrew Elyon, ‘Most High,’ a title of God.

chapters.n: The Lord keeps a register of his people, like a census book, and enrolls each as a native of Zion. Scripture often pictures God keeping a book of the names of the faithful.
The psalm ends in celebration: singers and dancers or musicians rejoice in Zion, saying that every source of life and blessing is found in her. Springs of water were precious in a dry land.

f.g: Fountains or sources; figuratively, the origin of all joy and life.

chapters.n: Heman, the psalm’s author by tradition, still calls God ‘the God of my salvation’ even in deep darkness. His constant crying out shows that faith can keep praying when no answer has yet come.
He asks God simply to hear him. ‘Incline thine ear’ pictures God bending down to listen closely to someone too weak to speak loudly.

f.g: Turn or bend your ear toward me; listen attentively.

chapters.n: His troubles have piled up until his soul feels full, and he senses death approaching. Many readers have found comfort that scripture gives honest words to such despair.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol, the realm of the dead.

chapters.n: Others already treat him as good as dead. He feels drained of all strength, like someone being lowered into a tomb.

f.g: A poetic name for the grave or the underworld.

chapters.n: ‘Free among the dead’ means cast loose among them — abandoned, no longer part of the living community. He fears being forgotten, as if beyond the reach of God’s care.

f.g: Set adrift among the dead; released from life’s ties, as one forsaken.

chapters.n: He feels God himself has placed him at the very bottom of the pit, surrounded by darkness and deep waters — images of utter helplessness.
His suffering feels like divine anger pressing down on him, and trouble rolls over him like ocean waves, one after another.
Even friends keep their distance, perhaps because illness made him ritually unclean or repulsive to them. He feels imprisoned with no way out.

f.g: Something loathed or shunned.

chapters.n: He has wept until his eyes are worn out, yet he keeps praying every day, hands lifted toward heaven in the ancient posture of prayer.

A series of questions begins: if he dies, how can he praise God? The psalmist argues that saving him lets God’s goodness be seen and celebrated among the living. Later revelation adds that God’s power reaches even the dead.
The questions continue in parallel lines: can God’s steady love and faithfulness be announced in the grave? The point is urgency — help me while I can still testify of you.

f.g: Hebrew Abaddon, another name for the place of the dead.

chapters.n: ‘The land of forgetfulness’ is a poetic name for the grave, where the dead seem forgotten. The psalmist longs to keep living as a witness of God’s wonders.
‘But’ marks his stubborn hope. ‘Prevent’ is old English for ‘come before’: his prayer will meet God first thing each morning.

f.g: Archaic: go before, anticipate — not ‘hinder.’

chapters.n: His most painful question: why does God seem to reject him and hide his face? Even prophets have asked this; compare Joseph Smith in Liberty Jail.
He has suffered and been near death since youth, so long that he is overwhelmed and bewildered. This hints at a lifelong illness or affliction.

f.g: Overwhelmed, numb, at a loss.

chapters.n: He experiences his troubles as waves of God’s fierce anger sweeping over him and cutting him off. The psalm voices how suffering can feel, not a final verdict on God’s character.

f.g: Silenced or destroyed me.

chapters.n: Terrors surround him like a rising flood that closes in from every side, day after day.

The psalm ends with no resolution: loved ones and friends are gone, and his only companion is darkness. Its inclusion in scripture teaches that honest lament is itself an act of faith, prayed to the God who hears.
Ethan the Ezrahite begins with a vow to praise forever. Two key words run through this psalm: God’s ‘mercies’ (his covenant love) and his ‘faithfulness’ (his reliability).

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — loyal, covenant love; steadfast kindness.
Hebrew ʾemunah — firmness, dependability.

chapters.n: The psalmist pictures God’s mercy as a building that keeps rising and his faithfulness as something set firmly in heaven itself, beyond any earthly change.
Now God speaks, recalling his covenant with David. He swore a solemn oath to his chosen servant.
The heart of the covenant: David’s descendants and throne would last forever. Christians and Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled ultimately in Jesus Christ, the Son of David.

f.w: Thy seed will I establish for ever

chapters.n: Heaven itself joins the praise. ‘The congregation of the saints’ here means the holy ones, the heavenly council around God’s throne.

f.g: ‘Holy ones’ — here likely heavenly beings in God’s presence.

chapters.n: No one in heaven compares to the Lord. ‘The sons of the mighty’ are the heavenly beings; even among them, none is like him.

f.g: Hebrew bene elim, ‘sons of God,’ heavenly beings.

chapters.n: Even the holy beings around God stand in awe of him. To ‘fear’ God here means deep reverence and respect.

f.g: Held in reverent awe.

chapters.n: ‘LORD God of hosts’ means the God who commands the armies of heaven. His faithfulness surrounds him like a garment.

f.g: Jehovah, commander of heavenly armies; a title of power.

chapters.n: In the ancient world, the sea stood for chaos. God rules it and calms its waves — a power Jesus later displayed on the Sea of Galilee.
Rahab here is a poetic sea-monster, a symbol of chaos and of Egypt. God crushed it, recalling his victory at the Red Sea.

f.g: A symbolic chaos-monster, often standing for Egypt.

chapters.n: Everything belongs to God because he made it — the heavens, the earth, and all that fills them.
North and south stand for the whole earth. Tabor and Hermon, two well-known mountains of northern Israel, are pictured as joyfully praising God’s name.

f.g: Mount Tabor in Galilee and Mount Hermon, Israel’s highest peak, on the northern border.

chapters.n: God’s arm and right hand are symbols of his power to act and to save.
God’s rule rests on justice and right judgment, while mercy and truth go before him like heralds. Divine power is always joined with goodness.
Happy are those who know the festival shout of worship. They live in the warm light of God’s face — his favor and presence.

f.g: The trumpet blast or shout of praise at Israel’s feasts.

chapters.n: God’s people find their joy in his name all day long, and his righteousness lifts them up.
God is the source of his people’s strength. A ‘horn’ is a symbol of strength and dignity, like a strong animal holding its head high.

f.g: Symbol of strength, power, and victory.

chapters.n: Israel’s ‘shield’ (defence) and king belong to God. The earthly king served under the Holy One of Israel, the true King.

f.g: Literally ‘shield’ — likely meaning the human king, who belongs to the Lord.

chapters.n: The psalm now retells God’s revelation, likely through the prophet Nathan. God chose a mighty young man from among the people to lead them.
God found David, a shepherd, and had him anointed with sacred oil as king. ‘Messiah’ means ‘anointed one.’

f.w: with my holy oil have I anointed him

chapters.n: God promises that his own hand and arm will steady and strengthen David. The king’s strength would come from the Lord.

f.w: mine arm also shall strengthen him

chapters.n: No enemy would succeed in oppressing David. ‘Exact upon’ means to oppress or extort from someone.

f.g: Oppress or take advantage of him, like a harsh creditor.

chapters.n: God himself would defeat David’s enemies, crushing them before his eyes.
God’s faithfulness and covenant love would stay with David, and in God’s name David’s strength would rise.
David’s rule would reach from the Mediterranean ‘sea’ to the ‘rivers,’ likely the Euphrates — the full borders promised to Abraham.
The king would call God ‘my father,’ a close covenant relationship. Jesus perfectly fulfilled this as the Son of God.
‘Firstborn’ means the heir with first rank and birthright, not necessarily the oldest. This points beyond David to Christ, the Firstborn and ‘prince of the kings of the earth.’
God’s covenant love toward David would never end; the agreement would stand firm.
David’s line and throne would last as long as the heavens. This hope fed Israel’s longing for the Messiah.
God anticipates that David’s descendants might disobey. Verses 30–31 set up the condition; verse 32 states the consequence.
The parallel lines repeat the idea: if they break God’s statutes and commandments.

f.g: Fixed decrees or laws.

chapters.n: Sin would bring correction, like a father disciplining a child with a rod. Discipline is not the same as abandonment.
Even when punishing, God would not fully withdraw his covenant love or let his faithfulness fail. This is the key promise the psalmist will plead later.
God will not break his covenant or change his word once spoken. His promises are utterly reliable.

f.w: nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips

chapters.n: God swears by his own holiness, the highest oath possible, since there is nothing greater to swear by.
David’s line will endure, and his throne will be as constant as the sun.
Like the moon, the throne will last forever. The ‘faithful witness in heaven’ may be the moon itself, steadily testifying to God’s promise.
A dramatic turn: ‘But.’ The psalmist now laments that God seems to have rejected his anointed king, perhaps after a military defeat or the fall of Jerusalem.

f.g: The reigning king of David’s line.

chapters.n: It feels as if God has cancelled the covenant and thrown the king’s crown into the dust, dishonoring it.

f.g: Treated as common or unholy; defiled.

chapters.n: The king is like a vineyard whose protective hedges are torn down, and his fortresses lie in ruins.

f.g: Walls or fences that protect a vineyard; here, the nation’s defenses.

chapters.n: Passersby plunder him freely, and neighboring nations mock him.

f.g: Plunder or rob him.

chapters.n: Instead of David’s hand being raised, God has lifted up his enemies’ hands and let them celebrate.

f.g: The power and victory of enemies.

chapters.n: God has dulled the king’s sword and not helped him stand firm in battle — the reverse of the earlier promises.

f.w: turned the edge of his sword
f.g: Blunted or turned back his sword.

chapters.n: The king’s splendor is ended and his throne overturned.

f.g: Possibly ‘his brightness’ or royal splendor.

chapters.n: The king has been cut down in his prime and covered in shame. Some think this fits young King Jehoiachin, taken captive to Babylon.
The lament becomes a direct prayer: How long? Will God stay hidden and angry forever?
Life is short; the psalmist asks God to act within his lifetime. Has God created human beings for nothing?
No one escapes death. Only God can rescue a soul from the grave — a hope fulfilled through Christ’s Resurrection.
The psalmist appeals to God’s own oath: Where are the acts of covenant love you swore to David?
He asks God to remember the insults his people suffer, carried in his heart like a heavy load.

f.g: Carry close to the heart, as one carries a burden or a child.

chapters.n: The enemies have mocked every step of God’s anointed. To insult the king was to insult the God who chose him.

f.g: Every move of the king; or, some think, the ‘coming’ of the Messiah.

chapters.n: This closing blessing ends Book Three of the Psalms (Psalms 73–89), not just this psalm. Each of the five books of Psalms ends with a similar doxology.

This psalm, titled ‘A Prayer of Moses,’ opens Book Four of the Psalms. Through every generation — even during Israel’s homeless wandering in the wilderness — the Lord himself has been their true home.
Before mountains or the earth existed, God already was. ‘From everlasting to everlasting’ means without beginning or end — the contrast that frames this whole meditation on human frailty.
God returns mortals to dust and says, ‘Return, children of men.’ This echoes the Creation and Fall, when Adam was told he would return to the ground.

f.g: Literally ‘crushed matter’ or dust.

chapters.n: To God, a thousand years pass like a single day already gone, or like one shift of a night watch. Time does not limit him as it does us.

f.g: One of the three or four periods into which the night was divided for guards — a few hours.

chapters.n: Human lives are swept away like by a flash flood, gone like a dream. People are like grass that sprouts fresh in the morning.
In the dry Middle East, grass can spring up green at dawn and be withered by evening under the hot sun or cut for fodder. Life is that brief.
Moses connects human frailty with sin: our troubles and mortality come under God’s judgment. This may reflect the wilderness generation who died before entering the promised land.
Nothing is hidden from God. Even secret sins lie exposed in the bright light of his face.
Our years end like a sigh or a story that is soon told. The Hebrew may mean ‘like a sigh’ or a murmur — quick and fading.

f.w: as a tale that is told
f.g: Hebrew hegeh — a sigh, moan, or murmur.

chapters.n: A normal life lasts about seventy years, or eighty for the strong. Even then, those years bring toil and sorrow, and soon we ‘fly away’ in death.

f.g: Seventy years (a score = 20).
Eighty.

chapters.n: Who truly understands how serious God’s judgment is? The reverence we owe him matches the weight of his holy anger against sin.

f.g: The reverent awe due to God.

chapters.n: The key verse: teach us to count our days — to realize life is short — so we can gain a wise heart. Knowing our time is limited should help us use it well.
Moses pleads, ‘Turn back to us, Lord! How long?’ ‘Let it repent thee’ means ‘have compassion’ or ‘relent.’

f.g: Relent; turn in compassion. It does not imply God has sinned.

chapters.n: ‘Early’ means in the morning. He asks God to fill them with covenant love at the start of each day so their whole lives will be joyful.

f.g: In the morning; at the dawn.

chapters.n: He asks for joy to balance the sorrow — as many glad days as there were years of affliction.

f.w: the days wherein thou hast afflicted us

chapters.n: May God’s great works be seen by his servants now, and his glory by their children. Faith looks ahead to coming generations.
The psalm ends asking for God’s ‘beauty’ or favor to rest upon his people, and for him to make their daily labor lasting. Brief human lives gain eternal worth when God blesses what we do.

f.g: Hebrew noʿam — pleasantness, kindness, favor.

f.w: establish thou the work of our hands

chapters.n: Whoever makes God their hiding place lives safely in his shade. ‘Most High’ and ‘Almighty’ are two titles stressing God’s supreme power to protect.

f.g: A hidden shelter or hiding place.
Hebrew Shaddai.

chapters.n: The psalmist personally confesses his trust: the Lord is his refuge and fortress. The rest of the psalm explains what that trust brings.
God rescues from hidden traps, like a bird-catcher’s net, and from deadly disease. ‘Noisome’ means harmful or destructive.

f.g: A bird-catcher’s trap — a picture of hidden danger.
Destructive, deadly.

chapters.n: A tender image: God shelters his people as a mother bird covers her young with her wings. His truth is like a large shield and a small shield together.

f.g: A small round shield; here paired with the large shield for full protection.

chapters.n: The believer need not fear dangers that come at any hour — night terrors or daytime attacks.
Plague that creeps in darkness and destruction that strikes at noon are named together to cover every time of day.

f.g: Lays waste; destroys.

chapters.n: Even if multitudes fall all around, the one who trusts God will not be overcome. This is poetry about God’s protection, not a guarantee that believers never suffer.
The faithful will simply watch as the wicked receive the results of their own choices.
The reason for this safety: the believer has made the Most High their home.

f.g: Dwelling place, home.

chapters.n: No disaster will overtake the faithful one’s home. Compare the Passover, when the destroyer passed over Israel’s houses.
God commands his angels to guard his people on every path. Satan later quoted this verse to tempt Jesus.

f.w: give his angels charge over thee

chapters.n: Angels carry the faithful as if in their hands, protecting them from stumbling. Jesus refused to test God by misusing this promise.

f.w: dash thy foot against a stone

chapters.n: The faithful will overcome fierce dangers, symbolized by lions and snakes. Jesus gave his disciples similar power over serpents.

f.g: A venomous snake.
Here a serpent or sea creature.

chapters.n: Now God himself speaks. He promises to rescue and lift up the one who clings to him in love and knows his name — that is, knows him personally.

f.g: Clung to me in love; held fast to me.

chapters.n: God promises to answer, to be present in trouble (not just to remove it), to rescue, and to honor.

f.w: I will be with him in trouble

chapters.n: The final promise: a full life and a vision of God’s salvation. For Latter-day Saints, ‘salvation’ ultimately points to eternal life through Jesus Christ.
This psalm’s heading calls it ‘A Psalm or Song for the sabbath day.’ It begins by declaring that giving thanks and singing to God is simply good and fitting.

f.g: Hebrew Elyon, a title of God’s supremacy.

chapters.n: God’s covenant love is announced in the morning and his faithfulness at night — praise that frames the whole day.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed, loyal covenant love.

chapters.n: Temple worship used stringed instruments. The ten-stringed lute and harp would have accompanied this song.

f.g: A stringed instrument, perhaps a type of lyre or harp.
Possibly a resounding or meditative melody.

chapters.n: God’s works bring the psalmist joy. Remembering creation and God’s acts was a key theme of the Sabbath.
God’s works are great, and his thoughts are deep beyond human measuring.
A ‘brutish’ person — dull and senseless like an animal — cannot grasp this. Spiritual understanding requires humility.

f.g: Stupid, senseless, like a beast.

chapters.n: The wicked may spring up quickly like grass, but that very quickness signals how soon they will wither. Their success is temporary.
This short verse is the center of the psalm: while evildoers fade, the Lord is exalted forever.
The repeated ‘lo, thine enemies’ builds emphasis like a drumbeat. Those who oppose God will be scattered.
The ‘horn’ means strength. The ‘unicorn’ in the KJV is the wild ox, a powerful animal. Anointing with fresh oil pictures being refreshed and honored.

f.g: Hebrew reʾem, the wild ox — not a mythical creature.

chapters.n: The psalmist expects to see his enemies defeated and to hear of their downfall.
The righteous are compared to two trees: the palm, which thrives in hard desert places and bears fruit, and the cedar of Lebanon, tall and long-lived.

f.g: The date palm — upright, fruitful, enduring heat.
Famous for strength and height; used to build the temple.

chapters.n: These trees are planted in the temple courts — nourished by being close to God.

f.w: planted in the house of the LORD

chapters.n: The faithful stay fruitful even in old age, full of life and vigor. ‘Fat’ here means healthy and full of sap.

f.g: Full of sap; healthy and vigorous.
