chapters.n: Their lasting fruitfulness testifies that the Lord is upright and dependable. ‘Rock’ is a title of God as a firm foundation.
‘The LORD reigneth’ begins a group of ‘enthronement psalms’ (93, 95–99) celebrating God as King. He is dressed in majesty and strength like royal robes, and the world he founded stands firm.

f.g: Belted, as a warrior ties on his belt to prepare for action.
Established, made firm.

chapters.n: God’s throne is not new; it has existed from ancient times, because he himself is eternal.
The ‘floods’ — rivers and seas — roar and raise their waves. In ancient thought, raging waters symbolized chaos and forces opposing God.

f.g: The repetition imitates waves surging higher and higher.

chapters.n: However loud the waves, the Lord on high is mightier still. No chaos — in nature or in life — is beyond his control.

f.w: mightier than the noise of many waters

chapters.n: God’s ‘testimonies’ — his covenant laws — are completely reliable, and holiness is what suits his temple forever.

f.g: God’s solemn declarations and laws.
Holiness is fitting for your temple.

chapters.n: The psalmist calls on God as the One who rightly avenges wrongs. ‘Shew thyself’ means ‘shine forth’ — appear and act. Vengeance belongs to God, not to us.

f.g: Literally ‘shine forth,’ as God appeared in glory.

chapters.n: He asks the Judge of all the earth to rise up and pay back the arrogant what they deserve.
The cry ‘how long?’ is repeated, showing deep frustration at seeing injustice go unpunished.
The wicked spill out arrogant, harsh words and brag about themselves.

f.g: Arrogant, insolent speech.

chapters.n: They crush God’s people, who are his ‘heritage’ — his own treasured inheritance.
They target the most vulnerable: widows, foreigners, and orphans — the very people God’s law commanded Israel to protect.
They act as if God doesn’t notice or care. This practical atheism lies behind much wickedness.
The psalmist turns to rebuke the oppressors directly, calling them senseless and foolish.

f.g: Senseless, like dumb animals.

chapters.n: A powerful argument: the God who designed ears and eyes certainly hears and sees. Our Creator is not less aware than his creations.
God disciplines whole nations and is the source of all human knowledge; surely he knows what the wicked do and will correct them.

f.g: Disciplines the nations.

chapters.n: God knows every human thought and sees how empty and fleeting they are. Paul quotes this verse.

f.g: Breath, vapor — something empty and passing.

chapters.n: In contrast to the wicked, the person God disciplines and teaches is truly blessed. God’s correction is a sign of his love.

f.w: Blessed is the man whom thou chastenest

chapters.n: God’s teaching brings inner calm through hard times while justice is prepared for the wicked.

f.g: The grave or trap being made ready — judgment is on its way.

chapters.n: The heart of the psalm’s hope: the Lord will never abandon his people.

f.w: will not cast off his people

chapters.n: Justice will once again line up with righteousness, and all the honest-hearted will follow it.
He asks: who will take my side against evildoers? The answer follows in the next verse.

f.w: Who will rise up for me
f.g: Who will stand as my defender, as in a courtroom?

chapters.n: Without the Lord’s help he would soon have been in ‘silence’ — the silence of the grave.

f.g: A poetic way to say ‘died.’

chapters.n: The moment he said, ‘I’m slipping!’ God’s covenant love held him up. Even admitting weakness brought help.
When anxious thoughts multiplied inside him, God’s comforts brought delight to his soul.

f.g: Anxious, troubled thoughts.

chapters.n: Can corrupt rulers who make injustice legal be partners with God? Never. Laws that oppress are not of God.

f.g: Creates harm under cover of law.

chapters.n: The wicked band together against the righteous and condemn innocent people to death.
‘But’ again marks the turn to trust: the Lord is his high tower, and God the rock where he can hide.
Evil will turn back on those who do it. God will cut them off — their own wickedness will bring their ruin.
An invitation to worship: come, sing, and shout for joy to the Lord, the solid ‘rock’ who saves us. This psalm became a traditional call to worship in Jewish and Christian services.

f.g: A loud shout of praise, like the cheer for a king.

chapters.n: Approach God with thanks and songs. Gratitude is the doorway into his presence.
The reason for praise: the Lord is the great King, far above every so-called god of the nations.
From the deepest depths of the earth to the highest mountain peaks, everything is in God’s hand.

f.g: Possibly ‘the peaks of the mountains.’

chapters.n: Sea and land both belong to God because he made them. Creation is the basis of his kingship.

f.w: his hands formed the dry land

chapters.n: A second invitation: bow down and kneel before our Maker. Worship involves the body as well as the heart.
We are God’s flock, cared for by his own hand. Then the tone shifts sharply: ‘Today, if you will hear his voice…’

f.w: To day if ye will hear his voice

chapters.n: Now God speaks: don’t be stubborn like Israel in the wilderness. ‘Provocation’ (Meribah) and ‘temptation’ (Massah) are the place names where Israel quarreled with God over water.

f.g: Hebrew Meribah, ‘quarreling.’
Hebrew Massah, ‘testing.’

chapters.n: The Israelites put God to the test and challenged him — even though they had seen his miracles.

f.g: Tested me.

chapters.n: For forty years God was grieved by that generation, whose hearts kept wandering and who never truly learned his ways.

f.g: Their hearts go astray.

chapters.n: So God declared they would not enter his ‘rest’ — the promised land. Hebrews and the D&C apply this ‘rest’ to entering the fulness of God’s glory.
The whole earth is invited to sing a ‘new song’ — fresh praise for a new act of God. A version of this psalm appears when David brought the ark to Jerusalem.
To ‘bless’ God’s name is to praise and honor it. His saving acts should be announced every day, like ongoing good news.

f.g: Proclaim the good news of his deliverance.

chapters.n: God’s glory is meant for every people, not just Israel. This anticipates the missionary call to all nations.

f.g: Among the nations (non-Israelites).

chapters.n: The Lord deserves the highest praise and reverence, above any other being people worship.

f.g: Revered, held in awe.

chapters.n: A wordplay: the nations’ gods (elohim) are mere idols (elilim, ‘nothings’), but the Lord made the heavens.

f.g: Hebrew elilim — ‘worthless things,’ a pun on elohim (gods).

chapters.n: Honor, majesty, strength, and beauty are pictured as attendants standing before God in his sanctuary.

f.g: The holy place, the temple.

chapters.n: ‘Give unto the LORD’ — that is, acknowledge and declare his glory and strength. All the families of the earth are invited.

f.g: Families, clans.

chapters.n: Worshipers bring offerings as they enter the temple courts. In ancient Israel no one came before the King empty-handed.
Worship God in holy splendor — perhaps in sacred clothing or a holy manner. ‘Fear before him’ means tremble in reverence.

f.g: Holy attire or holy majesty.

chapters.n: The message to share with every nation: the Lord is King! His rule brings stability and fair judgment.
All creation — heavens, earth, sea, and everything in it — is called to celebrate.
Fields and forests join in. Creation itself rejoices when God comes to set things right.

f.w: all the trees of the wood rejoice

chapters.n: The reason: the Lord is coming to judge the world fairly and faithfully. For Latter-day Saints this looks forward to Christ’s Second Coming and millennial reign.

f.w: he cometh to judge the earth

chapters.n: ‘The LORD reigns!’ So the whole earth — even the most distant islands and coastlands — should be glad.

f.g: Islands and distant coastlands; the far ends of the world.

chapters.n: Clouds and darkness surround God, as at Sinai, hiding his overwhelming glory. Yet his throne rests on righteousness and justice.
Fire goes before God, consuming his enemies. Fire is a frequent symbol of his presence and holiness.
His lightning lights up the world, and the earth trembles at the sight — imagery of a great storm announcing God’s arrival.
Mountains melt like wax before the Lord of all the earth — a picture of his overwhelming power when he appears.
The heavens proclaim God’s righteousness, and every nation sees his glory.
Those who worship carved idols will be put to shame. Even any ‘gods’ or heavenly beings are told to bow before the Lord.

f.g: Put to shame; disgraced.

chapters.n: Zion and the towns of Judah (‘daughters of Judah’) rejoice over God’s just judgments.

f.g: The towns and villages of Judah, or its women.

chapters.n: The Lord is the Most High, far above the whole earth and every other god.
Loving God means hating evil. He watches over the lives of his faithful ones and rescues them.

f.g: Faithful, devoted ones (Hebrew ḥasidim).

chapters.n: Light is ‘sown’ like seed for the righteous — it springs up and grows, bringing joy to the honest-hearted.
The psalm closes by calling the righteous to rejoice and give thanks as they remember God’s holy name.

f.g: Or ‘his holy name’ — what is remembered of him.

chapters.n: A new song for new wonders: God’s ‘right hand’ and ‘holy arm’ — his own power — have won the victory without human help.
God has made his salvation known openly, for all the nations to see.
God remembered his covenant love and faithfulness to Israel, and the ends of the earth saw him save. Mary’s song in Luke echoes this verse.

f.w: all the ends of the earth

chapters.n: All the earth is invited to break out in joyful shouts and songs. This verse inspired the hymn ‘Joy to the World.’
The harp and the singing voice combine in praise.

f.g: A lyre, the stringed instrument David played.

chapters.n: Trumpets and the ram’s horn blast out as at a king’s coronation. The Lord is hailed as King.

f.g: Hebrew shofar — the ram’s-horn trumpet.

chapters.n: The sea and everything living on the earth join the celebration.
Rivers clap their hands and mountains sing for joy — beautiful poetic images of all creation celebrating.

f.w: Let the floods clap their hands

chapters.n: Creation rejoices because the Lord is coming to judge the world with perfect fairness. Latter-day revelation ties this to the Second Coming.

f.w: for he cometh to judge the earth

f.g: Fairness, uprightness.

chapters.n: The Lord reigns, enthroned above the cherubim — the golden winged figures on the lid of the ark of the covenant. The proper response is trembling awe.

f.g: Cherubim (already plural in Hebrew): angelic guardians of God’s presence.

chapters.n: God is great in Zion, his chosen dwelling, and high above all peoples.
‘Terrible’ means awe-inspiring. The refrain ‘he is holy’ appears three times in this psalm (verses 3, 5, 9).

f.g: Awesome, inspiring reverent fear.

chapters.n: God is a mighty King who loves justice. He has established fairness and done what is right among Jacob’s descendants.

f.g: Fairness; uprightness.
The people of Israel.

chapters.n: Worship at his ‘footstool’ — the ark of the covenant, or the temple, where God’s presence touches earth.

f.g: The ark or temple, pictured as the footrest of God’s heavenly throne.

chapters.n: Moses, Aaron, and Samuel are remembered as great intercessors who prayed for the people — and God answered.
God spoke to them from the pillar of cloud, and they kept his decrees.
God forgave his people yet still punished their wrongdoing. ‘Inventions’ means their evil deeds. Mercy and justice work together.

f.g: Deeds, schemes, misdeeds.

chapters.n: The final refrain calls for worship on God’s holy hill, Zion, ending on the theme of the whole psalm: the Lord our God is holy.
This short psalm, headed ‘A Psalm of praise’ (or ‘thanksgiving’), invites every land on earth to shout joyfully to the Lord.

f.g: A loud shout of homage, as when greeting a king.

chapters.n: Serving God should be done with joy, not grudgingly. Coming into his presence with song is the right attitude of worship.
Know that the Lord is God and that he made us. An alternate Hebrew reading says ‘and we are his.’ Either way, we belong to him as sheep to a shepherd.

f.g: Many manuscripts read ‘and his we are’ — the two Hebrew words sound alike.

chapters.n: Worshipers are invited through the temple gates and into its courts with thanks and praise on their lips.

f.w: Enter into his gates with thanksgiving

chapters.n: Three reasons to praise: the Lord is good, his covenant love lasts forever, and his faithfulness endures through every generation.

f.g: Faithfulness, reliability.

chapters.n: David, speaking as king, promises to sing of covenant love and justice — the two qualities a godly ruler must reflect.
David resolves to live with integrity, even in private, at home. His question ‘When will you come to me?’ shows he longs for God’s presence.

f.g: Blameless, whole, with integrity — not flawless.

chapters.n: He will not look at anything worthless or wicked, and won’t let the deeds of those who turn from God stick to him. Guarding what we look at guards the heart.

f.w: no wicked thing before mine eyes

f.g: Stick, cling.

chapters.n: A twisted, perverse heart will have no place in him, and he will not be intimate with evil.

f.g: Perverse, crooked, stubborn.
Have close fellowship with.

chapters.n: As king he will remove anyone who secretly slanders others, and will not put up with arrogance.

f.g: Secretly.
A haughty, proud expression.

chapters.n: He will seek out the faithful to be his companions and officials. Good leaders choose good counselors.
Liars and deceivers will have no place in the king’s household or court.
‘Early’ means ‘every morning,’ when kings held court. He promises daily vigilance to keep Jerusalem, God’s city, free of evildoers.

f.g: Morning by morning — when judgment was given at the city gate.

chapters.n: The heading calls this ‘A prayer of the afflicted, when he is overwhelmed.’ It begins with a simple plea that God would truly hear.

f.w: let my cry come unto thee

chapters.n: He begs God not to turn away in his time of trouble but to listen closely and answer quickly.
His days vanish like smoke, and his body burns as if with fever, like coals in a fireplace.

f.g: A fireplace or burning coals.

chapters.n: His heart is struck and dried up like sun-scorched grass, so that he loses all appetite. Grief can affect the whole body.
Groaning and grief have left him so thin that his skin clings to his bones.
He compares himself to lonely birds of desolate places, symbols of isolation. The exact species are uncertain.

f.g: A bird of uncertain kind living in ruins or desert — possibly a jackdaw or owl.
Owls were associated with ruins and loneliness.

chapters.n: He lies awake like a solitary bird on a flat rooftop — sleepless and alone.

f.g: I lie awake, keeping watch.

chapters.n: Enemies taunt him constantly, and those who rage against him use his name as a curse.

f.g: They use my name in their curses.

chapters.n: Ashes, a sign of mourning, are like his daily bread, and his tears mix into his drink.
He feels God lifted him up only to throw him down, like a wind lifting and dropping a leaf.

f.w: lifted me up, and cast me down

chapters.n: His life is like a lengthening evening shadow that will soon disappear, and he withers like grass.
The turning point: ‘But thou, O LORD.’ Though he fades, God endures forever and is remembered in every generation.
He looks beyond his own pain to Zion’s future. God will rise and have compassion on her, for the appointed time has come. This may reflect hopes for rebuilding Jerusalem after the exile.
God’s servants love even Zion’s ruined stones and dust. Their love for the city mirrors God’s own.
Zion’s restoration will lead the nations and their kings to revere the Lord.

f.w: all the kings of the earth

chapters.n: When the Lord builds Zion, he will appear in glory. Latter-day Saints see this as a prophecy of the latter-day building of Zion before Christ’s return.
God pays attention to the prayers of the destitute — those stripped of everything — and never scorns them.

f.g: Stripped bare, utterly poor.

chapters.n: This hope is written down so future generations — people not yet born — will praise the Lord too.

f.w: written for the generation to come

chapters.n: God looks down from his heavenly sanctuary to see the earth.

f.w: looked down from the height of his sanctuary

chapters.n: He hears the groans of prisoners and frees those condemned to die — an image Latter-day Saints also connect with Christ’s work among the dead.

f.g: Literally ‘sons of death,’ those condemned to die.

chapters.n: Those he frees will proclaim the Lord’s name in Zion and Jerusalem.
Nations and kingdoms will gather together to serve the Lord.

f.w: the kingdoms, to serve the LORD

chapters.n: Back to his own situation: in the middle of his life’s journey, God has drained his strength and cut his days short.

f.g: Along the road of life; midway.

chapters.n: He pleads not to be taken in the middle of his life — contrasting his few years with God’s endless ones.

f.w: in the midst of my days

chapters.n: God laid the earth’s foundations long ago and made the heavens. Hebrews applies verses 25–27 to Jesus Christ as Creator.

f.w: laid the foundation of the earth

chapters.n: Even heaven and earth will wear out like old clothes, and God will change them like a garment. Scripture teaches the earth will be renewed and glorified.

f.g: Clothing, a robe.

chapters.n: But God never changes, and his years will never end. This constancy is the anchor of hope.
Because God endures, so will his people’s descendants. The psalmist’s personal hope widens into hope for the generations to come.

f.w: The children of thy servants shall continue

chapters.n: David speaks to his own soul, urging his whole inner being to praise God. To ‘bless’ the Lord is to praise and thank him with full devotion.

f.w: Bless the LORD, O my soul

chapters.n: He tells himself not to forget any of God’s ‘benefits’ — his kind acts. Forgetfulness is the enemy of gratitude.
The first gifts listed: forgiveness of all sins and healing of all diseases. Both are fulfilled in Jesus Christ, who forgave and healed.
God buys back (‘redeems’) life from the pit and crowns his people with steadfast love and compassion — as if making them royalty.

f.g: Buys back, rescues — the role of a kinsman-redeemer.
The pit, the grave.

chapters.n: God fills his people with good things, renewing their strength like the eagle, whose powerful flight symbolizes vigor.
God takes the side of the oppressed, working justice for them.
God revealed his ways to Moses and showed his mighty deeds to Israel. Moses asked to know God’s ways, and God answered.

f.w: made known his ways unto Moses

chapters.n: This verse echoes God’s self-description to Moses on Sinai — the central Old Testament statement of his character.

f.w: merciful and gracious, slow to anger

chapters.n: God does not keep accusing or stay angry forever. His discipline is temporary; his love is lasting.

f.g: Scold, contend, bring accusation.

chapters.n: God has not treated us as our sins deserve. This is grace — mercy beyond what is earned.

f.w: not dealt with us after our sins

chapters.n: God’s covenant love is as vast as the distance from earth to the sky.

f.w: as the heaven is high above the earth

chapters.n: East and west never meet; so completely does God remove our sins from us when we repent. He chooses not to hold them against us.

f.w: As far as the east is from the west

chapters.n: God feels tender compassion for his children like a loving father. Latter-day Saints believe he is literally the Father of our spirits.

f.w: Like as a father pitieth his children

f.g: Has tender compassion on.

chapters.n: God knows how we are made — that we are frail, formed from dust. He makes allowance for our weakness.

f.g: How we are formed or put together.

chapters.n: Human life is like grass or a wildflower — it blooms briefly.
A hot desert wind blows over the flower and it is gone, leaving no trace in the place it grew.
In contrast to our brief lives, God’s covenant love lasts forever toward those who revere him, reaching even to their grandchildren.
That everlasting mercy is for those who keep covenant and remember to obey. Covenant faithfulness opens the way to its blessings.
The Lord has set up his throne in heaven, and his kingdom rules over everything.
David now calls on the angels — mighty beings who obey God’s word — to join the praise.
All God’s ‘hosts’ — his heavenly armies and servants who do his will — are invited to bless him.

f.g: Armies; the heavenly multitudes.
Servants, attendants.

chapters.n: Finally all creation everywhere is called to praise — and the psalm ends where it began, with David’s own soul.

f.w: bless the LORD, O my soul

chapters.n: A companion to Psalm 103, this hymn praises God as Creator, loosely following the order of the Creation account. God is pictured as a king robed in honor and majesty.
God wears light like clothing and spreads out the sky like a tent curtain — recalling the first day of Creation, when light appeared.

f.w: stretchest out the heavens like a curtain

chapters.n: God builds his upper rooms on the waters above the sky, rides the clouds like a chariot, and travels on the wind.

f.w: the beams of his chambers in the waters

chapters.n: Winds and flames serve as God’s messengers. Hebrews applies this verse to angels.

f.g: Or ‘who makes the winds his messengers’ — the Hebrew words mean both.

chapters.n: God set the earth on firm foundations so it would not be shaken.

f.w: laid the foundations of the earth

chapters.n: In the beginning, deep waters covered the earth like a garment, even over the mountains.
At God’s rebuke and thunder, the waters fled — a picture of the third day, when dry land appeared.
The waters flowed over mountains and down valleys to the place God appointed for them.

f.w: the place which thou hast founded for them

chapters.n: God set a boundary the sea cannot cross, so it will not cover the earth again.
Now the waters become a blessing: springs flow through the valleys between the hills.
These streams water every animal, even the wild donkeys of the desert.

f.g: Wild donkeys, symbols of untamed desert life.

chapters.n: Birds nest beside the streams and sing in the branches.

f.g: Birds of the sky.

chapters.n: God waters the hills with rain from his ‘upper rooms,’ and the earth is filled with the results of his work.

f.g: From his upper rooms — the sky, source of rain.

chapters.n: God makes grass for livestock and plants for people to cultivate, so humans can grow food from the ground.

f.w: herb for the service of man

chapters.n: Wine, olive oil, and bread — the three staples of ancient Israel — are God’s gifts that gladden, refresh, and strengthen people.

f.w: oil to make his face to shine
f.g: Olive oil was used on skin and hair for refreshment and gladness.

chapters.n: God waters the great trees, like the cedars of Lebanon, which he himself planted.
These trees become homes for birds; the stork nests in the tall firs or junipers.

f.g: A large migratory bird well known in Israel.

chapters.n: Each creature has its proper home: the high mountains for wild goats, the rocks for small animals.

f.g: Rock badgers (hyraxes), small animals that live among rocks.

chapters.n: God made the moon to mark seasons and festivals; the sun knows when to set — recalling the fourth day of Creation.
God brings the darkness, and night animals come out to roam.
Even lions’ roaring is pictured as a prayer — they look to God for their food.
When the sun rises, the night predators slip back to their dens.

f.w: lay them down in their dens

chapters.n: Then humans go out to work until evening. Day and night are shared in God’s orderly design.
The psalmist bursts into wonder: God’s works are so many and so wisely made, and the earth is full of his creatures.

f.w: in wisdom hast thou made them all

f.g: Many and varied.

chapters.n: The vast sea teems with countless creatures, tiny and huge.
Ships sail the sea, and Leviathan, a great sea creature that others feared as a monster, is here just God’s plaything.

f.g: A great sea creature; in other poetry a symbol of chaos.

chapters.n: All living things depend on God to give them their food at the right time.
When God opens his hand, creatures gather what he provides and are satisfied.
When God hides his face, creatures are dismayed; when he withdraws their breath, they die and return to dust.
When God sends his Spirit (or breath), new life is created and the earth is renewed. Life is a continuing gift from him.

f.g: Hebrew ruaḥ: spirit, breath, or wind.

f.w: renewest the face of the earth

chapters.n: May God’s glory last forever, and may he rejoice in his works as he did at Creation, when he saw it was ‘very good.’

f.w: the LORD shall rejoice in his works

chapters.n: A mere glance from God makes the earth quake; his touch makes mountains smoke, as at Sinai.

f.w: he toucheth the hills, and they smoke

chapters.n: The psalmist vows to sing to God his whole life long.
He hopes his thoughts about God will be pleasing to God, and he will find his joy in the Lord.

f.g: Thoughts, musing; or the words of this song.

chapters.n: The only thing out of place in God’s good world is sin, so he prays that wickedness will end. The psalm closes with ‘Praise ye the LORD’ — in Hebrew ‘Hallelujah’ — its first appearance in the Psalms.

f.g: Hebrew hallelu-yah, ‘Hallelujah.’

f.w: let the wicked be no more

chapters.n: This history psalm retells God’s faithfulness from Abraham to the promised land. Its first fifteen verses were also sung when David brought the ark to Jerusalem. It opens by urging Israel to thank God and tell the world what he has done.

f.w: make known his deeds among the people

chapters.n: Sing to him, and talk about his wonderful works. Remembering God’s acts out loud keeps faith alive.

f.w: talk ye of all his wondrous works

chapters.n: Take pride in God’s holy name, and let all who seek him be joyful.

f.g: Boast, take pride in.

chapters.n: Keep seeking the Lord, his strength, and his presence (‘face’) always. Seeking God is a lifelong pursuit.
Remember his miracles, wonders, and the judgments he pronounced. ‘Remember’ is the key word of this psalm.
The audience is named: the descendants of Abraham and Jacob, God’s covenant people.
The Lord is Israel’s God, yet his authority covers the whole earth.

f.w: his judgments are in all the earth

chapters.n: God remembers his covenant forever — ‘a thousand generations’ means without end.
The covenant began with Abraham and was confirmed by oath to his son Isaac.
God renewed it with Jacob (renamed Israel) as an unbreakable, everlasting covenant.
The promise: the land of Canaan would be their portion and inheritance. ‘Lot’ means an allotted share.

f.g: Your allotted portion, like land measured out by a cord.

chapters.n: When the promise was made, the patriarchs’ families were tiny — just a few foreigners living in someone else’s land.
They wandered from one kingdom to another — to Egypt, Gerar, and back — as nomads.
God protected them, even rebuking kings such as Pharaoh and Abimelech on their behalf.

f.w: he reproved kings for their sakes

chapters.n: God’s warning: don’t harm my anointed ones or my prophets. The patriarchs are called ‘anointed’ and ‘prophets’ because they were set apart by God.
The story moves to Joseph. God allowed a famine that ‘broke the staff of bread’ — that is, cut off the food supply people leaned on.

f.g: Bread as the ‘staff’ that supports life.

chapters.n: God sent Joseph ahead of the family to Egypt, even though he went there as a slave. Joseph later saw God’s hand in it.

f.w: He sent a man before them

chapters.n: Joseph’s feet were bruised by shackles, and he was bound in iron in prison.

f.g: Shackles or chains for the feet.

chapters.n: He waited until his prophetic dreams came true; meanwhile God’s word tested and refined him.

f.w: the word of the LORD tried him
f.g: Tested or refined him, as metal is purified.

chapters.n: Pharaoh finally sent for Joseph and set him free.

f.w: The king sent and loosed him

chapters.n: Pharaoh made him master of his household and manager of all his possessions.
Joseph had authority over Pharaoh’s officials and taught Egypt’s elders wisdom.

f.g: Elders, counselors.

chapters.n: Jacob and his family moved to Egypt, called ‘the land of Ham’ because Egyptians were seen as descendants of Ham.

f.g: Lived as a foreigner.

chapters.n: In Egypt God made Israel multiply until they outnumbered and outstripped the Egyptians.
God allowed the Egyptians’ hearts to turn hostile, and they schemed against Israel. ‘Subtilly’ means craftily.

f.g: Craftily, deceitfully.

chapters.n: God raised up Moses and Aaron as deliverers.
They performed God’s miraculous signs in Egypt. The plagues that follow are listed in a poetic, not strictly chronological, order.
The ninth plague, darkness, is mentioned first. Moses and Aaron did not resist God’s command — or, as some read it, the Egyptians could not resist.
The first plague: the Nile turned to blood and the fish died.
The second plague: frogs swarmed everywhere, even in the royal bedrooms.
Swarms of flies and gnats filled every part of Egypt. ‘Divers’ means various; ‘coasts’ means borders or territory.

f.g: Borders, territory.

chapters.n: Instead of gentle rain came hail with lightning (‘flaming fire’) — the seventh plague.
The hailstorm destroyed vines, fig trees, and every tree in the land.
Locusts — here also called ‘caterpillers,’ perhaps a young stage of locust — came in uncountable numbers.

f.g: Probably young locusts.

chapters.n: They ate every plant left in the land.

f.w: devoured the fruit of their ground

chapters.n: The final plague: the death of every firstborn in Egypt, the ‘first fruits of their strength.’

f.w: the chief of all their strength
f.g: The first fruits of their manhood — the firstborn.

chapters.n: Israel left with silver and gold given by the Egyptians, and not one of them stumbled.
The Egyptians were relieved to see them go, having come to dread them.

f.w: Egypt was glad when they departed

chapters.n: God spread a cloud to shade them by day and fire to light their way at night.
When the people asked, God sent quail and fed them with manna, ‘bread from heaven.’ Jesus called himself the true bread from heaven.
God split the rock and water flowed like a river in the desert. Paul says that rock was Christ.
The reason for all this: God remembered his sacred promise to Abraham.
God brought his chosen people out singing and shouting for joy.
He gave them the lands of other nations, and they inherited fields and cities others had built.

f.w: inherited the labour of the people

chapters.n: The purpose of it all: so they would keep God’s laws. Blessings are given to help us live as covenant people. ‘Praise ye the LORD’ is ‘Hallelujah.’

f.w: That they might observe his statutes

chapters.n: Psalm 105 told of God’s faithfulness; Psalm 106 confesses Israel’s unfaithfulness. It opens with ‘Hallelujah’ and a familiar refrain: God is good and his covenant love lasts forever.
No one can fully describe God’s mighty acts or praise him enough.
Happy are those who act justly and do right always — a standard Israel’s history will show they often failed to meet.

f.g: Maintain justice.

chapters.n: The psalmist asks to be remembered with the kindness God shows his people and to experience his salvation.

f.g: Come to me with help.

chapters.n: He wants to share in the prosperity and joy of God’s chosen people.

f.g: Israel, God’s own treasured people.

chapters.n: Confession begins: ‘We have sinned with our fathers.’ He includes his own generation, not just blaming the past. The three verbs echo Solomon’s and Daniel’s confessions.

f.w: We have sinned with our fathers

chapters.n: In Egypt the ancestors failed to grasp God’s wonders and rebelled at the Red Sea, complaining when Pharaoh’s army appeared.
Yet God saved them anyway — ‘for his name’s sake,’ to show his power and keep his word, not because they deserved it.
At God’s rebuke the sea dried up, and he led them through the deep as easily as walking across open country.
God rescued them from the enemy — ‘redeemed’ them, as a kinsman buys back a relative.
The returning waters covered the Egyptian army; not one survived.
Then they believed and sang his praise — the Song of Moses.
But they quickly forgot and did not wait for God’s guidance. Gratitude faded fast.
They craved food intensely in the wilderness and put God to the test.

f.g: Craved greedily.

chapters.n: God gave them the quail they demanded but sent a wasting disease among them. Getting what we want is not always a blessing.
Some were jealous of the leadership of Moses and of Aaron, the priest set apart (‘saint’) for the Lord.

f.g: Holy one; one consecrated to God.

chapters.n: In Korah’s rebellion, the ground opened and swallowed the rebels Dathan and Abiram with their households.
Fire from the Lord consumed the 250 men who had offered incense in defiance.
At Horeb (Sinai), while Moses was on the mountain, they made and worshipped a metal calf.

f.g: An idol made of melted, cast metal.

chapters.n: A bitter irony: they traded the glorious God for the statue of a grass-eating ox.

f.g: Likeness, image.

chapters.n: They forgot God their Savior, who had worked great deeds in Egypt.
Those deeds were wonders in ‘the land of Ham’ (Egypt) and awe-inspiring acts at the Red Sea.

f.g: Awe-inspiring deeds.

chapters.n: God would have destroyed them, but Moses ‘stood in the breach’ — like a soldier filling a gap in a broken wall — to plead for them. Moses foreshadows Christ the Intercessor.

f.w: stood before him in the breach

chapters.n: At the edge of the promised land, they rejected the ‘pleasant land’ and doubted God’s promise after the spies’ report.
They grumbled in their tents and refused to listen to the Lord.
So God raised his hand in an oath that they would die in the wilderness.

f.w: lifted up his hand against them
f.g: Swore an oath (raising the hand).

chapters.n: He also warned their descendants would be scattered among the nations if they kept rebelling — later fulfilled in exile.

f.w: to scatter them in the lands

chapters.n: At Peor in Moab they joined in worship of the Baal of that place and ate sacrifices offered to lifeless idols.

f.g: Offerings to lifeless gods, or rites for the dead.

chapters.n: Their actions provoked God, and a plague broke out among them.

f.g: Evil deeds.

chapters.n: Phinehas, Aaron’s grandson, stepped in and acted against the open sin, and the plague stopped.

f.g: Stopped, held back.

chapters.n: His zeal was credited to him as righteousness, and God gave him a covenant of lasting priesthood.
At Meribah, ‘the waters of strife,’ the people’s complaints led even Moses into trouble.

f.g: Hebrew Meribah, ‘quarreling.’

chapters.n: They embittered his spirit so that he spoke rashly — and Moses was not allowed to enter the land.

f.g: Spoke rashly, without thinking.

chapters.n: In Canaan, they failed to remove the idolatrous nations as God had commanded.

f.w: They did not destroy the nations

chapters.n: Instead they intermarried with them and copied their practices.
They worshipped the Canaanite idols, which became a trap.
Worst of all, they sacrificed their own children to demons — the false gods behind the idols.

f.g: Hebrew shedim, demons or false spirits.

chapters.n: They shed innocent blood, killing their own children for Canaan’s idols, and defiled the land itself.

f.w: the land was polluted with blood

chapters.n: Their deeds made them unclean. Idolatry is pictured as spiritual adultery — unfaithfulness to their covenant ‘husband,’ God.

f.g: Committed spiritual adultery — idolatry as covenant betrayal.

chapters.n: God’s anger burned so fiercely that he loathed his own people’s behavior.
He handed them over to foreign nations, and their enemies ruled them — the repeated cycle of the book of Judges.

f.w: gave them into the hand of the heathen

chapters.n: They were crushed and humbled under their oppressors.
Again and again God rescued them, but they kept choosing rebellion and sinking lower.

f.w: Many times did he deliver them

chapters.n: Still God noticed their distress and heard their cry.
He remembered his covenant and relented because of his abundant love. ‘Repented’ here means he turned from punishment to mercy.

f.g: Relented; changed course toward mercy.

chapters.n: God even caused their captors to treat them with compassion.

f.w: made them also to be pitied

chapters.n: The final prayer: save us and gather us from among the nations so we can praise you again. This fits the exile; Latter-day Saints see it echoed in the latter-day gathering of Israel.

f.w: gather us from among the heathen
f.r: 1 Chronicles 16:35; Deuteronomy 30:3-4; 1 Nephi 10:14; Articles of Faith 1:10

chapters.n: This doxology closes Book Four of the Psalms (Psalms 90–106). All the people respond, ‘Amen. Hallelujah.’

f.w: let all the people say, Amen

chapters.n: Book Five of the Psalms opens with a great thanksgiving hymn. The familiar refrain — God is good and his covenant love endures forever — sets the theme.
Those whom God has ‘redeemed’ — rescued and bought back — should say so out loud. Testimony is the natural response to deliverance.

f.w: Let the redeemed of the LORD say so

chapters.n: God gathered his people from every direction. This fits the return from exile and is echoed in latter-day revelation on the gathering of Israel.

f.w: gathered them out of the lands

chapters.n: The first of four pictures of rescue: travelers lost in the desert, unable to find a town to live in.

f.g: On a desolate, empty road.

chapters.n: Hungry and thirsty, they were close to fainting. Their whole life was ebbing away.

f.g: Their life grew weak.

chapters.n: This first refrain appears four times: in their trouble they cried to the Lord, and he rescued them.

f.w: they cried unto the LORD in their trouble

chapters.n: God led them on a straight road to a city where they could settle.

f.g: A straight, level road.

chapters.n: The second refrain, also repeated four times: if only people would thank the Lord for his steadfast love and wonders.

f.w: Oh that men would praise the LORD

chapters.n: God satisfies the thirsty and hungry with good things — both body and soul. Jesus promised the same to those who hunger for righteousness.

f.w: filleth the hungry soul with goodness

chapters.n: The second picture: prisoners sitting in darkness, chained in suffering and iron.

f.g: Deep darkness, gloom like death.

chapters.n: Their captivity came because they rebelled against God’s words and despised his counsel.

f.g: Despised, scorned.

chapters.n: God humbled them with hard labor; they stumbled with no one to help. Sometimes hardship turns people back to God.
Yet when they cried out, he saved them.

f.w: he saved them out of their distresses

chapters.n: He led them out of the darkness and snapped their chains. Latter-day Saints also see in this Christ’s power to free the captive and the dead.

f.g: Apart, to pieces.

chapters.n: The praise refrain repeats: thank him for his goodness.
God smashes bronze gates and cuts through iron bars — nothing can hold his people when he frees them.

f.g: Brass here means bronze.

chapters.n: The third picture: people who became sick through their own foolish sin.

f.g: Those who act senselessly and sinfully.

chapters.n: They lost all appetite and came close to death’s gates.
The refrain again: they cried, and he saved them.
God ‘sent his word’ and healed them. Christians see the ultimate fulfillment in Jesus, the Word made flesh, who healed with a word.

f.w: He sent his word, and healed them

chapters.n: Thanks again for God’s goodness and wonders.
Those healed should offer thank-offerings and joyfully tell what God has done.
The fourth picture: sailors and merchants who travel the wide sea. Israel was not a seafaring nation, so the sea seemed especially dangerous.

f.w: go down to the sea in ships

chapters.n: Out on the deep, they witness God’s mighty works.
At God’s command a storm wind rises and lifts the waves high.
Ships rise to the sky and plunge to the depths; the sailors’ courage melts away.

f.g: Their courage dissolves in fear.

chapters.n: They stagger like drunk men, and all their skill is useless — literally, ‘all their wisdom is swallowed up.’

f.g: Hebrew: ‘all their wisdom is swallowed up.’

chapters.n: Then they cry to the Lord, and he brings them out.

f.w: Then they cry unto the LORD

chapters.n: He hushes the storm to a whisper and the waves fall still — just as Jesus did on the Sea of Galilee.

f.w: He maketh the storm a calm

chapters.n: The sailors rejoice in the quiet, and God guides them to the harbor they longed for.

f.g: The port they longed for.

chapters.n: The final praise refrain for God’s goodness and wonders.

f.w: Oh that men would praise the LORD

chapters.n: Praise should be public — in the assembly of the people and among the leaders.
The psalm turns to a wisdom reflection: God can turn rivers into desert and springs into dry ground.

f.w: He turneth rivers into a wilderness

chapters.n: Fertile land can become a salty wasteland because of its people’s wickedness — as with Sodom and Gomorrah.

f.g: Literally ‘a salt land.’

chapters.n: He can also do the reverse: turn desert into pools and dry ground into springs.

f.w: the wilderness into a standing water

chapters.n: There he settles the hungry, who build a city to live in.
They plant fields and vineyards that produce a rich harvest.
God blesses them with many children and flourishing herds.
But fortunes can reverse: people may be reduced and humbled by oppression and sorrow.

f.g: Diminished, reduced in number.

chapters.n: God pours contempt on proud rulers and makes them wander in a trackless wasteland.
Meanwhile he lifts the needy out of their affliction and makes their families grow like flocks.

f.w: setteth he the poor on high

chapters.n: The upright will see this and be glad, while the wicked are left speechless.

f.w: all iniquity shall stop her mouth

chapters.n: The closing lesson: the wise will pay attention to these patterns and come to understand the Lord’s steadfast love.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed, loyal covenant love.

chapters.n: This psalm joins two earlier passages: verses 1–5 repeat Psalm 57:7–11, and verses 6–13 repeat Psalm 60:5–12. David’s heart is ‘fixed’ — steady and resolved — to praise God with his whole being.

f.g: Steadfast, firmly set.
My soul, my innermost being.

chapters.n: He calls his instruments to wake up, and promises to wake the dawn itself with his music.

f.g: Or ‘I will awaken the dawn.’
Two kinds of stringed instruments.

chapters.n: He will praise God not just in Israel but among all nations.
God’s covenant love is higher than the heavens and his faithfulness reaches the clouds.

f.w: thy mercy is great above the heavens

chapters.n: David prays that God’s glory will be honored throughout heaven and earth.
The second section begins: rescue your beloved people with your strong right hand.
God speaks from his sanctuary, claiming the land as his to distribute. Shechem (west of the Jordan) and Succoth (east of it) represent the whole territory.

f.g: A central town in the hill country of Ephraim.
A valley east of the Jordan.
Measure out, apportion.

chapters.n: God names Israel’s tribal regions as his own. Ephraim is his helmet (‘strength of mine head’) and Judah his royal scepter.

f.g: My scepter — the tribe of kings.

chapters.n: The enemy nations are pictured as lowly servants: Moab a washbasin, Edom a place to toss sandals — a gesture of ownership.

f.g: A basin for washing feet — a humble, menial object.
Throwing a sandal over land claimed ownership.

chapters.n: David asks who will lead him into the fortified city of Edom — probably the rock city later known as Petra or Bozrah.

f.g: A fortified city, likely Edom’s capital.

chapters.n: Only God can lead them — even though he seemed to have rejected them in a recent defeat.
Help from humans is worthless; only God can truly save.

f.w: vain is the help of man

chapters.n: The closing confidence: with God, we will act bravely, and he will trample our enemies.

f.w: Through God we shall do valiantly

chapters.n: David begs God not to stay silent. He addresses him as ‘God of my praise’ — the One he has always praised — even while enemies attack.

f.g: Don’t be silent; speak and act.

chapters.n: Wicked and deceitful people have opened their mouths against him with lies. The attack is mainly through words — slander and false accusation.
They surround him with hateful words and attack him for no reason.
In return for his love they accuse him, but he responds by giving himself to prayer — literally, ‘but I am prayer.’

f.g: Hebrew: ‘but I — prayer,’ as if he is prayer itself.

chapters.n: They repay his goodness with evil and his love with hatred.

Verses 6–19 are a harsh series of curses. Many scholars think they quote what the enemies were saying against David; others read them as David’s own plea for justice. ‘Satan’ here means ‘an accuser’ standing in court.

f.g: Hebrew satan, ‘accuser’ or ‘adversary’ — a prosecutor in court.

chapters.n: May he be found guilty when tried, and may even his prayers count against him.
May his life be short and someone else take his position. Peter applied this verse to Judas Iscariot, whose apostleship was filled by Matthias.
May his children lose their father and his wife become a widow — the curse extends to the whole family, as ancient curses often did.
May his children wander as beggars, searching for food far from their ruined homes.

f.g: Homeless wanderers.

chapters.n: May creditors seize everything and strangers plunder his earnings.

f.g: A creditor who seizes property.
Plunder.

chapters.n: May no one show him kindness or pity his orphans.

f.g: Show steadfast kindness.

chapters.n: May his family line end and his name be erased in the next generation.

f.w: let their name be blotted out

chapters.n: May God remember his parents’ sins too. In the Old Testament, families were seen as bound together in blessing and curse.
May their sins stay always before the Lord, so that even their memory disappears.

f.w: cut off the memory of them

chapters.n: The reason given: he never showed kindness, but hounded the poor and the heartbroken to death. The curses mirror his own cruelty.
He loved cursing, so let it come back on him; he didn’t want blessing, so let it stay far away. People reap what they love.
He wore cursing like clothing; let it soak into his body like water and into his bones like oil.

f.g: Inner body, insides.

chapters.n: Let it wrap around him like a robe and a belt he can never take off.

f.g: A belt or sash.

chapters.n: May this be the Lord’s payment to those who accuse and slander him. Whatever the curses’ origin, David leaves the judgment with God.
The tone shifts: ‘But you, O God the Lord, act for me for your name’s sake.’ David appeals to God’s character and covenant love.
He is poor and needy, and his heart is pierced within him.
He fades like an evening shadow and is shaken off like a locust brushed from a garment.

f.w: tossed up and down as the locust
f.g: Shaken off like an insect flicked away.

chapters.n: His knees are weak from fasting and his body has grown thin.

f.w: My knees are weak through fasting

chapters.n: People mock him, shaking their heads in scorn — just as onlookers later did to Jesus on the cross.
‘Help me, save me according to your steadfast love.’
He wants his rescue to be so clear that his enemies will know God did it.
Let them curse — God’s blessing outweighs every human curse.

f.w: Let them curse, but bless thou

chapters.n: May his accusers be clothed in their own shame like a cloak.

f.g: A cloak or outer robe.

chapters.n: David vows to praise the Lord loudly and publicly.

The final picture: in the courtroom of life, the accuser stood at the wicked man’s right hand (v. 6), but the Lord stands at the right hand of the poor as defender. Christ is our Advocate with the Father.

f.w: stand at the right hand of the poor

chapters.n: The most-quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament. ‘The LORD’ (Jehovah) speaks to David’s ‘Lord’ (adon, master). Jesus used it to show the Messiah is more than David’s son — he is David’s Lord, exalted to God’s right hand.

f.w: The LORD said unto my Lord
f.g: LORD = YHWH; Lord = adoni, ‘my master.’

chapters.n: From Zion, God will extend the king’s scepter — his royal power. He will rule even in the middle of his enemies.

f.g: The scepter of your power.

chapters.n: A difficult verse. On the day the king’s power is displayed, his people will volunteer freely, dressed in holy splendor. His youthful strength is renewed like dew born from the dawn.

f.g: Freewill offerings — they give themselves gladly.
Fresh vigor, like morning dew; possibly ‘your young warriors.’

chapters.n: God swears an oath: this king is a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek — the king-priest of Salem who blessed Abraham. Hebrews applies this to Christ. Latter-day Saints also hold the Melchizedek Priesthood, named for this ancient high priest.

f.g: Will not change his mind.

chapters.n: The Lord at the king’s right side will crush rulers on the day of his wrath. The roles of God and his anointed blend together.

f.w: in the day of his wrath

chapters.n: He will judge the nations and defeat their leaders across the earth — vivid ancient battle imagery for God’s final victory over evil.

f.w: He shall judge among the heathen

f.g: Rulers, or ‘the head’ — a chief enemy.

chapters.n: Refreshed by drinking from a stream along the way, the victorious king lifts his head in triumph. Some see a hint of the Messiah’s suffering and exaltation.

f.g: Rise in renewed strength and victory.

chapters.n: This psalm is an acrostic: after ‘Hallelujah,’ each half-line begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The psalmist praises God wholeheartedly, both among close friends and in the larger congregation.

f.g: Hebrew hallelu-yah.

chapters.n: God’s works are great, and those who delight in them study them closely. Faith includes curiosity about God’s ways.

f.g: Studied, searched into, pondered.

chapters.n: All God does is full of splendor and majesty, and his righteousness never ends.

f.g: Majestic, splendid.

chapters.n: God made his wonders memorable — through festivals like Passover — so his people would never forget his grace and compassion.
He gave food — like manna in the wilderness — to those who reverence him, and never forgets his covenant.

f.g: Food (any kind, not only flesh).

chapters.n: He showed his power by giving Israel the lands of other nations.
Everything God does is faithful and just; all his commandments can be trusted.

f.g: Truth, faithfulness.

chapters.n: His commands stand firm forever, grounded in truth and uprightness.
God sent redemption to his people — as at the Exodus, and ultimately through Jesus Christ — and made his covenant permanent. ‘Reverend’ means awe-inspiring.

f.g: Worthy of reverence; awesome. In scripture used only of God.

chapters.n: The famous conclusion: reverence for the Lord is where wisdom begins. Real understanding comes from living his commandments, not just knowing them.

f.w: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom

chapters.n: A twin to Psalm 111 and also an acrostic. Psalm 111 praised God’s character; Psalm 112 shows that character reflected in the person who reverences him and delights in his commandments.
The children of such a person will be strong and influential; the upright family line is blessed.

f.g: His descendants.

chapters.n: Prosperity fills his house, and his righteousness lasts forever — the very phrase used of God in Psalm 111:3.
Light dawns for the upright even in dark times. He is gracious, compassionate, and just — the same qualities as God (111:4).
A good person is generous and lends freely, and conducts business with justice.

f.g: Justice, fairness.

chapters.n: He will never be shaken, and the righteous will be remembered forever.
Bad news doesn’t terrify him, because his heart is firmly anchored in trust in the Lord.

f.g: Steady, settled.

chapters.n: His heart is secure and unafraid; he will see his enemies’ threats come to nothing.

f.g: Upheld, steady.

chapters.n: He gives generously to the poor. Paul quotes this verse to encourage cheerful giving. His ‘horn’ (dignity) will be lifted in honor.

f.w: he hath given to the poor

f.g: Symbol of strength and dignity.

chapters.n: The wicked see it and are angry, grinding their teeth in frustration, but their desires will come to nothing — a contrast that echoes Psalm 1.

f.w: the desire of the wicked shall perish

chapters.n: Psalms 113–118 are the ‘Egyptian Hallel,’ sung at Passover. Jesus and his disciples likely sang part of it after the Last Supper. It opens by calling God’s servants to praise his name.

f.g: Hallelujah — this begins the Hallel (‘praise’) psalms.

chapters.n: May God’s name be praised now and forever — praise without end in time.

f.w: from this time forth and for evermore

chapters.n: From sunrise to sunset — from east to west — praise without limit in space.

f.w: From the rising of the sun

chapters.n: The Lord is exalted above every nation, and his glory is above the heavens.
Who compares to the Lord, who sits enthroned on high?

f.w: Who is like unto the LORD

chapters.n: Yet this exalted God stoops down to look at heaven and earth. God’s greatness includes his willingness to come near.

f.g: Stoops down, lowers himself.

chapters.n: He lifts the poor from the dust and the needy from the ash heap or garbage dump, where outcasts sat. Hannah’s song uses these words.

f.g: An ash heap or refuse pile outside a town.

chapters.n: He seats them among princes — a total reversal of fortune.
He gives the childless woman a home and the joy of children — as he did for Sarah, Rachel, and Hannah. In that culture, barrenness brought deep sorrow and shame.
A short, vivid poem about the Exodus. Israel left Egypt, a land whose language was foreign to them.

f.g: A people speaking a foreign tongue.

chapters.n: At the Exodus, God made Israel his own: Judah became his holy dwelling and Israel his kingdom.
Two water miracles frame the journey: the Red Sea parted at the start, and the Jordan River stopped at the end so Israel could enter Canaan.

f.w: The sea saw it, and fled

chapters.n: The mountains leaped like rams and the hills like lambs — playful poetry for the earthquake at Sinai.
The psalmist teasingly asks the sea and the river what made them run away.

f.g: What was wrong with you? What happened to you?

chapters.n: He asks the mountains and hills the same question. The answer is coming in the next verse.
The answer: tremble, earth, before the Lord, the God of Jacob! Creation itself responds to his presence.
He turned hard rock into a pool and flint into a spring. The God who shakes mountains also provides water for thirsty people — a sign Paul connects to Christ.

f.w: turned the rock into a standing water

f.g: Very hard stone.

chapters.n: ‘Not to us, but to your name be the glory.’ The psalmist asks God to act for the sake of his own covenant love and faithfulness, not Israel’s merit. Compare the premortal Christ: ‘the glory be thine forever.’
Why should the nations mock, asking where Israel’s invisible God is?
The answer: our God is in heaven and does whatever he wills. He has no statue because he is real and free.

f.w: our God is in the heavens

chapters.n: By contrast, the nations’ idols are just silver and gold shaped by human craftsmen.
The satire begins: idols have mouths but can’t speak, and eyes but can’t see.

f.w: They have mouths, but they speak not

chapters.n: They have ears but cannot hear prayers, and noses but cannot smell the incense offered them.
Their hands can’t touch, their feet can’t walk, and not even a whisper comes from their throats.

f.w: neither speak they through their throat
f.g: They can’t even make a murmur.

chapters.n: The sharp point: people become like what they worship. Trusting in lifeless things makes people spiritually lifeless.

f.w: They that make them are like unto them

chapters.n: The call to trust begins, likely sung as a call-and-response: ‘O Israel, trust in the LORD’ — and the choir answers, ‘He is their help and their shield.’

f.w: he is their help and their shield

chapters.n: The ‘house of Aaron’ — the priests — are called to trust too.

f.g: The priestly family, descendants of Aaron.

chapters.n: Finally, ‘ye that fear the LORD’ — all who revere God, possibly including foreigners who worshipped him.
The Lord has remembered us and will bless each group named — Israel and the priests.

f.w: The LORD hath been mindful of us

chapters.n: He will bless everyone who reveres him, from the least to the greatest.
May the Lord multiply you and your children.
You are blessed by the Creator of heaven and earth — far greater than any idol.
Heaven belongs to God, but he has entrusted the earth to humankind to care for and use — a stewardship.

f.w: the earth hath he given to the children of men

chapters.n: The dead, who go down into the silence of the grave, cannot join in earthly praise.
But we, the living, will praise the Lord now and forever. Hallelujah!

f.w: from this time forth and for evermore

chapters.n: A heartfelt testimony: ‘I love the LORD, because he heard me.’ Answered prayer deepens love for God.

f.g: Humble pleas for help.

chapters.n: Because God bent down to listen, the psalmist will keep praying all his life.

f.g: Bent down to listen.

chapters.n: Death’s ropes wrapped around him and the terrors of the grave seized him. He was in deep trouble and grief.

f.g: Literally ‘the cords of death,’ like ropes.
Hebrew Sheol, the grave or realm of the dead.

chapters.n: He cried out in a short, urgent prayer: ‘O LORD, save my life!’

f.w: Then called I upon the name of the LORD

chapters.n: God is gracious, righteous, and merciful — kindness and justice together.
The Lord protects the ‘simple’ — the humble and unsophisticated who rely on him.

f.g: The naive or unprotected; those who can’t defend themselves.

chapters.n: He tells his soul to return to calm rest, because God has been so generous.

f.w: Return unto thy rest, O my soul

chapters.n: God rescued his life from death, his eyes from tears, and his feet from stumbling.
Restored to life, he will live in God’s presence among the living.
He kept believing even when severely afflicted, and spoke because he believed. Paul quotes this as a model of faith-filled testimony.

f.w: I believed, therefore have I spoken

chapters.n: In panic he had concluded that no human could be relied on — only God proved trustworthy.

f.g: In my alarm or panic.

chapters.n: ‘How can I ever repay the Lord?’ — the natural question of a grateful heart.

f.g: What shall I give back?

chapters.n: He will lift a cup of thanksgiving, perhaps a drink offering at the temple, and call on God’s name. Jews drink cups of blessing at Passover; Latter-day Saints may think of the sacramental cup.
He will fulfill the vows he made while in trouble, publicly before God’s people.
The death of God’s faithful ones is ‘precious’ — costly, weighty — to him. He does not take it lightly; each life matters, and he cares for his saints in life and death.

f.g: Costly, of great worth, not lightly permitted.

chapters.n: He declares himself God’s servant, born into his service like the son of a servant woman. God has untied the ropes of death that bound him.

f.g: Born a servant in God’s household — belonging to him from birth.

chapters.n: He will offer a thanksgiving sacrifice and call on the Lord.
He repeats his vow for emphasis: he will keep his promises publicly.

f.w: in the presence of all his people

chapters.n: The setting is the temple courts in Jerusalem. The psalm ends with ‘Hallelujah.’

f.w: the courts of the LORD's house

chapters.n: The shortest psalm and shortest chapter in the Bible has a huge reach: every nation and every people is called to praise Israel’s God. Paul quotes it to show the gospel is for Gentiles too.
Two reasons: God’s covenant love toward us is mighty, and his faithfulness lasts forever. Hallelujah!

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — steadfast covenant love; ‘great’ also means ‘prevailing, mighty.’
Faithfulness, reliability.

chapters.n: The last of the Passover Hallel psalms — likely the hymn Jesus sang with his disciples before Gethsemane. It begins and ends with the same call to thanksgiving.
A responsive call: let all Israel declare that God’s covenant love lasts forever.
Let the priests, Aaron’s family, say it too.
And let all who revere the Lord join in — the same three groups as Psalm 115.

f.w: them now that fear the LORD

chapters.n: In a tight spot he called to God, and God answered by setting him in a ‘large place’ — wide open freedom.

f.g: Open space; freedom from being hemmed in.

chapters.n: With the Lord on his side, he has nothing to fear from any human. Hebrews quotes this verse.

f.w: what can man do unto me?

chapters.n: The Lord is among his helpers, so he will see his enemies defeated.

f.g: Is on my side, among my helpers.

chapters.n: Trusting God is better than relying on people. Some have noted this verse sits near the middle of the Bible’s verses.

f.w: better to trust in the LORD

chapters.n: Even powerful rulers are less reliable than God.
The speaker — perhaps a king leading worship — recalls being surrounded by hostile nations, yet driving them off in the Lord’s name.

f.w: in the name of the LORD

f.g: Cut off, ward off.

chapters.n: The repetition of ‘compassed me about’ makes us feel the enemies closing in.

f.g: Surrounded me.

chapters.n: They swarmed like angry bees, but burned out as quickly as a fire of thorns.

f.g: Dry thorns blaze up fast and die out fast.

chapters.n: The enemy pushed hard to make him fall, but the Lord helped him.

f.g: Pushed violently.

chapters.n: These words come from the Song of Moses at the Red Sea: the Lord is my strength, my song, and my salvation.

f.w: The LORD is my strength and song

chapters.n: Shouts of joy and victory ring out from the tents of the righteous: the Lord’s right hand acts mightily.

f.g: Tents, dwellings.
Acts with mighty power.

chapters.n: The triple praise of God’s ‘right hand’ — his power — builds to a climax.

f.w: The right hand of the LORD is exalted

chapters.n: ‘I will not die but live, and tell what the Lord has done.’ Christians hear in this the victory of the risen Christ.

f.w: I shall not die, but live

chapters.n: The Lord disciplined him severely but did not let him die. Hardship refined him rather than destroyed him.
Arriving at the temple, he asks for the ‘gates of righteousness’ to open so he can enter and give thanks.
The priests answer: this is the Lord’s gate; only the righteous may enter. Jesus called himself the gate through which we enter.
Inside, he thanks God for answering him and becoming his salvation.
A stone rejected by the builders became the cornerstone. Jesus applied this to himself, rejected by the leaders yet made the foundation of God’s house. The Book of Mormon uses the same image.

f.w: The stone which the builders refused

f.g: The cornerstone or capstone that holds the building together.

chapters.n: This reversal is God’s doing, and it amazes us.

f.w: it is marvellous in our eyes

chapters.n: ‘This is the day the Lord has made’ — the day of his saving act. Christians sing it of Easter, the day of Christ’s Resurrection.

f.w: This is the day which the LORD hath made

chapters.n: ‘Save now, we pray!’ — in Hebrew, hoshiʿah-na, the source of ‘Hosanna.’ The crowds shouted this as Jesus entered Jerusalem.

f.g: Hebrew hoshiʿah-na — ‘Hosanna.’

chapters.n: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD’ — sung by the crowds on Palm Sunday and quoted by Jesus about his return.

f.w: Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the LORD

chapters.n: God has given us light. Bind the festival sacrifice with cords to the horns of the altar — perhaps leading a procession with branches up to the altar. Christ is the ultimate sacrifice.

f.g: Horn-shaped projections at the altar’s four corners.

chapters.n: A personal declaration: ‘You are my God; I will praise and exalt you.’
The psalm closes as it began — a frame of thanks for God’s goodness and enduring love.

f.w: O give thanks unto the LORD

chapters.n: The longest chapter in the Bible is a giant acrostic: 22 stanzas of 8 verses, one for each Hebrew letter, and every verse in a stanza starts with that letter. This first stanza (Aleph) opens like Psalm 1 — happy are those whose path is blameless.

f.g: Blameless, whole, living with integrity.
Hebrew torah — instruction, teaching, not only rules.

chapters.n: Happiness belongs to those who keep God’s ‘testimonies’ and seek him wholeheartedly. Nearly every verse of this psalm uses one of about eight words for God’s word.

f.g: God’s solemn witness and covenant terms.

chapters.n: Such people avoid wrongdoing because they follow God’s paths. Obedience is pictured as walking a road.
The psalmist now speaks to God directly, as he will for the rest of the psalm: you commanded us to keep your ‘precepts’ carefully.

f.g: Specific instructions or charges given by God.

chapters.n: A sigh of longing: if only my life were steady in keeping your ‘statutes’! He knows his weakness and wishes for consistency.

f.g: Fixed, engraved decrees.
Made firm, steady.

chapters.n: When he pays attention to all God’s commandments, he won’t be put to shame.

f.g: Look carefully at; pay attention to.

chapters.n: As he learns God’s just rulings, he will praise him with an honest heart. Learning God’s ways leads to worship.

f.g: God’s just decisions and rulings.

chapters.n: He resolves to obey, and pleads not to be abandoned. Determination and dependence go together.
Stanza Beth. How can a young person keep their life pure? By guarding it according to God’s word — a question every generation asks.

f.g: By what means? How?

chapters.n: He has sought God with all his heart, yet still asks for help not to drift away.
He has treasured God’s word in his heart, like hiding a valuable, to guard against sin. Scripture memorized and pondered becomes protection.

f.w: Thy word have I hid in mine heart

chapters.n: He praises God and asks him to be his teacher — a request repeated often in this psalm.
He has spoken aloud all the rulings God has given. Sharing the word helps us keep it.

f.w: With my lips have I declared

chapters.n: Following God’s testimonies brings him as much joy as great wealth would.

f.w: as much as in all riches

chapters.n: He will think deeply about God’s instructions and keep his eyes on God’s paths.

f.g: Ponder, muse, speak quietly to oneself.

chapters.n: He will delight in God’s decrees and never forget his word.

f.w: I will not forget thy word

chapters.n: Stanza Gimel. He asks God to treat him generously so he can live and keep his word. Life itself is for obedience.

f.g: Treat generously, reward.

chapters.n: A beloved prayer: open my eyes to see wonders in your law. Understanding scripture requires spiritual sight that God gives.
He feels like a foreigner on earth, just passing through; God’s commandments are his guide in unfamiliar territory.

f.w: I am a stranger in the earth

chapters.n: His soul is crushed with constant longing for God’s rulings.

f.g: Is crushed, worn out.

chapters.n: God rebukes the arrogant who stray from his commandments; they bring a curse on themselves.

f.g: The arrogant, insolent — a recurring enemy in this psalm.

chapters.n: He asks God to roll away the scorn others heap on him because of his faithfulness.

f.g: Literally ‘roll away.’

chapters.n: Even powerful officials plotted against him, but he kept meditating on God’s decrees. Faith doesn’t wait for opposition to stop.

f.g: Officials, rulers.

chapters.n: God’s testimonies are his delight and his ‘counsellors’ — literally ‘men of my counsel,’ his trusted advisers.
Stanza Daleth. His soul clings to the dust — he feels flattened, near death. ‘Quicken’ means give life; he asks God to revive him.

f.g: Make alive, revive.

chapters.n: He told God everything about his life, and God answered. Now he asks for teaching.

f.g: I have openly told you my life, confessing all.

chapters.n: If God helps him understand, he will talk about God’s wonders. Understanding leads to testimony.
His soul weeps or drips away with sorrow. He asks God to strengthen him through his word.

f.g: Drips away with grief, like tears.

chapters.n: He asks God to keep him from deceptive ways and to graciously give him his law.

f.g: Falsehood, deception, unfaithfulness.

chapters.n: He has chosen the way of faithfulness and set God’s rulings before him like a guide.

f.w: I have chosen the way of truth

chapters.n: He has clung to God’s testimonies; he asks not to be disappointed.

f.g: Clung to — the same Hebrew word as ‘cleaveth’ in v. 25.

chapters.n: When God enlarges his heart — gives it understanding and freedom — he will run eagerly in the way of the commandments, not just trudge.

f.g: Broaden my understanding; set me free.

chapters.n: Stanza He. Every verse here is a request. ‘Teach me your way, and I will keep it to the end.’
Give me understanding, and I will obey wholeheartedly. True obedience comes from understanding, not mere compliance.
Lead me along the path of your commandments, for I delight in it.
Turn my heart toward your testimonies, not toward greed. The heart has to be pointed somewhere.

f.g: Greed, selfish gain.

chapters.n: Turn my eyes away from worthless things, and give me life in your way. What we look at shapes who we become.

f.g: Emptiness, worthless things.

chapters.n: Confirm your promise to your servant, who is devoted to revering you.

f.g: Establish, make good, fulfill.

chapters.n: Take away the disgrace I dread, for your judgments are good.

f.g: Disgrace, scorn.

chapters.n: He has longed for God’s instructions; he asks for new life through God’s righteousness.

f.g: Give me life by your saving justice.

chapters.n: Stanza Vau. Let your covenant love and salvation come to me, as you promised.

f.w: thy salvation, according to thy word

chapters.n: Then he will have an answer for those who taunt him, because he trusts God’s word.
He asks God never to take the word of truth from his mouth — never let him lose his testimony.
So he will keep God’s law always — ‘continually for ever and ever.’

f.g: The piled-up words stress unbroken constancy.

chapters.n: He will walk freely, in wide open space, because he seeks God’s precepts. Obedience brings true freedom.
He will speak of God’s testimonies even before kings, without shame.
God’s commandments, which he loves, are his delight.
He will lift his hands toward God’s commandments — a gesture of prayer, reverence, and eager reaching.

f.w: My hands also will I lift up

chapters.n: Stanza Zain. ‘Remember your word to me’ — the promise that gave him hope. Faith rests on God’s promises.

f.w: Remember the word unto thy servant

chapters.n: His comfort in suffering is that God’s word has given him life.

f.w: This is my comfort in my affliction

chapters.n: Arrogant people have mocked him terribly, but he has not turned aside from God’s law.

f.g: Mockery, ridicule.
Turned aside.

chapters.n: Remembering God’s ancient rulings — his past faithfulness — comforts him.
He is seized with burning anger — ‘horror’ — at those who abandon God’s law.

f.g: Burning indignation, a hot wind of anger.

chapters.n: God’s decrees have been his songs in the house where he lives as a pilgrim — this temporary earthly life.
He remembers God’s name even at night, and keeps his law.
This blessing has been his because he kept God’s precepts — or, ‘this has been my practice: keeping your precepts.’

f.g: This has been mine — this has been my way of life.

chapters.n: Stanza Cheth. The Lord is his ‘portion’ — his share of the inheritance. Like the Levites, who received no land, his treasure is God himself.
He sought God’s favor with his whole heart — literally ‘I stroked your face,’ an idiom for earnestly seeking favor.

f.g: Hebrew idiom: ‘I sought your face.’

chapters.n: He reflected on his life and turned his feet back to God’s testimonies. This is repentance: thinking, then turning.
He hurried and did not delay in obeying. Postponing obedience is a quiet form of disobedience.
The cords or gangs of the wicked have entangled and robbed him, but he hasn’t forgotten God’s law.

f.g: Cords, ropes; or bands of robbers.

chapters.n: He gets up at midnight to give thanks — like Paul and Silas singing in prison at midnight.
He is a friend of all who revere God and keep his commands. Good companions strengthen faith.
The whole earth is full of God’s covenant love; he asks to be taught.

f.w: The earth, O LORD, is full of thy mercy

chapters.n: Stanza Teth. Every verse begins with the letter for ‘good.’ God has dealt well with his servant, just as he promised.
He asks for good judgment and knowledge, because he trusts God’s commandments.

f.g: Good discernment, good taste.

chapters.n: Before affliction he wandered; now he keeps God’s word. Hard times can bring us back.

f.w: Before I was afflicted I went astray

chapters.n: ‘You are good and do good’ — a simple, deep statement of God’s character.
The arrogant smeared him with lies, but he keeps God’s precepts with his whole heart.

f.g: Smeared, plastered over — as with a coat of lies.

chapters.n: Their hearts are dull and insensitive, like fat; but he delights in God’s law.

f.g: Dull, unfeeling, spiritually insensitive.

chapters.n: It was good for him to be afflicted, so he could learn God’s statutes. Suffering became a school.

f.w: It is good for me that I have been afflicted

chapters.n: God’s instruction is worth more than thousands of pieces of gold and silver.

f.w: better unto me than thousands of gold

chapters.n: Stanza Jod. God made and shaped him with his own hands; now he asks for understanding to learn God’s commands. The Creator is also the Teacher.
Other believers will be encouraged to see him, because he has waited on God’s word.

f.w: will be glad when they see me

chapters.n: He acknowledges that God’s rulings are right and that God afflicted him in faithfulness — even trials come from a faithful God.
He prays for God’s covenant love to comfort him, as promised.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed, steadfast love.

chapters.n: Let your tender compassion come to me so I may live; your law delights me.

f.g: Deep compassion, like a mother’s love.

chapters.n: May the arrogant be ashamed for wronging him with lies; he will keep pondering God’s precepts.

f.g: Twisted the truth to wrong me.

chapters.n: He asks that fellow believers — those who know God’s testimonies — would turn to him in fellowship.
May my heart be whole and blameless in your statutes, so I’m never ashamed.

f.g: Whole, blameless, complete.

chapters.n: Stanza Caph — the low point of the psalm. His soul faints with longing for God’s salvation, but he still hopes in his word.

f.g: Is exhausted with longing.

chapters.n: His eyes are worn out from watching for God’s promise: ‘When will you comfort me?’
He feels like a leather wineskin hung near the fire — shriveled, blackened, and useless. Yet he does not forget God.

f.g: A leather wineskin dried and cracked by smoke.

chapters.n: How many days does he have left? When will God bring justice against his persecutors?

f.w: How many are the days of thy servant?

chapters.n: The arrogant dug pits to trap him — in defiance of God’s law.
God’s commands are faithful, while his persecutors are false. ‘Help me!’

f.g: With lies; without cause.

chapters.n: They nearly wiped him off the earth, but he didn’t abandon God’s precepts.

f.g: Finished off, destroyed.

chapters.n: He asks for renewed life through God’s steadfast love, so he can keep God’s testimony.
Stanza Lamed — the turning point. God’s word stands firm forever in heaven, unshaken by earthly trouble.

f.w: thy word is settled in heaven

chapters.n: God’s faithfulness spans all generations; he founded the earth and it stands.
Heaven and earth continue by God’s ordinances, for all creation serves him.
If God’s law had not been his delight, he would have died in his suffering.
He will never forget God’s precepts, because through them God gave him life.

f.w: with them thou hast quickened me

chapters.n: ‘I am yours — save me.’ Belonging to God is the basis of his plea.
The wicked lie in wait to destroy him, but he focuses his mind on God’s testimonies.

f.g: Give careful attention to.

chapters.n: Everything earthly, however perfect, has limits; but God’s commandment is boundless.

f.g: A limit to every human achievement.
Immeasurably wide.

chapters.n: Stanza Mem. ‘Oh, how I love your law!’ He thinks about it all day — the emotional heart of the psalm.

f.w: O how love I thy law!

chapters.n: God’s commandments, always with him, make him wiser than his enemies.

f.w: for they are ever with me

chapters.n: Meditating on God’s testimonies gives him more insight than all his teachers.

f.w: more understanding than all my teachers

chapters.n: Obedience has given him more understanding than even the elders. Wisdom comes by living the truth, not age alone.

f.g: The elders, the aged.

chapters.n: He has kept his feet from every evil path so he can keep God’s word.

f.g: Held back, restrained.

chapters.n: He has not turned from God’s rulings, because God himself has taught him.
God’s words taste sweeter than honey — not a burden but a delight.

f.w: sweeter than honey to my mouth

chapters.n: God’s precepts give him understanding, so he hates every false path.
Stanza Nun. One of scripture’s best-known verses: God’s word is a lamp for my feet and a light for my path. Ancient lamps lit only the next few steps — enough to keep walking.

f.w: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet

chapters.n: He has made a solemn vow, and will keep it: to obey God’s just rulings. Covenants are promises we follow through on.

f.w: I have sworn, and I will perform it

chapters.n: He is deeply afflicted, and asks God to revive him as promised.
He offers his words of praise as a voluntary sacrifice, asking God to accept them and teach him.
His life is constantly ‘in his hand’ — always at risk — yet he doesn’t forget God’s law.

f.w: My soul is continually in my hand
f.g: Idiom: my life is constantly in danger.

chapters.n: The wicked set traps for him, but he didn’t stray from God’s precepts.
God’s testimonies are his inheritance forever — the joy of his heart.
He has set his heart on doing God’s decrees always, to the very end.

f.g: Bent, turned my heart toward.

chapters.n: Stanza Samech. He hates double-minded, divided loyalty, but loves God’s law. ‘Vain thoughts’ likely means half-hearted people.

f.g: Possibly ‘the double-minded’ — those divided in loyalty.

chapters.n: God is his hiding place and his shield; he waits in hope for God’s word.
He tells evildoers to leave him alone — he will keep God’s commandments.
Hold me up as you promised, so I may live and not be let down in my hope.
With God holding him up he will be safe, and will keep his eyes on God’s statutes.

f.w: Hold thou me up, and I shall be safe

chapters.n: God rejects all who stray from his statutes; their deceptions are empty lies.

f.g: Rejected, set at nothing.
