chapters.n: God removes the wicked like ‘dross’ — the impurities skimmed off melted metal. That is why he loves God’s testimonies.

f.g: Scum removed in refining metal.

chapters.n: His body shivers in awe of God, and he reverences God’s judgments.
Stanza Ain. He has done what is just and right, and asks not to be left to oppressors.
‘Be surety for thy servant’ — guarantee his welfare, as someone who co-signs for a debt. Christ is called the ‘surety’ of a better covenant.

f.g: Stand as guarantor; pledge yourself for me.

chapters.n: His eyes are worn out watching for God’s salvation and his righteous promise.

f.w: Mine eyes fail for thy salvation

chapters.n: Treat your servant according to your covenant love, and teach me.
‘I am your servant’ — so give me understanding to know your testimonies.
It is time for the Lord to act, because people have broken his law. Latter-day revelation likewise urges urgent labor in the last days.

f.w: It is time for thee, LORD, to work

f.g: Broken, annulled.

chapters.n: Therefore he loves God’s commandments more than gold, even the purest gold.
Therefore he counts all God’s precepts right in every matter, and hates every false path.

f.g: In everything — the whole of God’s word.

chapters.n: Stanza Pe (‘mouth’). God’s testimonies are wonderful, so his soul keeps them.

f.g: Extraordinary, beyond human ability.

chapters.n: When God’s words enter — or are ‘opened up’ — they bring light and understanding even to the simple.

f.w: The entrance of thy words giveth light

f.g: The inexperienced, teachable.

chapters.n: He opened his mouth and panted like a thirsty animal, longing for God’s commands.
Turn to me and be gracious, as you always do for those who love your name.

f.g: As is your custom, your habit.

chapters.n: Make my steps steady by your word, and let no sin rule over me.

f.g: Make my steps firm and directed.

chapters.n: Free me from human oppression, and I will keep your precepts.
Let your face shine on your servant — an echo of the priestly blessing.
Rivers of tears flow from his eyes because people don’t keep God’s law. Love for God includes grief over sin.

f.w: Rivers of waters run down mine eyes

chapters.n: Stanza Tzaddi (the letter for ‘righteous’). The Lord is righteous, and his judgments are upright.
The testimonies God commanded are righteous and completely faithful.

f.g: Utterly trustworthy.

chapters.n: His zeal burns him up because his enemies ignore God’s words. Jesus’ disciples recalled a similar line when he cleansed the temple.
God’s word is refined and pure like tested metal, so his servant loves it.

f.g: Refined, tested in fire.

chapters.n: He is small and despised, but doesn’t forget God’s precepts. Faithfulness doesn’t depend on status.
God’s righteousness is everlasting, and his law is truth.
Trouble and anguish have seized him, yet God’s commandments are his delight.
God’s testimonies are righteous forever. ‘Give me understanding, and I will live.’

f.w: give me understanding, and I shall live

chapters.n: Stanza Koph. He cries out with his whole heart for an answer, and promises obedience.

f.w: I cried with my whole heart

chapters.n: ‘I cry to you; save me, and I will keep your testimonies.’
‘Prevented’ means ‘came before’: he was up before dawn, crying for help and hoping in God’s word.

f.g: Came before, anticipated — not ‘stopped.’

chapters.n: His eyes are open before each night watch so he can meditate on God’s word through the night.

f.g: Divisions of the night when guards changed.

chapters.n: Hear me by your steadfast love; give me life according to your just ways.
Those who pursue evil draw near to attack him, but they are far from God’s law.

f.g: Wicked schemes, evil intent.

chapters.n: The enemies are near — but God is nearer. All his commands are true.
He has long known that God established his testimonies to last forever.
Stanza Resh. Look at my suffering and rescue me, for I have not forgotten your law.
‘Plead my cause’ — be my defense attorney. ‘Redeem me and give me life.’
Salvation is far from the wicked, because they don’t seek God’s statutes.

f.w: Salvation is far from the wicked

chapters.n: God’s compassions are great; give me life according to your just decrees.
Though persecutors are many, he doesn’t turn from God’s testimonies.

f.g: Turn aside, swerve.

chapters.n: He looked at the faithless and felt disgust, because they don’t keep God’s word.

f.g: Felt loathing, disgust.

chapters.n: ‘See how I love your precepts’ — give me life by your steadfast love.

f.w: Consider how I love thy precepts

chapters.n: The ‘sum’ or whole of God’s word is truth, and every just ruling lasts forever.

f.g: Or ‘the sum’ — the entirety of your word.

chapters.n: Stanza Schin. Rulers persecute him without cause, but his heart trembles in awe only before God’s word.

f.w: standeth in awe of thy word

chapters.n: He rejoices over God’s word like someone discovering great treasure taken in battle.

f.w: as one that findeth great spoil

chapters.n: He hates and detests lies, but loves God’s law.

f.g: Detest, regard with horror.

chapters.n: Seven times a day he praises God — seven meaning complete, continual praise.

f.g: Seven symbolizes fullness; praise all day long.

chapters.n: Those who love God’s law have great peace, and nothing makes them stumble. ‘Offend’ here means cause to trip.

f.g: Cause to stumble.

chapters.n: He has waited for God’s salvation while doing his commandments — hope and action together.

f.w: I have hoped for thy salvation

chapters.n: His soul keeps God’s testimonies and loves them deeply.
He keeps God’s instructions because his whole life is open before God.

f.w: all my ways are before thee

chapters.n: Stanza Tau, the last letter. He prays that his cry will reach God and bring understanding.

f.w: Let my cry come near before thee

chapters.n: May my plea reach you; rescue me as you promised.

f.g: A humble request for favor.

chapters.n: When God teaches him, praise will pour from his lips like a bubbling spring.

f.g: ‘Utter’ means pour forth, bubble over.

chapters.n: His tongue will sing of God’s word, for all God’s commands are right.

f.w: My tongue shall speak of thy word

chapters.n: He has chosen God’s precepts, so he asks for God’s helping hand.
He longs for God’s salvation and delights in his law.

f.w: I have longed for thy salvation

chapters.n: Let me live so I can praise you, and let your rulings help me.
A humble ending: after 175 verses of devotion, he admits he has wandered like a lost sheep and asks God to come find him. Jesus is the Good Shepherd who seeks the lost.

f.w: I have gone astray like a lost sheep

chapters.n: Psalms 120–134 are each titled ‘A Song of degrees’ (or ‘ascents’) — likely sung by pilgrims going ‘up’ to Jerusalem for the festivals. The journey begins far away, in distress: he cried to the Lord, and God answered.

f.w: In my distress I cried unto the LORD

chapters.n: He asks to be rescued from liars and slanderers. Words can wound as deeply as weapons.
He turns to address the lying tongue itself: what punishment do you deserve?
The answer: sharp warrior’s arrows and burning coals of the broom tree, whose wood burns very hot — fitting payback for words that pierce and burn.

f.g: Charcoal from the broom bush, known for burning long and hot.

chapters.n: He feels like an exile among hostile peoples. Meshech (far north, near the Black Sea) and Kedar (Arabian desert nomads) stand for barbarous, distant places.

f.g: Meshech, a people of far-off Asia Minor.
Nomadic Arab tribe descended from Ishmael.

chapters.n: He has lived too long among people who hate peace.
‘I am peace’ — but whenever he speaks, they want war. This sense of not belonging sets up the pilgrim’s longing for Jerusalem, the ‘city of peace.’

f.g: Hebrew: ‘I am peace.’

chapters.n: A pilgrim looks up at the hills on the road to Jerusalem — beautiful, but also where robbers hid and pagan shrines stood. ‘Where does my help come from?’ is best read as a question.

f.w: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills

chapters.n: The answer: my help comes from the Lord, the Maker of heaven and earth — not from the hills, but from the One who made them.
A new voice, perhaps a fellow pilgrim or priest, reassures him: God won’t let your foot slip on the rocky path, and your guardian never dozes off.

f.w: will not suffer thy foot to be moved

chapters.n: The guardian of Israel never sleeps. Unlike pagan gods mocked for sleeping, Israel’s God is always awake.
The Lord is your keeper and your shade at your right side — like a protector walking beside you on the hot road.

f.g: Guardian, watchman — the key word of this psalm (six times).

chapters.n: No sunstroke by day, and no harm by night. The pair covers every hour of the journey.

f.w: The sun shall not smite thee

chapters.n: God will guard you from all harm and watch over your life.

f.g: Keep your life.

chapters.n: He will guard your going out and coming in — every departure and return, all of life’s daily movement — now and forever.

f.w: thy going out and thy coming in
f.g: A Hebrew phrase for all of life’s activities.

chapters.n: Credited to David, this song captures a pilgrim’s joy when invited to go to the temple. Latter-day Saints often apply it to the joy of temple worship today.

f.w: Let us go into the house of the LORD

chapters.n: At last their feet are standing inside Jerusalem’s gates — the journey is over.
Jerusalem is built as a city ‘joined together,’ tightly knit — a picture of unity among God’s people.

f.g: Closely joined, bound firmly together.

chapters.n: Here the tribes of Israel go up, as God commanded, to give thanks to his name.

f.g: The decree or ordinance given to Israel.

chapters.n: Jerusalem was also the seat of justice, where David’s royal family judged the people.
‘Pray for the peace of Jerusalem’ — a wordplay, since ‘Jerusalem’ sounds like ‘peace’ (shalom). Those who love her will be secure.

f.w: Pray for the peace of Jerusalem
f.g: Hebrew wordplay: shaʾalu shalom yerushalayim.

chapters.n: May peace be within your walls and security in your fortresses.

f.g: Security, ease.

chapters.n: For the sake of family and friends, he blesses the city: ‘Peace be within you.’
Most of all, because God’s house is there, he will seek the city’s good. Love for God’s house becomes love for his people.

f.w: Because of the house of the LORD

chapters.n: The psalm begins with a look upward. Psalm 121 lifted eyes to the hills; here eyes go straight to God, enthroned in heaven.

f.w: Unto thee lift I up mine eyes

chapters.n: Like servants watching their master’s hand for a signal — for orders, provision, or help — God’s people keep watching him until he shows mercy.

f.g: Servants watched for hand signals from their masters.

f.w: until that he have mercy upon us

chapters.n: The plea is doubled for urgency: have mercy, have mercy! They are sick of being scorned.
They are fed up with the mockery of the comfortable and the arrogant — people at ease who look down on the faithful.
A song of David, sung responsively: the leader begins, ‘If the Lord had not been on our side…’ and calls Israel to repeat it.
Repetition drives the point home: without God, when enemies attacked, all would have been lost.

f.w: the LORD who was on our side

chapters.n: Enemies would have swallowed them alive, like a monster or the grave. ‘Quick’ means alive.

f.g: Alive.

chapters.n: A second image: a flash flood would have swept over them.

f.w: the stream had gone over our soul

chapters.n: The ‘proud,’ raging waters would have drowned them.

f.g: Raging, swelling waters.

chapters.n: Praise God, who did not let them be torn apart by their enemies’ teeth like prey.
They escaped like a bird from a hunter’s trap — the trap broke and they flew free.
The closing confession: our help is in the name of the Lord, the Maker of heaven and earth.

f.w: Our help is in the name of the LORD

chapters.n: Those who trust the Lord are as stable as Mount Zion itself — unshakable and enduring.

f.w: as mount Zion, which cannot be removed

chapters.n: Jerusalem is ringed by higher hills; just so, the Lord surrounds his people with protection forever.

f.w: the mountains are round about Jerusalem

chapters.n: The wicked’s ‘rod’ — their scepter or rule — will not stay over the land given to the righteous, so that the righteous aren’t pressured into evil.

f.g: The scepter — rule — of the wicked.
The land allotted to the righteous.

chapters.n: A prayer: Lord, do good to those who are good and honest-hearted.
Those who turn aside to crooked paths will be led away with evildoers. The psalm closes with a blessing: peace be upon Israel.
This psalm likely remembers the return from Babylonian exile. When God brought the captives home, it felt too good to be real — like a dream.

f.w: turned again the captivity of Zion
f.g: Restored Zion’s fortunes; brought back the exiles.

chapters.n: They laughed and sang, and even foreign nations admitted, ‘The Lord has done great things for them.’

f.w: The LORD hath done great things for them

chapters.n: Israel echoes the nations: yes, the Lord has done great things for us, and we are glad.

f.w: The LORD hath done great things for us

chapters.n: Now a prayer for full restoration: refresh us like the dry streambeds of the Negev (‘the south’), which suddenly fill with rushing water after rain.

f.g: Dry wadis in the Negev desert that flood after winter rains.

chapters.n: Those who sow with tears will reap with shouts of joy. Sorrow and faithful effort lead to future harvest.

f.w: They that sow in tears shall reap in joy

chapters.n: A farmer weeps as he plants precious seed during hard times, but will return singing with armfuls of harvest. Many see in this the work of missionaries and the joy of gathering souls.

f.g: Bundles of harvested grain.

chapters.n: Titled ‘for Solomon,’ the temple builder. Unless the Lord builds a house — a home, a family, or a temple — the builders’ work is wasted; unless he guards a city, the watchman stays awake for nothing.

f.w: Except the LORD build the house

chapters.n: Anxious overwork — rising early, staying up late, eating the bread of worry — is pointless without God. He gives rest to those he loves.

f.g: Food eaten in anxious toil.

chapters.n: Children are a gift and inheritance from God, not just the result of human effort.

f.w: children are an heritage of the LORD

chapters.n: Children born when parents are young are like arrows in a warrior’s hand — strength and protection for the family.

f.w: As arrows are in the hand of a mighty man
f.g: Children as a family’s defense and future.

chapters.n: Happy is the man with a full quiver of them. When disputes arose at the city gate — where courts were held — his sons would stand up for him.

f.g: A case for holding arrows.
The city gate, where elders held court and business.

chapters.n: A companion to Psalm 127: everyone who reveres the Lord and walks in his ways is blessed — the blessing reaches into ordinary home life.

f.w: Blessed is every one that feareth the LORD

chapters.n: You will enjoy the fruits of your own work — a blessing, since invaders or famine often robbed farmers of their harvest.

f.w: thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands

chapters.n: The wife is like a fruitful grapevine in the inner rooms of the home; children are like young olive shoots around the table — full of promise and future fruit.

f.g: Young olive shoots that grow up around the parent tree.

chapters.n: This is how the one who reverences the Lord will be blessed.

f.g: Look! — calling attention to the point.

chapters.n: The blessing now comes from the temple in Zion. May you see Jerusalem prosper your whole life long.

f.w: The LORD shall bless thee out of Zion

chapters.n: May you live to see your grandchildren, and may peace rest on Israel. Personal blessing and community blessing go together.
Israel speaks as one person looking back on its history: since its ‘youth’ in Egypt, enemies have attacked it again and again. The leader invites the people to say it together.

f.g: From Israel’s beginnings as a nation, in Egypt.

chapters.n: Yet for all their attacks, the enemies have never defeated Israel. God’s covenant people survive.

f.w: they have not prevailed against me

chapters.n: A vivid image of cruelty: enemies dragged plows across Israel’s back, cutting long furrows — like the welts of a whipping.

f.w: The plowers plowed upon my back

chapters.n: But the righteous Lord cut the ropes that harnessed Israel to the plow — he set his people free.

f.w: cut asunder the cords of the wicked

chapters.n: A prayer that all who hate Zion will be put to shame and driven back.

f.g: Put to shame, thrown into confusion.

chapters.n: May they be like grass sprouting on a flat clay rooftop — it springs up but withers quickly with no deep soil.

f.g: Flat mud roofs sprouted thin grass that soon dried up.

chapters.n: Such grass is useless: a reaper can’t gather even a handful, nor a binder an armful.

f.g: Ties harvested grain into bundles.

chapters.n: No passerby will offer the usual harvest greeting, ‘The Lord bless you!’ — as Boaz and his workers greeted each other.

f.w: The blessing of the LORD be upon you

chapters.n: From deep waters — a picture of overwhelming trouble and guilt — the psalmist cries to the Lord. Traditionally counted among the penitential psalms.
‘Lord, hear me; let your ears pay attention to my pleas.’
If God kept a record of every sin, no one could stand before him. We all depend on mercy.

f.g: Keep a record of sins.

chapters.n: But God forgives — and this leads to reverence, not carelessness. Forgiveness draws us to God in grateful awe.
He waits for the Lord with his whole soul, hoping in God’s promise.
He longs for God more than night watchmen long for the dawn — and he repeats it, because their longing is so intense.

f.w: they that watch for the morning
f.g: Night watchmen on the city walls, eager for dawn and the end of their shift.

chapters.n: He invites all Israel to hope in the Lord, whose covenant love is sure and whose redemption is abundant.
God himself will redeem Israel from all its sins. Christians see this fulfilled in Jesus, who came to save his people from their sins.

f.w: he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities

chapters.n: A short, gentle psalm of humility attributed to David. His heart isn’t proud, his eyes don’t look down on others, and he doesn’t obsess over matters too lofty for him.

f.g: Proud, arrogant.

chapters.n: He has calmed and quieted his soul like a weaned child resting on its mother — no longer fussing for milk, simply content to be near her. Mature trust is peaceful.
He invites all Israel to share this quiet hope in the Lord, now and forever.

f.w: Let Israel hope in the LORD

chapters.n: The psalmist asks God to remember David and all the hardships he endured — especially his devotion to finding a home for the ark of the covenant.

f.g: Hardships, or the trouble he took.

chapters.n: David made a solemn vow to ‘the Mighty One of Jacob,’ an ancient title of God.
He vowed not to rest in the comfort of his own house…

f.g: My own tent or home.

chapters.n: …nor sleep…

f.w: I will not give sleep to mine eyes

chapters.n: …until he found a dwelling place for the Lord. David longed to build a temple, though God let his son Solomon build it.

f.w: an habitation for the mighty God of Jacob

chapters.n: The worshipers recall the ark’s story: they heard of it in Ephrathah (the Bethlehem region) and found it in ‘the fields of Jaar,’ likely Kiriath-jearim, where it rested for years.

f.g: Ephrathah, the region of Bethlehem.
Possibly ‘the fields of Jaar’ — Kiriath-jearim.

chapters.n: ‘Let us go to his dwelling and worship at his footstool’ — the ark, pictured as the footrest of God’s throne.
These words echo the call Moses used when the ark set out: ‘Arise, O LORD!’ Solomon used them at the temple dedication.

f.w: Arise, O LORD, into thy rest

f.g: The ark, symbol of God’s mighty presence.

chapters.n: May the priests be dressed in righteousness and the faithful shout for joy.
For David’s sake, don’t reject the current king, the Lord’s anointed.

f.w: turn not away the face of thine anointed

chapters.n: God made a sure oath to David: one of his own descendants would sit on his throne. Christians see this fulfilled in Jesus Christ.

f.w: Of the fruit of thy body

chapters.n: The promise had a condition: if David’s children kept God’s covenant, their line would rule forever.

f.w: If thy children will keep my covenant

chapters.n: The Lord chose Zion and desired it as his home.
God speaks: ‘This is my resting place forever; here I will live.’

f.w: This is my rest for ever

chapters.n: God promises abundant food for Zion, so even her poor will have bread.

f.w: I will satisfy her poor with bread

chapters.n: God answers verse 9 with something greater: her priests will be clothed not only with righteousness but with salvation.
God will make a ‘horn’ — a strong king — sprout from David’s line, and keep a lamp burning for him. The ‘branch’ and ‘lamp’ became messianic images.

f.w: the horn of David to bud

chapters.n: David’s enemies will be clothed with shame, but his crown will shine. Contrasting ‘clothing’ runs through the psalm.

f.g: His crown will sparkle or bloom.

chapters.n: How good and lovely it is when brothers and sisters live together in unity! Pilgrims from every tribe gathering in Jerusalem would have felt this keenly.

Unity is like the fragrant anointing oil poured on Aaron’s head when he was consecrated high priest — so abundant it flowed down his beard to the collar of his robe. It is holy and spreads to bless everyone.

f.w: the precious ointment upon the head

f.g: The collar or edge of the garment.

chapters.n: Unity is also like the heavy dew of Mount Hermon, Israel’s tallest peak, falling on Zion’s hills — refreshing and life-giving. There God commands his blessing: life forevermore.

f.g: Hermon’s abundant dew was famous for watering the land.

chapters.n: The final Song of Ascents. Pilgrims leaving the temple call on the priests and Levites who serve through the night to keep praising the Lord.

f.w: which by night stand in the house of the LORD

chapters.n: ‘Lift your hands toward the holy place and bless the Lord’ — raised hands were a gesture of prayer and praise.
The priests answer with a blessing on the departing pilgrim: may the Creator of heaven and earth bless you from Zion. The worshipers who came for blessing go home blessed.
A ‘Hallelujah’ psalm built largely from phrases of other scriptures. It calls God’s servants to praise his name.

f.w: praise him, O ye servants of the LORD

chapters.n: The call goes especially to those who serve in the temple and its courts.

f.w: Ye that stand in the house of the LORD

chapters.n: Praise him because he is good, and because praising him is itself delightful.
God chose Jacob’s family as his own ‘peculiar treasure’ — his special possession, not ‘odd’ but uniquely his.

f.g: A treasured personal possession.

chapters.n: The psalmist personally testifies: ‘I know the Lord is great, above all gods.’
God does whatever he pleases in every realm — heaven, earth, seas, and depths. No idol has such power.

f.w: Whatsoever the LORD pleased, that did he

chapters.n: He controls the weather: raising clouds, making lightning with rain, and bringing wind out of his storehouses.

f.g: Clouds, mists.

chapters.n: He struck down Egypt’s firstborn — the final plague that freed Israel.
He sent signs and wonders against Pharaoh and his officials.

f.g: Signs, miraculous evidences.

chapters.n: He defeated powerful nations and kings in Israel’s path.
Sihon and Og, two kings east of the Jordan, were famous early victories, followed by Canaan’s kingdoms.
He gave their land to Israel as an inheritance.
God’s name and fame will endure through every generation. ‘Memorial’ means the name by which he is remembered.

f.g: Your renown; the name by which you are remembered.

chapters.n: The Lord will vindicate his people and have compassion on his servants. This line is quoted from the Song of Moses.

f.g: Have compassion; relent.

chapters.n: By contrast, idols are only metal shaped by human hands. Verses 15–18 echo Psalm 115.
They have mouths but no speech, eyes but no sight.

f.w: eyes have they, but they see not

chapters.n: They have ears but no hearing — and no breath. The living God breathes life; idols have none.

f.w: neither is there any breath in their mouths

chapters.n: Those who make and trust idols become as lifeless as their gods.

f.w: They that make them are like unto them

chapters.n: A call to praise goes to all Israel and to the priestly house of Aaron.
The Levites and all who revere God are called too. This list adds ‘house of Levi’ to Psalm 115’s list.
The psalm ends: blessed be the Lord from Zion, who lives in Jerusalem. Hallelujah!
Known as the ‘Great Hallel,’ this psalm was sung responsively: a leader announced each line and the congregation answered with the refrain 26 times, ‘for his mercy endureth for ever.’

f.g: His ḥesed — loyal, covenant love — lasts forever.

chapters.n: Thank the ‘God of gods’ — the one supreme God over any power people might worship.
Thank the ‘Lord of lords,’ the ruler over every ruler — a title later given to the risen Christ.
The story of praise begins with Creation: God alone does great wonders.
He made the heavens with skill and wisdom.
He spread out the land above the waters, as the ancients pictured it.

f.w: stretched out the earth above the waters

chapters.n: He made the great lights in the sky.
The sun to govern the day…

f.w: The sun to rule by day

chapters.n: …and the moon and stars to govern the night. Creation is the first evidence of God’s enduring love.
The story moves to the Exodus: God struck Egypt’s firstborn.
He brought Israel out from among the Egyptians.
He did it with a ‘strong hand’ and ‘outstretched arm’ — Exodus language for his mighty power.
He split the Red Sea in two.

f.w: divided the Red sea into parts

chapters.n: He led Israel through the middle of it.
But he threw Pharaoh and his army into the sea. Rescue for Israel was judgment for the oppressor.

f.g: Literally ‘shook off,’ like shaking something off a garment.

chapters.n: He led his people through the wilderness for forty years.

f.w: led his people through the wilderness

chapters.n: He struck down great kings who opposed Israel.
He killed famous, mighty kings.

f.g: Majestic, renowned rulers.

chapters.n: Sihon, king of the Amorites, who refused Israel passage…
…and Og, the giant king of Bashan.
He gave their land as an inheritance…

f.w: gave their land for an heritage

chapters.n: …an inheritance to Israel, his servant.
Now the story becomes personal: God remembered us when we were humbled and low — perhaps in exile.

f.w: remembered us in our low estate

chapters.n: He rescued us from our enemies.

f.g: Literally ‘tore us away from.’

chapters.n: He feeds every living creature. God’s love reaches beyond Israel to all creation.

f.w: Who giveth food to all flesh

chapters.n: The closing call: give thanks to the God of heaven, whose love never ends.
One of the most moving laments in scripture, written during the Babylonian exile (after 587 BC). By Babylon’s rivers and canals the captives sat and wept, remembering Zion.

f.g: The Euphrates and Tigris and their irrigation canals.

chapters.n: They hung up their lyres on the poplar trees — too heartbroken to play.

f.g: Probably Euphrates poplars.

chapters.n: Their captors mockingly demanded entertainment: ‘Sing us one of those Zion songs!’

f.g: Our tormentors, those who plundered us.

chapters.n: How can we sing the Lord’s sacred songs in a foreign, pagan land? Holy things shouldn’t be turned into amusement.

f.g: A foreign land.

chapters.n: The psalmist swears an oath: if I forget Jerusalem, may my right hand — my harp-playing hand — lose its skill.

f.g: Skill, ability.

chapters.n: May my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth — so I could never sing again — if I don’t make Jerusalem my highest joy.

f.g: Literally ‘the head of my joy.’

chapters.n: The lament turns to a cry for justice. Edom, Israel’s ‘brother’ nation, cheered as Babylon destroyed Jerusalem: ‘Tear it down to the ground!’

f.g: Raze it — strip it bare, level it.

chapters.n: Babylon itself is addressed as ‘daughter’ — a poetic name for a city. The psalmist is confident it will face justice for what it did, as the prophets foretold.

A shocking line of raw grief and rage, echoing the brutal warfare Babylon had inflicted on Jerusalem’s own children. Scripture honestly records this cry for justice; it is a prayer handing vengeance to God, not a command to imitate. Jesus taught us to love and pray for enemies.

f.w: dasheth thy little ones against the stones

chapters.n: This begins a final group of psalms credited to David (138–145). He praises God wholeheartedly — even ‘before the gods,’ boldly honoring the Lord in the face of any rival powers or rulers.

f.g: Possibly heavenly beings, the gods of the nations, or human rulers.

chapters.n: He bows toward the temple and praises God’s covenant love and faithfulness. God has honored his word — his promise — even above his own reputation.

f.w: magnified thy word above all thy name
f.g: Exalted your promise above everything else known of you.

chapters.n: When he cried out, God answered and made him bold, putting strength into his soul.

f.w: strengthenedst me with strength in my soul

chapters.n: All earth’s kings will praise the Lord when they hear his words.

f.w: All the kings of the earth

chapters.n: They will sing of the Lord’s ways, for his glory is great.

f.w: great is the glory of the LORD

chapters.n: Though the Lord is exalted, he cares for the humble; but he keeps his distance from the proud, seeing them from afar.
Even in the middle of trouble, God will preserve his life, stretching out his hand against enemies and saving him with his right hand.

f.w: Though I walk in the midst of trouble

chapters.n: The Lord will finish what he has begun in David’s life. His love lasts forever, so David asks him not to abandon the work of his own hands.

f.w: The LORD will perfect that which concerneth me
the works of thine own hands

chapters.n: One of the most personal psalms. David marvels that the Lord has searched him through and through and knows him completely.
God knows when he sits down and when he gets up, and understands his thoughts from far away.

f.w: thou understandest my thought afar off

chapters.n: God sifts through his travels and his rest, and is familiar with all his habits.

f.g: Sifts, examines, surrounds.

chapters.n: Before a word even reaches his tongue, God already knows it completely.
God surrounds him behind and in front, resting his hand on him — both protection and loving closeness.

f.g: Surrounded, hemmed in.

chapters.n: Such knowledge is too wonderful and lofty for him to grasp.
Where could he go to escape God’s Spirit or presence? Nowhere — and that is a comfort, not a threat.

f.w: Whither shall I go from thy spirit?

chapters.n: Whether he rises to heaven or lies down in Sheol, the world of the dead, God is there.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol, the grave or world of the dead.

chapters.n: Even if he flew on the wings of dawn to the farthest sea in the west…

f.g: Swift as the light of sunrise spreading across the sky.

chapters.n: …God’s hand would still guide and hold him.

f.w: thy right hand shall hold me

chapters.n: If he hoped darkness would hide him, the night itself would become light around him.

f.w: Surely the darkness shall cover me

chapters.n: Darkness hides nothing from God; to him night shines like day.

f.w: the darkness and the light are both alike to thee

chapters.n: God formed his innermost being and knit him together in his mother’s womb.

f.g: Kidneys — the inner self, the seat of emotions.

f.w: covered me in my mother's womb
f.g: Wove me together.

chapters.n: He praises God for making him in an awe-inspiring, wonderful way. God’s works are marvelous, and he knows it deep within.
His frame was not hidden from God when he was being formed in secret, skillfully woven as if in the depths of the earth — a poetic picture of the womb.

f.g: Skillfully embroidered or woven.

f.w: the lowest parts of the earth
f.g: A poetic image for the hidden place of formation.

chapters.n: God saw him as an unformed embryo, and every one of his days was written in God’s book before any of them began. Latter-day Saints also see in God’s foreknowledge our premortal existence.

f.g: My unformed body; embryo.

chapters.n: God’s thoughts toward him are precious and vast.

f.w: How precious also are thy thoughts unto me

chapters.n: They outnumber the grains of sand. When he wakes, God is still with him.

f.w: more in number than the sand
when I awake, I am still with thee

chapters.n: The tone shifts sharply. David asks God to end the violent wicked and tells bloodthirsty men to leave him.

f.g: Men guilty of bloodshed; violent people.

chapters.n: They speak of God with malice and misuse his name.
He asks rhetorically: don’t I hate those who hate you, Lord, and loathe those who rebel against you?

f.g: Do I not loathe or feel disgust?

chapters.n: He hates them with complete hatred, counting God’s enemies as his own. This voices total loyalty to God; the New Testament later teaches us to hate evil while loving and praying for enemies.

f.w: I hate them with perfect hatred

chapters.n: Then a humble turn: rather than only judging others, he asks God to search him too. ‘Try me’ means test me as metal is tested; ‘thoughts’ means anxious thoughts.

f.g: Test me, as metal is tested.

chapters.n: ‘See if there is any hurtful way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.’ The psalm ends in a prayer for guidance toward eternal life.

f.g: Any path of pain or idolatry.

chapters.n: David asks for rescue from evil and violent people. This psalm resembles others written when David was hunted by enemies.

f.g: Literally ‘man of violent deeds.’

chapters.n: They plot evil in their hearts and constantly stir up conflict.

f.g: Plan evil schemes.

chapters.n: Their words are venomous — tongues sharpened like a snake’s, with viper poison behind their lips. Paul quotes this to describe human sinfulness.

f.w: adders' poison is under their lips

f.g: A musical or liturgical pause marker.

chapters.n: ‘Guard me from the wicked who plan to trip me up.’

f.g: To trip up my steps; make me fall.

chapters.n: The arrogant have hidden traps, cords, nets, and snares along his path — like a hunter setting snares for birds.

f.g: Traps or snares.

f.w: spread a net by the wayside

chapters.n: In response, David declares his loyalty: ‘You are my God; hear my pleas.’
God is the strength of his salvation, who protected his head like a helmet in battle.

f.w: thou hast covered my head in the day of battle

chapters.n: Don’t let the wicked get what they want, or they will become proud.

f.g: Don’t let his scheme succeed.

chapters.n: May the harm their own lips planned fall back on their heads.

f.w: the mischief of their own lips cover them

chapters.n: Strong images of judgment: burning coals, fire, and deep pits — echoing the fate of Sodom and the rebels of Korah’s day.
Slanderers will not last, and evil will hunt down the violent person. Evil carries its own punishment.

f.g: Literally ‘a man of tongue’ — a slanderer.

chapters.n: David knows God will defend the cause of the afflicted and secure justice for the poor.

f.w: maintain the cause of the afflicted

chapters.n: The righteous will thank God’s name, and the upright will live in his presence — the ultimate reward.

f.w: the upright shall dwell in thy presence

chapters.n: David calls urgently: ‘Lord, hurry to me; listen when I call.’
May his prayer rise to God like the fragrant incense in the temple, and his raised hands be like the evening offering. Prayer itself is a form of sacrifice.
He asks God to station a guard at his mouth and watch the door of his lips. Controlling speech is a spiritual discipline.

f.w: Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth

chapters.n: ‘Don’t let my heart lean toward evil, or let me join evildoers or enjoy their delicacies.’ The perks of wicked company are a temptation too.

f.g: Delicacies, luxurious foods.

chapters.n: He welcomes correction from the righteous as a kindness — like soothing oil on the head rather than a blow. Even so, he keeps praying against the wicked’s deeds.

f.w: Let the righteous smite me; it shall be a kindness

f.g: Fine oil for anointing the head — refreshing and honoring.

chapters.n: A difficult verse. When the wicked leaders are thrown down from the cliffs, people will finally listen and find David’s words pleasant and true.

f.g: Down the sides of a rocky cliff.

chapters.n: Another obscure line: their (or our) bones lie scattered at the mouth of the grave like chips of wood or clods turned up by a plow.

f.g: The entrance to Sheol, the realm of the dead.

chapters.n: But David keeps his eyes on God, trusting him. ‘Don’t leave my life defenseless’ — literally, ‘don’t pour out my soul.’

f.g: Don’t pour out my life; don’t leave me exposed.

chapters.n: Keep me from the traps and snares the wicked have set.

f.g: Snares, traps.

chapters.n: Let the wicked fall into their own nets while David passes by safely.

f.w: Let the wicked fall into their own nets

f.g: Meanwhile; at the same time.

chapters.n: The heading says David prayed this ‘when he was in the cave’ — probably hiding from King Saul at Adullam or En-gedi. He cries out loud to the Lord.

f.w: I cried unto the LORD with my voice

chapters.n: He pours out his complaint and lays all his trouble before God. Honest prayer includes telling God our troubles.
When his spirit grew faint, God still knew the path he was on — even while enemies hid traps along it.

f.g: Secretly.

chapters.n: He looked to his right — where a defender would stand in court — and found no one. No one cared about him; there was nowhere to run.

f.w: I looked on my right hand
f.g: The place where a protector or advocate stood.

f.w: no man cared for my soul

chapters.n: So he cried to God: ‘You are my refuge and my portion’ — all he needs, while still alive.
‘Listen, for I am brought very low; save me from pursuers too strong for me.’
He asks to be freed from his ‘prison’ — the cave, or his overwhelming trouble — so he can praise God. Then the righteous will gather around him because God has been good to him.

f.w: Bring my soul out of prison
the righteous shall compass me about

chapters.n: The last of the seven traditional penitential psalms. David appeals not to his own merit but to God’s faithfulness and righteousness.
‘Don’t put me on trial, for no living person is righteous before you.’ Paul echoes this verse in teaching that we are saved by grace.

f.w: in thy sight shall no man living be justified

chapters.n: The enemy has hunted him, crushed him to the ground, and forced him into darkness like the long-dead.

f.w: as those that have been long dead

chapters.n: His spirit grows faint and his heart is numb with dismay.

f.g: Appalled, stunned.

chapters.n: He finds strength in remembering how God acted in the past. Pondering God’s works restores hope.

f.w: I remember the days of old

chapters.n: He reaches out his hands to God; his soul thirsts for him like dry, cracked ground thirsts for rain.
‘Answer me quickly; my spirit is failing. Don’t hide your face, or I’ll be like those going down to the grave.’

f.w: hide not thy face from me

f.g: The grave.

chapters.n: ‘Let me hear your steadfast love in the morning; show me the way to walk.’ Each new day starts with seeking God’s guidance.

f.w: cause me to know the way

chapters.n: ‘Rescue me from my enemies; I run to you for shelter.’

f.w: I flee unto thee to hide me

chapters.n: A beautiful prayer: ‘Teach me to do your will, for you are my God. Let your good Spirit lead me on level ground.’

f.w: Teach me to do thy will

f.g: Level ground — a smooth, safe path.

chapters.n: ‘Give me life for your name’s sake; bring me out of trouble because you are righteous.’

f.g: Revive me, give me life.

chapters.n: In his covenant love, may God silence the enemies, ‘for I am your servant.’ Belonging to God is the final ground of his plea.
This royal psalm borrows heavily from Psalm 18. David praises the Lord, his ‘Rock,’ who trains him for battle — his skill as a warrior came from God.

f.w: which teacheth my hands to war

f.g: Literally ‘my rock.’

chapters.n: A stack of titles for God: his steadfast love, fortress, high tower, deliverer, and shield. God keeps the people peaceful under David’s rule.

f.g: My steadfast love (ḥesed).

chapters.n: Amazement: what are humans, that God notices or cares about them? Compare Psalm 8 and Moses’ vision.
People are like a breath, and their days like a passing shadow. Yet God cares for them.

f.g: A breath, a vapor.

chapters.n: David asks God to part the sky and come down, touching mountains so they smoke — like at Sinai.

f.w: Bow thy heavens, O LORD, and come down

chapters.n: ‘Flash your lightning and scatter the enemy; shoot your arrows and rout them.’
Reach down from on high and pull me out of the deep waters — out of the hands of foreigners.

f.g: Foreigners, hostile outsiders.

chapters.n: These enemies speak lies, and even their ‘right hand,’ raised to swear oaths, is false.

f.g: Their sworn oaths (sworn with raised right hand) are lies.

chapters.n: He promises a new song of praise on a ten-stringed harp.
God gives victory to kings and rescued David from the deadly sword.
The plea from verses 7–8 is repeated like a refrain.
The psalm turns to a vision of peace: sons growing strong like healthy young plants, daughters like beautifully carved corner pillars of a palace.

f.w: as plants grown up in their youth

f.g: Carved corner pillars, graceful and strong.

chapters.n: Barns full of every kind of produce, and flocks multiplying by thousands in the fields.

f.g: Granaries, storehouses.

chapters.n: Strong oxen, no breaches in the city walls, no exile, and no cries of distress in the streets — complete security.

f.w: no breaking in, nor going out
f.g: No breach of the walls, no going into captivity.

chapters.n: Happy is the people with such blessings — and above all, happy is the people whose God is the Lord.

f.w: happy is that people, whose God is the LORD

chapters.n: The last psalm credited to David, and an acrostic praising God as King. David will lift up God’s name forever.

f.g: Lift up high, exalt.

chapters.n: Praise is not occasional: he will bless God every single day, forever.

f.w: Every day will I bless thee

chapters.n: The Lord is great and deserves great praise. His greatness can’t be fully explored.
Each generation passes on the story of God’s mighty acts to the next — parents to children.

f.w: One generation shall praise thy works to another

chapters.n: He will reflect on the splendor of God’s majesty and his wonders.

f.w: the glorious honour of thy majesty

chapters.n: People will speak of God’s awe-inspiring deeds, and David will declare his greatness.

f.g: Awe-inspiring deeds.

chapters.n: They will overflow with memories of God’s goodness and sing joyfully of his righteousness.

f.g: Bubble over, pour forth.

chapters.n: This echoes God’s self-revelation to Moses: gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love.

f.w: slow to anger, and of great mercy

chapters.n: God is good to everyone, and his compassion covers all he has made.

f.w: The LORD is good to all

chapters.n: All creation praises God, and his faithful ones bless him.

f.w: All thy works shall praise thee

f.g: Faithful ones (ḥasidim).

chapters.n: The faithful talk of the glory of God’s kingdom and his power.
Their purpose: to make God’s mighty acts and majestic kingdom known to all people.

f.w: To make known to the sons of men

chapters.n: God’s kingdom is everlasting, his rule unending.
The King lifts up all who fall and straightens those bent under burdens. His greatness shows in his care for the weak.

f.w: The LORD upholdeth all that fall

chapters.n: All creatures look hopefully to God, and he provides their food at the right time.

f.w: The eyes of all wait upon thee

chapters.n: He opens his hand and satisfies the needs of every living thing.
God is just in all his ways and kind in all he does.

f.g: Or ‘loving’ — Hebrew ḥasid, faithful and kind.

chapters.n: The Lord is near to everyone who calls on him sincerely — ‘in truth,’ with honest intent.

f.w: The LORD is nigh unto all them that call upon him

chapters.n: He fulfills the desires of those who revere him, hears their cry, and saves them.

f.w: He will fulfil the desire of them that fear him

chapters.n: The Lord protects all who love him, but the wicked he will destroy.

f.w: preserveth all them that love him

chapters.n: David will keep praising, and he invites ‘all flesh’ — every living being — to bless God’s holy name forever. This sets up the great praise finale of Psalms 146–150.

f.w: let all flesh bless his holy name

chapters.n: The first of five closing ‘Hallelujah’ psalms (146–150), each beginning and ending with ‘Praise ye the LORD.’ The psalmist urges his own soul to praise.

f.g: Hebrew hallelu-yah.

f.w: Praise the LORD, O my soul

chapters.n: He will praise God for as long as he lives and breathes.
Don’t put your ultimate trust in rulers or in any mortal — they cannot save.

f.w: Put not your trust in princes

chapters.n: When a person’s breath leaves, they return to the ground, and all their plans die with them. A wordplay: ‘man’ (adam) returns to ‘earth’ (adamah).

f.g: His plans come to nothing.

chapters.n: True happiness belongs to the one whose help is the God of Jacob and whose hope is in the Lord.

f.w: the God of Jacob for his help

chapters.n: This God made heaven, earth, sea, and everything in them — and he keeps faith forever, unlike mortal princes.
He brings justice to the oppressed, food to the hungry, and freedom to prisoners. Jesus’ ministry fulfilled these very works.
He opens blind eyes, lifts up the bowed-down, and loves the righteous — works Jesus did during his ministry in Israel and among the Nephites.

f.w: openeth the eyes of the blind
raiseth them that are bowed down

chapters.n: He protects foreigners and supports orphans and widows — society’s most vulnerable — but turns the path of the wicked into a dead end.

f.g: Makes crooked, frustrates.

chapters.n: Unlike mortal rulers who die, the Lord reigns forever — Zion’s God for every generation. Hallelujah!

f.w: The LORD shall reign for ever

chapters.n: This psalm opens and closes with “Praise ye the LORD” (Hebrew hallelu-yah). Praise is called good, pleasant, and fitting—worship is not a chore but something that suits and delights God’s people.

f.g: Hebrew hallelu-yah, “praise Jah (Jehovah).” Psalms 146–150 all begin and end this way.
comely = fitting, beautiful, proper.

chapters.n: Many scholars think this psalm was sung after the exiles returned from Babylon, when Jerusalem was being rebuilt. The Lord gathers scattered Israel—a theme Latter-day Saints also see in the latter-day gathering.

f.w: gathereth together the outcasts of Israel

chapters.n: The same God who rebuilds a city also heals one broken heart at a time. He binds wounds like a careful physician. Isaiah used this language for the Messiah’s mission, which Jesus read as his own.
God counts the countless stars and knows each by name. The point sits right after verse 3: the Lord of the vast universe is personally attentive to the hurting individual.

f.w: calleth them all by their names

chapters.n: A short summary of God’s greatness: his power is great and his understanding has no limit. Nothing about our lives is beyond what he can comprehend.

f.g: Literally “his understanding has no number”—it cannot be counted, echoing the counted stars of verse 4.

chapters.n: God reverses human rankings: he raises the humble and brings the proud wicked down. This “great reversal” runs through scripture, from Hannah’s song to Mary’s.
A second call to praise begins the psalm’s middle section. Thanksgiving is set to music on the harp, Israel’s common instrument for worship.

f.g: Hebrew kinnor, a lyre—a small hand-held stringed instrument, David’s instrument.

chapters.n: God is praised as the one behind the weather: clouds, rain, and grass even on high, rocky slopes. In a dry land like Israel, rain was a clear sign of God’s daily care.
God feeds animals too, even noisy young ravens—birds the law counted unclean. Jesus pointed to the ravens to teach that God will surely care for his children.
Military muscle—war horses and the strong legs of soldiers—does not impress God. Ancient kings trusted cavalry and infantry; the psalmist says that kind of strength is not what the Lord values.

f.g: An image for a runner’s or soldier’s physical might.

chapters.n: What does delight God? People who revere him and keep hoping in his mercy. Faith and trust please him more than raw power.

f.g: To “fear” the Lord is to revere and trust him, not to be terrified of him.

chapters.n: The third section begins. Jerusalem and Zion are two names for the same holy city, repeated in classic Hebrew parallelism—the second line echoes the first.

f.g: Originally the hill of David’s city, then a name for Jerusalem and God’s people. In Latter-day Saint usage, also “the pure in heart” (D&C 97:21).

chapters.n: Strong gate bars meant a city was secure. God has made Jerusalem safe and blessed the families inside—fitting for a people who had just rebuilt their walls.

f.g: Heavy beams that locked city gates shut at night or in war.

chapters.n: Peace on the borders and plenty of the best wheat: security and prosperity both come from the Lord.

f.g: Literally “the fat of the wheat”—the richest, best grain.

chapters.n: God’s word is pictured as a swift messenger running across the earth to carry out his will. What he commands happens quickly.
Winter weather pictured with homely similes: snow falls like white wool, frost is scattered like fine ash. Even the cold seasons are God’s handiwork.

f.g: hoarfrost = white frost crystals that form on the ground or plants.

chapters.n: Hail is tossed down like crumbs of bread, and his cold is more than anyone can endure. The rhetorical question humbles the reader before God’s power.

f.g: morsels = crumbs or small bits, here describing hail.

chapters.n: The same word that brought the freeze now brings the thaw: a warm wind blows, ice melts, and streams run again. God rules both winter and spring.
The climax: the God who commands nature has also spoken his law to Israel. Revelation to his covenant people is an even greater gift than rain or harvest.
Israel had a unique privilege: no other nation had received God’s revealed covenant law. Privilege brings responsibility—and gratitude. The psalm closes as it began, with “Hallelujah.”

f.w: He hath not dealt so with any nation

chapters.n: This psalm is a grand roll call of all creation, summoned to praise God. It begins at the very top—the heavens and the heights—and will work its way down to the earth.

f.g: Hebrew hallelu-yah, “praise Jah (Jehovah).”

chapters.n: The first worshippers called are the angels and the “hosts,” God’s heavenly armies. Even beings in God’s presence are invited to keep praising him.

f.g: hosts = armies, multitudes; here the angelic multitudes. “Lord of hosts” uses the same word.

chapters.n: Sun, moon, and stars are told to praise their Maker. Neighboring nations worshipped the heavenly bodies as gods; here they are only creatures giving glory to the true God.
“Heavens of heavens” means the highest heavens. The “waters above the heavens” reflects the ancient picture of the sky in Genesis, with waters above the firmament.

f.g: A Hebrew superlative: the highest heavens.

f.w: waters that be above the heavens

chapters.n: Why should all these praise God? Because they owe their very existence to him: he spoke, and they came into being.

f.w: he commanded, and they were created

chapters.n: God not only made the heavens but set them in fixed, dependable order. His laws for creation stand firm, a sign of his faithfulness.

f.g: stablished = established, set firmly in place.

f.w: a decree which shall not pass

chapters.n: Now the call turns to the earth, starting with the ocean depths and the great sea creatures. Even the creatures people feared most are part of the choir.

f.g: Hebrew tanninim—great sea creatures or sea monsters, as in Genesis 1:21; not the dragons of fantasy.

chapters.n: Weather is called to praise: fire (lightning), hail, snow, mist, and storm winds. Even wild storms are doing what God sends them to do.

f.g: vapour = mist, cloud, or smoke.

chapters.n: The landscape joins in—mountains and hills, fruit trees and the towering cedars of Lebanon, the most prized trees of the ancient Near East.

f.g: Cedars of Lebanon, huge evergreen trees used for Solomon’s temple.

chapters.n: Every kind of animal is named: wild beasts, livestock, crawling creatures, and birds. The list follows the categories of the creation story.
Finally humanity: from rulers and judges down to all peoples. Those who hold power on earth are no exception—they too must bow before God.
Every age and gender is included—young men and young women, the elderly and children. Praise is not just for priests or the old; everyone has a voice.

f.g: maidens = young unmarried women.

chapters.n: The reason for all this praise: God’s name alone is truly exalted, and his glory is greater than earth and heaven together. All creation finds its purpose in honoring him.
The psalm ends with God’s covenant people. A horn symbolized strength; God has raised Israel’s strength, and they are “a people near unto him”—close to him by covenant.

f.g: A symbol of strength and victory, from the horns of a strong animal.

chapters.n: A “new song” celebrates a fresh act of God’s goodness. This hymn is sung by the gathered “saints”—the faithful, covenant people—in public worship.

f.g: Hebrew ḥasidim—the faithful, loyal ones who keep covenant love (ḥesed) with God.

chapters.n: Israel is called to rejoice in the God who made them a people. He is not only their Creator but their King.
Worship here is joyful and physical: dancing, tambourines, and lyres. Israel’s praise could be full of movement and music, as when Miriam led the women after the Red Sea.

f.g: timbrel = a hand drum or tambourine.

chapters.n: The reason for joy: the Lord delights in his people and adorns the humble with salvation, like clothing them in beauty.
The faithful are to rejoice in the honor God gives them, singing even on their beds—praise that fills both public worship and private moments of night.

f.g: Here likely the honor or splendor God gives his people.

chapters.n: This verse pairs praise with a two-edged sword. Many think it reflects Israel’s early wars or a coming day of judgment. Christians have often read the sword spiritually, as the word of God.
The “vengeance” here is God’s justice on nations that oppressed his people, not personal revenge. Elsewhere scripture is clear that vengeance belongs to the Lord.

f.g: heathen = the nations, the peoples who did not know Israel’s God.

chapters.n: Proud kings and nobles who once bound Israel are now pictured bound themselves. It is a picture of reversal: the oppressors are brought under God’s rule.

f.g: fetters = shackles for the feet.

chapters.n: The judgment is “written”—already decreed by God, not invented by people. To share in carrying out God’s righteous purposes is called an honor for all his faithful. The Hallelujah closes the psalm.

f.w: this honour have all his saints

chapters.n: The final psalm is the grand finale of the whole book. It answers where to praise: in God’s holy sanctuary on earth and in the vast heavens where his power is displayed.

f.g: The temple, God’s holy dwelling; possibly also his heavenly sanctuary.
The expanse of the sky, which shows God’s strength.

chapters.n: Why praise? Because of what God has done (his mighty acts) and who he is (his surpassing greatness).
How to praise? With the whole orchestra. The trumpet here is the shofar, a ram’s horn blown on holy days; the psaltery and harp were stringed instruments played by Levites.

f.g: Hebrew shofar, a ram’s-horn trumpet used to announce feasts and holy events.
psaltery = a stringed instrument, likely a kind of harp (Hebrew nevel).

chapters.n: Percussion, dance, strings, and pipes join in. Every kind of music is welcome when offered to God.

f.g: Not a modern pipe organ; Hebrew ʿugav, likely a flute or pipe.
timbrel = a tambourine or hand drum.

chapters.n: Two kinds of cymbals are named, perhaps a softer pair and a loud, clashing pair. The music swells to its loudest point.
The book of Psalms ends with a call for every living, breathing thing to praise the Lord. The breath God gave us is meant to return to him in praise. The Psalter closes with one last Hallelujah.

f.g: The final “Hallelujah” of the book, a fitting end to its Hebrew title, Tehillim, “Praises.”
